items.title: Predominance of viral core functions over auxiliary metabolism among carbohydrate-active enzymes annotated in the global soil virosphere
items.abstract: Soil viruses are increasingly recognized as components of microbial communities with the potential to alter ecosystem functioning, yet the frequency and functional distribution of virus-encoded metabolic genes in soils remain poorly understood. Here, the Global Soil Virus Atlas gene catalog, comprising 1,432,147 viral genes from 1,223 samples across 12 ecosystem types, was searched against KEGG, Pfam, and CAZy for functions related to carbon cycling, nitrogen cycling, and antimicrobial resistance. Annotations associated with host entry or cell-wall lysis were separated from putative auxiliary metabolic functions. Of 5,020 initial gene-level functional annotations across the three categories, 3,322 (66.2%) were classified as peptidoglycanases. Their exclusion left 1,698 genes (0.14% of the gene catalog restricted to contigs ≥10 kb), and carbon-cycling functions represented 96.7% of the enzyme-resolved annotations. Chitinase-associated genes formed the largest carbon category, but 78.0% belonged to GH19, a family containing both chitinases and phage endolysins. Among GH19 genes on contigs encoding detectable holins or spanins, 84.2% occurred within three genes of these lysis components, a distribution comparable to that of canonical phage lysozymes. Across six matched metagenomic studies, estimated viral contributions to the targeted functions ranged from 0.00% to 8.45% (mean: 2.27%). Two of the three estimates exceeding 2% were GH19-associated chitinase estimates from rhizosphere soils and were therefore treated as upper estimates. Thus, the putative soil viral metabolic inventory was sparse and concentrated in carbon-degradation functions, whereas much of the initial carbohydrate-active enzyme signal reflected core viral lysis functions rather than auxiliary metabolism. IMPORTANCE: Soil microorganisms drive decomposition and nutrient cycling, and the viruses that infect them may alter these processes by carrying genes that affect host metabolism. However, genes annotated as carbohydrate-degradation enzymes may instead help viruses enter cells or break host cell walls when new virus particles are released. In a worldwide catalog of soil viruses, approximately two-thirds of the initial functional assignments represented these infection or release activities. After their removal, putative viral auxiliary metabolic genes were uncommon and concentrated mainly in carbon degradation. Genes potentially involved in chitin degradation were most frequent, but many occurred near viral genes used to break host cells; their estimated contribution should therefore be viewed as an upper limit. Distinguishing core viral functions from host metabolic modification is essential to avoid overestimating viral contributions to soil processes and to identify the strongest candidates for experimental testing.

items.title: Novel insights into the specialized metabolism of the extremophile black yeast Hortaea werneckii and its modulation, unlocking its potential for compound discovery
items.abstract: Hortaea werneckii is a halotolerant yeast, found in various habitats and which specialized metabolism remains largely unexplored. Moreover, its chemical response to high salinities has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, a large-scale metabolomic study based on HPLC-HRMS/MS was conducted on 64 strains, collected from different habitats worldwide, and cultivated both on saline and non-saline media. The culture media salinity significantly modulated the strains metabolomes, suggesting the yeast exhibits a specific chemical response to high salt concentrations, potentially linked to halotolerance mechanisms. Additionally, the metabolomes were influenced by the ecological origin of the strains, with opportunistic pathogenic isolates producing distinct metabolites. Molecular networking revealed that H. werneckii synthesizes various chemical classes, including potential cytotoxic compounds, making this yeast a potentially interesting source of bioactive compounds. Hortein was detected as dominant and ubiquitous, emerging as a potential chemical marker for the species. This study highlights several compounds of interest, related to the chemical ecology and pathogenicity of H. werneckii . As most of them remain unidentified, future research should prioritize their isolation and identification, to improve our understanding of this extremophile organism and harness its potential in natural product discovery.

items.title: TaxoAttention: fusing semantic and hierarchical taxonomic models with attention-guided augmentation for mosquito identification
items.abstract: Accurate species-level identification of mosquitoes remains a critical bottleneck in vector surveillance, particularly when dealing with morphologically similar taxa or field-damaged specimens. In this study, we introduce a deep learning framework that integrates hierarchical taxonomic structure with attention-based feature learning to improve classification performance under real-world imaging conditions. The model combines a semi-fixed, taxonomy-informed feature stream with a fully trainable semantic stream. It further employs dynamic attention-guided augmentation, designed to focus training on diagnostically relevant regions, such as wing venation, tarsal banding, and palpal morphology, and to reduce the influence of the background. Evaluated on a standardized, predominantly field-collected dataset (MosquitoTax-200) representing 32 species across Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex with 200 images per species, our approach achieves 84.6% macro-averaged precision (mAP), 5.0 percentage points above an Xception baseline trained with standard cross-entropy loss and used as a control. This work highlights the potential of biologically grounded AI tools to scale species identification in vector control operations and to support training and quality assurance in entomological diagnostics.

items.title: Lynx reintroduction from a bottlenecked source exposes a lethal genetic defect
items.abstract: Abstract Conservation programmes worldwide use reintroductions and translocations as management tools to support endangered species. However, such efforts often result in small and isolated populations that face genetic challenges associated with reduced gene flow and inbreeding. Inbreeding depression is a well-known risk in such programmes, as increased homozygosity can expose recessive deleterious alleles, compromise fitness and threaten population persistence. Yet, no causal variant for a lethal disease has previously been identified in a wild population. Here we combine long-term health and population data with genomic analyses to identify a recessive loss-of-function allele causing lethal organ mineralization in young Eurasian lynx ( Lynx lynx ) from a reintroduced population in Switzerland. Spatio-temporal analyses revealed that the allele was introduced from one of the source populations and increased in frequency through founder effects and inbreeding. Our findings establish the first direct link between reintroduction history and a lethal genetic disease in the wild, illustrating how population genetic processes interact to shape the fate of a recessive deleterious allele and emphasize the vulnerability of small, isolated populations following reintroduction.

items.title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
items.abstract: Seasonal breeders often depend on predictable resource pulses, yet climate change may alter reliability without shifting average timing. Here, using satellite chlorophyll records and two decades of individual breeding data for a tropical seabird, we show that weakened breeding synchrony and declining and less consistent reproductive success were associated with increasingly variable bloom timing without a consistent directional shift. Focusing on average timing alone could mean that climate impacts on species are overlooked. The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

items.title: Species-rich and genomically diverse: Comparative genomics reveals how fusions, fissions, and sex chromosomes have shaped beetle evolution
items.abstract: Chromosome evolution in animals reflects a balance between long-term conservation of ancestral linkage groups and lineage-specific chromosomal rearrangements that reshape genome structure. Beetles (Coleoptera), the most species-rich animal order, exhibit extensive diversity in karyotype, yet the extent to which their chromosomes retain deep ancestral structure remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 190 chromosome-level genome assemblies spanning 39 families and 16 superfamilies to characterize genome diversity, evaluate the conservation of ancestral linkage groups (Stevens elements), identify neo-sex chromosomes, and explore the role of repetitive elements in driving karyotypic change. Our results reveal that beetle genomes are highly diverse, varying substantially in genome size, chromosome number, GC content, and transposable element (TE) composition. Despite this diversity, Stevens elements appear conserved across much of the radiation, with several superfamilies maintaining strong chromosome synteny over more than 200 million years of evolution. In contrast, some clades, and specifically the leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae), have undergone extensive genomic changes including numerous chromosomal fusions and fissions and changes in genome size. Using synteny-based approaches across beetles, we identified 37 species (approximately 19.5%) having patterns consistent with neo-sex chromosomes, a substantially higher frequency than previous estimates. These putative X-autosome fusions vary in complexity and age, often clustered within lineages that are prone to chromosomal instability. The ancestral X chromosome appears conserved for over 300 million years, with stable gene content and reduced TEs relative to autosomes. These findings help establish beetles as a promising system to uncover the evolutionary forces that maintain and disrupt ancestral linkage groups and drive the formation of neo-sex chromosomes.

items.title: Recent thermohaline shifts in the Adriatic Sea and their potential consequences
items.abstract: The Adriatic Sea has warmed and salinified rapidly over the past two decades, and the changes are not uniform with depth. We combine 33 664 quality-controlled shipboard and Argo temperature and salinity casts from 1950–2025 into two climatologies, test the individual casts for regime shifts, and use the Argo profiles from the Southern Adriatic Pit to quantify the vertical structure of the changes. Between the 1950–1999 and 2000–2025 climatologies the southern Adriatic salinified at every depth and season, by 0.11–0.53, and warmed by up to 1.6 °C everywhere except at the uppermost levels in summer and autumn, where the sampling differs between the two periods. Amplification relative to the rest of the Mediterranean is strongly depth-dependent: below 700 m the southern Adriatic warms at 6.2 times the median rate of the other Mediterranean sub-basins, whereas above 200 m its warming is not amplified. The occurrence of near-surface salinity maxima (“surface saline lakes”) rises abruptly after 2014, in both ship and float records, from a few per cent of warm-season casts to about 40 %; this regime shift is only provable if vertical resolution and platform are accounted for. The intermediate salinity maximum has lost its dominant band: the detected maxima no longer cluster in one depth interval. Where two maxima coexist they have moved apart and diverged in density, so they are not one migrating core. Over 2014–2024 the steric contribution in the Southern Adriatic Pit is negative, dominated by halosteric contraction, so that local sea level rise must be mass-driven. Salt fingering has intensified below the classical intermediate core, allowing salt transport towards deeper layers. Three consequences follow, set out here as hypotheses. First, deep ventilation may persist under milder winters, because water that is already saline needs less cooling to sink, but each ventilation event may then deliver less oxygen, because the water that sinks is warmer. Second, exchange of oxygen, nutrients and carbon between the surface and intermediate layers may be either suppressed or enhanced beneath more frequent surface saline lakes, depending on whether stratification or double diffusion prevails. Third, Adriatic ecosystems, in which warming-linked mortality and species redistribution are already documented, face a basin changing faster at depth than at the surface. Testing these hypotheses requires sustained high-resolution observations.

items.title: Edukasi Konservasi Mangrove dan Pemanfaatan Potensi Lokal sebagai Upaya Pemberdayaan Masyarakat Pesisir Desa Sungsang, Banyuasin
items.abstract: Mangrove ecosystems play a vital role in maintaining coastal ecological balance and providing social and economic benefits. Sungsang Village, Banyuasin II District, Banyuasin Regency, has mangrove resources that can be developed through conservation and sustainable utilization. These efforts require greater community knowledge and awareness of mangrove preservation. This community service program aimed to improve community knowledge, awareness, and skills in mangrove conservation and value-added product development. Activities included education on mangrove functions and benefits, demonstrations and practical training in local material processing, packaging and marketing training, and community mentoring. Evaluation involved pre-tests and post-tests to assess knowledge improvement. The results showed increased understanding of mangrove ecological functions, conservation, and sustainable resource utilization. Participants also improved their skills in product development and gained knowledge of packaging and marketing strategies. Integrating conservation education with local product is expected to strengthen community participation in mangrove preservation and promote sustainable resource utilization while integrating ecological, social, and economic dimensions.

items.title: Physicochemical gradients shape zooplankton and bivalve communities along the Sô River–Lake Nokoué continuum in Benin: implications for environmental health monitoring
items.abstract: Tropical river-lagoon systems are dynamic environments in which physicochemical variability can influence aquatic community structure. This study characterized the composition, taxonomic richness, occurrence, and spatiotemporal variation of zooplankton and bivalve communities along the Sô River-Lake Nokoué continuum in southern Benin. Monthly biological sampling was conducted at 11 stations from August 2024 to March 2025, including four stations in the Sô River (S1-S4) and seven in Lake Nokoué (S5-S11). A total of 24 zooplankton families and nine bivalve families were recorded. Eurotatoria dominated the zooplankton community, accounting for 56% of total relative density and exhibiting the highest taxonomic richness. Bivalves showed lower family-level richness but were recorded across the study area. Principal component analysis revealed a marked physicochemical gradient associated primarily with salinity, electrical conductivity, and total dissolved solids, distinguishing riverine from lagoonal conditions. Redundancy analysis identified associations between zooplankton community composition and dissolved oxygen and salinity, whereas bivalve community composition was associated with pH and temperature. These results highlight the environmental heterogeneity of the Sô River-Lake Nokoué continuum and provide an ecological baseline for future aquatic monitoring. Because pathogens, human exposure, and disease outcomes were not assessed, the findings do not establish a direct relationship between the observed community patterns and waterborne disease risk.

items.title: A comprehensive benchmark and dual-encoder baseline for terraced field extraction in complex mountainous regions
items.abstract: Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.

items.title: Molecular, chemical, and conventional fisheries methods reveal early invasion dynamics and range expansion of an invasive fish in a large North American estuary
items.abstract: Abstract Round Goby (Neogobius melanostomus) have quickly expanded throughout the Hudson River Estuary since their initial detection in 2021, yet patterns of establishment, dispersal, and population status remain poorly understood. We studied Round Goby distribution, relative abundance, establishment, and natal origins in the Hudson River Estuary from 2022–2024 using environmental DNA (eDNA), beach seining, and otolith microchemistry. These approaches provided complementary information on spatial expansion and connectivity between the Hudson and Mohawk rivers, where hydrological and anthropogenic connections can influence aquatic organism movement across river networks. Concurrent eDNA sampling and seining showed agreement in detections, supporting eDNA as a complementary monitoring tool in large tidal rivers. Throughout the study period eDNA detections increased spatially and temporally in the lower Hudson River Estuary, with most positive detections in 2024 occurring across approximately 70 km of brackish habitat, indicating downstream range expansion and likely establishment in brackish waters. Despite continued range expansion, cumulative captures during 2022–2024 were lower than in 2021, suggesting the population has not undergone rapid exponential growth. Otolith microchemistry revealed overlapping but distinguishable natal signatures between Hudson and Mohawk River fish, demonstrating demographic connectivity and indicating that the expanding Hudson River Estuary population is supported by both local recruitment and downstream immigrants from the Mohawk River. Together, these results identify the Hudson–Mohawk connection, facilitated in part by the NYS Canal system, as an important invasion pathway and highlight the value of combining detection and provenance approaches to resolve invasion dynamics across connected freshwater and estuarine habitats.

items.title: Public Spatial Perceptions from PPGIS Studies Using Qualitative Content Analysis in Existing, Candidate, and Outside Protected Areas
items.abstract: Pre-designation stakeholder spatial perceptions remain underexamined despite their relevance to protected area (PA) designation. Using Public Participation Geographical Information System (PPGIS), by convenience sampling, 97 participants (69 locals and 25 visitors) mapped 377 open-ended values and concerns statements across existing PA (EPA), candidate PA (CPA), and outside CPA (OCPA) in eastern Hokkaido, Japan. Inductive coding yielded 1042 code instances organized into 122 codes, 17 sub-themes, and four themes. Gi* hotspot values (n = 719) and concerns (n = 323) were compared to identify value–concern zones, and a participant-based location quotient identified distinctive themes. Values (69%) concentrated on ecology, landscape, recreation, and conservation; concerns concentrated on energy infrastructure, ecological loss, human–wildlife conflicts, and facilities. Potential conflict zones (overlapping value and concern hotspots) were concentrated on the Notsuke Peninsula and Shunkunitai within the EPA, combining shared values with habitat loss. Concern-dominant zones, marked by energy infrastructure and habitat loss, lay mainly outside the EPA. Locals and visitors shared values but differed in concerns; only locals raised human–wildlife conflicts. Codes related to all six elements of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services conceptual framework, though abiotic elements fell outside its contribution categories. Pre-designation PPGIS provides spatial evidence for boundary delimitation, zoning, and identifying potential conflicts.

items.title: Climate Change and Governance Gap in South Asia
items.abstract: Abstract Climate Change is one of the most concerning non-traditional security threats which is affecting the world at an unprecedented pace. South Asia is the most vulnerable region in terms of climate change with countries across the region are facing challenges like sea-level rise, biodiversity loss, uneven patterns of rainfall, global warming, climate-induced migration, food scarcity, extreme floods and much more which are further responsible for the critical nexus of food and water security. This research paper provides critical analysis on how these problems creates a governance gap in South Asia and requires the need for a comprehensive regional governance framework which is a major gap in this research. This paper also analyzes the various protocols, declarations and reports related to Climate Change which are not responsive towards the specific vulnerabilities of South Asia. Ineffectiveness of South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation i.e. SAARC- major regional grouping of South Asia- particularly due to political disputes and conflicts between countries is also the major factor in governance gap. This paper adopts Qualitative research methodology which includes the analysis of both primary and secondary sources. Finally, this paper proposes the need for a Polycentric governance framework for the effective coordination and cooperation in South Asia.

items.title: The Ecology of Open Science Landscapes
items.abstract: This repository contains the materials from the Unconference 5 of the 2026 SORTEE Conference, held on October 13-14, 2026. This unconference discussed how and if we can use ecological diversity metrics to help us understand states of open scholarship culture. We discussed whether components of ecological diversity metrics (richness, evenness, turnover) can inspire ways to describe openness in research. Prompts included: what are meaningful dimensions of open science? Can they be measured or compared without oversimplification? Where does the ecological analogy break down? The goal was to map candidate metrics, identify shared definitions, and outline potential empirical or conceptual follow-up work. items.title: Perceived priorities, experiences and provision gaps in urban green spaces: evidence from university students in Pécs, Hungary
items.abstract: Urban green spaces play a vital role in enhancing the liveability and sustainability of cities, particularly for university students. This study applies a socially differentiated importance–experience framework to the evaluation of urban green spaces by university students in Pécs, Hungary. The sample was not representative of the target population, primarily because foreign students were overrepresented. Post-stratification weights were therefore applied to align the sample with the composition of the student population at the University of Pécs. Using these weights, Multiple Factor Analysis identified three dimensions for both the importance and experience measures, as well as six dimensions representing the gap between the corresponding importance and experience ratings. Each dimension was subsequently modelled using post-stratification-weighted linear regression. The explanatory variables describing patterns of green-space use were preselected using the Boruta feature-selection algorithm. The findings reveal substantial importance–experience gaps for several basic attributes, including public toilets, accessibility for people with reduced mobility, benches, cleanliness, waste bins and vegetation. Associations with citizenship and patterns of green space use were dimension-specific rather than indicating consistently less experiences among respondents with foreign citizenship. The results suggest that the students’ evaluations of urban green spaces reflect a multidimensional interplay of practical, environmental, and social attributes. Future research should examine comparative settings and incorporate qualitative methods to explore variation among more precisely defined user groups and across urban contexts. Given the non-representative sample and the aggregation of respondents with foreign citizenship into a single group, the results should be interpreted cautiously, particularly regarding gender-specific patterns and heterogeneity within the foreign-citizenship group.

items.title: Population Diversity of Tecomella undulata across South Asia: Diversity identification Markers, Possible Causes, and Potential for Conservation
items.abstract: Tecomella undulata (Sm.) Seem., the sole species of its genus in the family Bignoniaceae, is a keystone tree of the arid and semi-arid tracts of South Asia, valued equally for its ecological role in desert stabilization and its long history of use in traditional medicine. Habitat fragmentation, unsustainable timber and herbal extraction, weak natural regeneration, grazing pressure and a warming/drying climate has together pushed the species toward endangered status in the Thar Desert of Sindh, Pakistan. Since there is a lack of such study which integrate anatomical, phytochemical, and molecular analysis as diversity identification markers, this review explores and summarizes the available information on population diversity identification using molecular (chiefly ISSR and RAPD), anatomical structure and the phytochemical profile as markers to understand variations in T. undulata populations. Published marker-based work shows substantial genetic diversity retained within populations despite geographic isolation, while anatomical and phytochemical surveys, though comparatively sparse, point to xeromorphic adaptations and stress induced shifts in secondary metabolism that likely track local aridity and soil conditions. We argue that combining molecular, anatomical and phytochemical data is not simply additive but necessary though other approaches like common garden experiment may also be needed to fully distinguish genetically fixed divergence from environmentally plastic response, and thereby to identify populations that are both genetically distinct and ecologically or medicinally valuable. This information would give conservation planners, across South Asian range, an evidence based strategy for prioritizing germplasm collection, in situ protection, and restoration efforts before further population decline erodes the genetic resources

items.title: Contrasting local responses but similar regional turnover in phytoplankton and rotifer assemblages in saline–alkaline wetlands, Northeast China
items.abstract: Freshwater salinization and alkalization are emerging threats to global biodiversity, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions. Although ecological impacts of freshwater salinization and alkalization on local biodiversity have received increasing attention, it remains unclear how diversity patterns of organisms in different trophic levels respond at a regional scale. Here, we investigated rotifer and phytoplankton assemblages across 61 wetlands spanning a broad saline–alkaline gradient in the Songnen Plain, Northeast China. We quantified local (alpha) diversity, partitioned beta diversity into turnover and nestedness components, and evaluated how saline–alkaline conditions are associated with assemblage and diversity. Our results showed salinization in wetlands was often associated with high pH, nutrient enrichment, shallower surface water and lower macrophyte coverage, association with a significant decline in local phytoplankton diversity but no significant effect on rotifer diversity. Rotifer assemblages were mainly shaped by water depth, and macrophyte coverage, while phytoplankton assemblages were more influenced by TOC, NH 4 + -N, water temperature, and macrophyte coverage. Phytoplankton diversity in local wetlands was negatively associated with pH and inorganic nitrogen concentrations, whereas rotifer diversity was associated with water temperature, water depth, and nutrient concentrations. Despite these contrasting local responses, both groups exhibited high spatial compositional dissimilarity among investigated wetlands. Mean total beta diversity reached 0.89 for rotifers and 0.91 for phytoplankton, with turnover accounting for 74.16% and 67.03% of the assemblage dissimilarities, respectively. These findings reveal the profound impacts of freshwater salinization and alkalization on wetland organisms. We highlight the importance of integrating both alpha and beta diversity dimensions in monitoring biodiversity response to these emerging threats in freshwater ecosystems under global environmental change.

items.title: THE CATASTROPHIC VIRAL–MICROBIAL HOMEOSTASIS HYPOTHESIS: Environmental Disruption, Viral Dormancy, Host Transition, and the Emergence of Epidemic Disease Series: Canonical Monograph Series in Biophysical Political Economy (Monograph No. 14 / Book XIV)
items.abstract: Book XIV of the Canonical Monograph Series in Biophysical Political Economy establishes a unified biophysical, ecological, virological, and immunological treatise investigating the emergence of infectious disease crises in the wake of planetary and anthropogenic catastrophes. Serving as the cellular and microbiological counterpart to the macro-geomechanics of Book XIII, this monograph dismantles the classical reductionist assumption of spontaneous pathogen creation (the myth of de novo pathogenesis). It demonstrates that environmental cataclysms—such as explosive volcanic winters, severe climatic oscillations, floods, famines, and wars—do not manufacture novel biological killers out of an empty void. Instead, macro-disturbances fundamentally reorganize the regulatory balance of power within ancient, preexisting microbial ecosystems. Anchored in a rigorous Four-Register Epistemic Protocol and a 70-Pillar Scientific Canon, the treatise traces this biological cascade across ten canonical chapters and three operational divisions: Division I: The Ecological Trigger and the Dual Viral Rheostat (Chapters 1–3) The Tambora Catalyst (1815–1817): Examines the April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora, the 1816 "Year Without a Summer," and the subsequent ignition of the First Global Cholera Pandemic in the Bay of Bengal. Integrates estuarine zooplankton (copepod) ecology and Viable-but-Non-Culturable (VBNC) bacterial dormancy with famine-induced human hypochlorhydria (loss of the gastric acid barrier) and mucosal atrophy. The Dual Viral Response & Lytic–Lysogenic Inversion: Demonstrates that environmental trauma does not alter viral activity uniformly. Ambient shock simultaneously deactivates free-swimming predatory bacteriophages (removing top-down population control and creating a regulatory vacuum) while activating bacterial cellular SOS responses that trigger dormant prophages to excise, replicate, and horizontally transfer lethal exotoxin cassettes (such as cholera toxin and Shiga toxin) via lysogenic conversion. Bacteriophages as Planetary Rheostats & The BAM Shield: Formulates the dual role of the viral ocean in enforcing "kill-the-winner" microbial biodiversity versus encoding pathogenicity. Details the Bacteriophage Adherence to Mucus (BAM) model, showing how phages tethered to mucosal glycoproteins form an animal-independent, non-host-derived immune shield that collapses during host nutritional starvation. Division II: The Human Interface and Pathological Scaling (Chapters 4–6) The Holobiont Under Siege: Replaces Cartesian biological isolation with the human holobiont paradigm. Traces the physical breakdown of the Three Physiological Gates of Defense (the respiratory mucociliary escalator, the gastric hydrochloric acid furnace, and the zonulin-regulated intestinal tight-junction monolayer) alongside the collapse of gut anaerobic colonization resistance and the compression of wildlife zoonotic spillover corridors. Multi-Scalar Pathological Topography: Deconstructs the fallacy of linear disease progression. Proves that cellular dysbiosis, local community clusters, regional epidemics, and global pandemics are discontinuous topological regimes governed by specific environmental compatibility gates, metapopulation mobility networks, and contact degree variance. Extends the analytical matrix beyond viruses to bacteria, thermally adapted fungi, vector-borne parasites, and free-living amoebic refuges. The Opportunistic Expansion Principle & Competitive Niche Vacancy: Synthesizes multidimensional niche theory, resource depletion rules, and the fluctuating resource hypothesis. Demonstrates why the primary beneficiary of an ecological catastrophe is rarely the organism directly targeted by the shock, but the opportunistic survivor whose natural competitors and viral predators were disproportionately decimated—illustrated through post-antibiotic Clostridioides difficile colitis and post-trauma angioinvasive mucormycosis. Division III: The Matrix's Tragic Triage and Sovereign Transcendence (Chapters 7–10) The "Good Matrix" Paradox & Non-Equilibrium Regulation: Evaluates the planetary homeostat through cybernetic regulation theory and multi-stable ecological attractors. Explains how five natural biological counter-brakes halt runaway outbreaks, while showing why an unfeeling planetary regulator settles for alternative stable attractors marked by hysteresis and chronic host strain. The Stealth Constant: Deconstructs the illusion of tranquil inter-epidemic intervals. Maps covert biological colonization, persister cells, intracellular phagolysosomal sequestration, and antigenic camouflage, demonstrating how sub-clinical populations sample host telemetry and undergo sudden, synchronized phase transitions when quorum-sensing autoinduction thresholds are breached. The Tragic Bio-Triage, The 90% Containment Law, & The Organ Ghetto: Demonstrates why the planetary homeostat intercepts over ninety percent of potential pandemic trajectories by choosing virulence and velocity attenuation over complete eradication. Reveals how this stalemated containment walls pathogens inside human vital organs (liver, kidneys, joints, central nervous system)—creating an "Organ Ghetto" that forces human hosts to endure chronic fatigue, cyclic fevers, and neuro-inflammatory sickness behavior as biological buffer tissue for collective survival. Algorithmic Immunology and the Avicenna Sovereign Shield: Enforces the Anti-Expendability Charter across medicine and planetary public health. Replaces the blind sacrifice of natural bio-triage with the Four Pillars of the Avicenna Sovereign Shield: sub-clinical metagenomic telemetry, non-cytotoxic phage biocontrol and enzymatic quorum quenching, mucosal tight-junction and BAM shield restoration, and decentralized clean water and nutritional sovereignty—dissolving the organ ghetto and achieving 99.8% population protection with zero biological expenditure.

items.title: Comparative assessment of bacterial diversity in small water bodies of the Eastern Pamir mountains using amplicon-based and metagenomic approaches
items.abstract: Microbial diversity in remote extreme environments remains poorly understood. We investigated sediment microbial communities in small water bodies of the Eastern Pamir cold desert using V3–V4 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and metagenomics, to assess taxonomic and functional diversity. Amplicon data showed high Pseudomonadota abundance and taxa overlooked in the 2019 analysis, including Vampirovibrionaceae. Reanalysis of the amplicon data increased taxonomic assessment from 54% to 93% without changes in the number of unique sequences. Comparison of amplicon and metagenome-derived 16S profiles revealed limited overlap: only 15% of metagenomic V3–V4 sequences were detected in amplicons. Fourteen of 37 phyla were exclusive to ASVs, whereas three (of 20) to MAGs. Metagenomics recovered 86 MAGs spanning 26 classes, predominantly from Bacteroidota. Sulfur oxidation and sulfate reduction pathways occurred mainly in Pseudomonadota. Phototrophic potential was identified in 25 MAGs, largely Bacteroidota and established phototrophic lineages; most possessed complete nitrogen-fixation pathways. Eight genera detected with all methods belonged to halophilic or halotolerant lineages. These findings highlight salinity as an important driver of bacterial community composition in Eastern Pamir benthic communities and identify differences between methods. Integrating amplicon sequencing and metagenomics provides complementary insights into microbial diversity and metabolic potential in remote extreme environments.

items.title: Phylogenetic conservatism of dietary niches in Neotropical leaf-nosed bats
items.abstract: Abstract The tendency of lineages to retain their ancestral niche over time is known as phylogenetic niche conservatism (PNC ). Studies considering Eltonian niche characteristics (i.e. biotic interactions) have increased in recent years. However, the question of whether Eltonian niches are conserved remains largely unexplored. The aim of this study was to test for PNC in the Eltonian niches, namely the dietary niches of phyllostomid bats. More specifically, we look for PNC patterns at three phylogenetic scales: family, subfamily and species levels; and in two features of Eltonian niche: dietary breadth and position. We used phylogenetic comparative methods to test the PNC at family and subfamily levels; for species level, we used an approach that compares the dietary niche similarities between species pairs. Our results are largely consistent with PNC of dietary niches, but different patterns emerged when we assessed dietary niche position or breadth, and at different phylogenetic scales. At family level, we found evidence for PNC in dietary niche breadth, but not for dietary niche position. Conversely, at subfamily level we found evidence for PNC in dietary niche position but not for dietary niche breadth. At species level, we found that dietary niches of sister species resemble each other more than non-sister species do, providing evidence of PNC. Our findings highlight the importance of considering that Eltonian niche do not evolve in the same way over time, nor among subclades. Therefore, not assuming but testing PNC is fundamental for understanding the processes underlying the evolution of dietary niches.

items.title: Coupled MaxEnt-InVEST modelling identifies habitat suitability, quality and conservation gaps of Garrulax maximus
items.abstract: Introduction Habitat degradation and conservation gaps severely threaten China's endemic montane birds, yet few studies have integrated habitat suitability with quality assessment. Methods Using the nationally protected Giant Laughingthrush ( Garrulax maximus ) across five provinces in western China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we coupled optimized MaxEnt, InVEST, and GIS approaches to quantify potential distribution, habitat quality, conservation gaps, and environmental drivers. Results The MaxEnt model performed robustly (mean AUC = 0.946). Climate dominated distribution (69.3% cumulative contribution), with annual precipitation (bio12, 35.7%) as the core limiting factor. The species occupied a cold-humid niche: annual precipitation 631.60–794.65 mm, driest-quarter temperature −7.12–2.75 °C, and elevation 2496.79–4012.78 m. High-suitability areas centered on the western Sichuan Basin rim, decreasing outward. Notably, a spatial mismatch emerged between habitat quality and suitability: Yunnan held the largest high-quality habitat (17.28 × 10 4 km 2 ) but limited priority conservation areas, whereas Sichuan, with less high-quality habitat (13.63 × 10 4 km 2 ), contained the largest priority zones (6.95 × 10 4 km 2 ), indicating complementarity rather than substitution. Conservation gaps were extensive (54.26%–75.98%), mainly along reserve boundaries and buffers, revealing structural deficiencies from overemphasizing core zones while neglecting corridors. Discussion These findings underscore the urgency of reassessing and expanding protected area networks to cover priority zones. Our integrated framework offers a scientific reference for conserving the Giant Laughingthrush and managing montane birds within the Hengduan Mountains biodiversity hotspot, with implications for broader conservation planning in ecologically sensitive regions.

items.title: How Fishes Live in an Ice-Covered Ocean
items.abstract: The Arctic Ocean lies at the northernmost point of our planet, where the sun does not set in summer and does not rise in winter, and where temperatures are cold enough to keep your ice cream frozen. Floating on top is a sheet of sea ice that expands in winter and shrinks in summer. For Arctic animals, living in this environment means dealing with extremes in temperature, sea ice, light, and food. Arctic fishes have survived thanks to their unique adaptations, but now they also must survive climate change and the thinning of sea ice. Luckily, north of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland, there is a large portion of sea ice that is much older and thicker than the rest. This is the Last Ice Area, and as thick sea ice disappears from other areas, this region could act as a refuge for Arctic fishes looking for shelter under the cold ice.

items.title: Primordial quark stars made of a long-lived false vacuum
items.abstract: A false vacuum could be a profound ingredient of fundamental physics, yet its direct detection in laboratories is hindered when the lifetime is exponentially long. Conventional static phase diagrams often discard metastable false vacuum, we show that, however, in a dynamical treatment of a first-order QCD phase transition at large quark chemical potential that strongly suppresses tunneling, cosmologically long-lived, and thus indispensable false vacuum naturally arises, and makes nontrivial contribution to constituting primordial quark objects. We identify two distinct branches of such primordial quark objects: quark star crusted with false vacuum, and nugget specifically referring to quark star in global false vacuum, which may account for a population of small compact stars. Some long-lived primordial objects may have survived until the late Universe, and hopefully sow the seeds of high red-shift galaxies. Its false vacuum decay can power ultra-energetic long $γ$-ray bursts and kHz gravitational waves within multi-messenger facilities, rendering itself an astrophysical and thus testable phenomenon.

items.title: The Synthetic Absorption Line Spectral Almanac (SALSA)
items.abstract: We create the first large-scale mock spectroscopic survey of gas absorption sightlines traversing the interstellar medium (ISM), circumgalactic medium (CGM), and intergalactic medium (IGM) surrounding galaxies of virtual Universes. That is, we create mock, or synthetic, absorption spectra by drawing lines-of-sight through cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, using a new mesh-free Voronoi ray-tracing algorithm. The result is the Synthetic Absorption Line Spectral Almanac (SALSA), which is publicly released on a feature-rich online science platform (www.tng-project.org/spectra). It spans a range of ions, transitions, instruments, observational characteristics, assumptions, redshifts, and simulations. These include, but are not limited to: (ions) HI, OI, CI, MgI, MgII, FeII, SiII, CaII, ZnII, SiIII, SiIV, NV, CII, CIV, OVI; (instruments) SDSS-BOSS, KECK-HIRES, UVES, COS, DESI, 4MOST, WEAVE, XSHOOTER; (model choices) with/without dust depletion, noise, quasar continua, foregrounds; (redshift) from z=0 to z~6; (ancillary data) integrated equivalent widths, column densities, distances and properties of nearby galaxies; (simulations) IllustrisTNG including TNG50, TNG-Cluster, EAGLE, and SIMBA. We also provide line-of-sight integrals, including Faraday rotation measure (RM) probing magnetic fields, and dispersion measure (DM) as traced by fast radio bursts (FRBs). This scope is not fixed, and will grow and evolve with community interest and requests over time. The resulting dataset is generic and broadly applicable, enabling diverse science goals such as: (i) studies of the underlying physical gas structures giving rise to particular absorption signatures, (ii) galaxy-absorber and halo-absorber correlations, (iii) virtual surveys and survey strategy optimization, (iv) stacking experiments and the identification of faint absorption features, (v) assessment of data reduction methods and completeness calculations, (vi) inference of physical properties from observables, and (vii) apples-to-apples comparisons between simulations and data.

items.title: Loop Quantum Gravity Black Holes Surrounded by Quintessence
items.abstract: Quantum gravity corrections act on the near-horizon geometry of a black hole (BH), while dark energy acts on its asymptotic region, and how the two imprints combine is still poorly understood. We study a static, spherically symmetric BH of Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) surrounded by a quintessence field. The metric function carries the LQG parameters [Formula: see text] and the quintessence parameters [Formula: see text], and for suitable values it has three horizons, a structure found neither in pure LQG BHs nor in classical quintessence BHs. We analyze null and timelike geodesics, photon spheres and the shadow seen by a static observer placed between the event and the cosmological horizons. Sixth-order WKB quasinormal modes (QNMs) of scalar and electromagnetic fields confirm stability over the ranges examined. The quantum term behaves as a short-range repulsive correction: it shrinks the photon sphere and the shadow, raises the QNM oscillation frequency and lowers the light deflection. Quintessence works the other way on the photon sphere, the ringing frequency and the bending. With the Gauss-Bonnet method we obtain a weak deflection angle valid for [Formula: see text], which we check against direct numerical integration, and in which quintessence dominates at large impact parameters and the LQG terms at small ones.

items.title: The Electromagnetically Isolated Global Signal Estimation Platform (EIGSEP)
items.abstract: Abstract The Electromagnetically Isolated Global Signal Estimation Platform (EIGSEP) is a new instrument designed to measure the global 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn and the Epoch of Reionization, redshifted to frequencies below 250 MHz. To reduce spectral structure in the antenna beam associated with ground scattering, EIGSEP uses a shaped bowtie antenna suspended in a canyon, designed to keep terrain and conducting structures about 100 m away. We describe the current system design of EIGSEP, including the rotating antenna platform, a transmitter antenna to characterize the beam of the bowtie antenna, and auxiliary ground antennas. We then discuss the EIGSEP calibration scheme, which incorporates traditional Dicke switching in the receiver, and novel approaches that include beam mapping, beam modulation, and interferometric cross-correlation. The instrument has been deployed near Marjum Pass, Utah, for testing and initial data collection. We discuss the site characteristics and present the measured response of the suspended and rotating antenna to an external transmitter. We also present an in situ measurement of the antenna reflection coefficient, whose delay spectrum shows no detectable terrestrial scattering at delays below 590 ns, the round-trip light travel time to the nearest canyon terrain, demonstrating the electromagnetic isolation of the antenna. Absolutely calibrated sky spectra and the characterization of the antenna beam are deferred to forthcoming work.

items.title: Modeling individual nearby radio galaxies as ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray accelerators
items.abstract: Abstract Nearby radio galaxies are among the most promising candidates for the acceleration of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs). In this work, we develop a physically motivated, source-resolved framework to quantify the contribution of the three nearest Fanaroff–Riley Class I (FR-I) radio galaxies – Centaurus A, Virgo A, and Fornax A – to the UHECR flux measured by the Pierre Auger Observatory. Acceleration spectra derived from detailed jet-acceleration models are combined with numerical simulations of extragalactic propagation, while the more distant radio-galaxy population is treated as a continuous background. By fitting our simulation exclusively to the measured UHECR energy spectrum, we determine the relative contribution of each source and constrain the fraction of jet power converted into UHECR luminosity. We find that a small number of nearby radio galaxies can account for the highest-energy UHECR flux with acceleration efficiencies of order $$10^{-3}$$ 10 - 3 – $$10^{-2}$$ 10 - 2 , while the background contribution remains subdominant. Some resulting scenarios yield mass-composition trends broadly consistent with observations at the highest energies and predict distinct levels of secondary neutrino fluxes. These results demonstrate that physically grounded, source-specific modeling of nearby radio galaxies provides a physically motivated contribution to the interpretation of the highest-energy UHECR component.

items.title: A Search for Rotation Measure Flare Candidates in Repeating Fast Radio Bursts
items.abstract: Abstract Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration extragalactic radio transients of unknown origin. Rotation measures (RMs) probe their local magnetoionic environments and provide important clues to their nature. While RM variability has been observed in several repeating FRBs, it is typically gradual or stochastic. Recently, observations of FRB 20220529A revealed an abrupt RM excursion followed by rapid recovery on weeklong timescales, termed an “RM flare,” suggesting a potentially distinct form of RM variability associated with localized magnetized plasma. In this work, we perform a systematic search for RM flare candidates in repeating FRBs with multi-epoch RM measurements. Using an iterative Gaussian smoothing method to estimate the baseline and a 3 σ significance threshold for candidate selection, we identify one tentative RM flare candidate in FRB 20121102A and one marginal signal in FRB 20240114A, in addition to the event in FRB 20220529A. Our results suggest that RM flares, if confirmed, may not be rare among repeating FRBs and point to highly dynamic magnetized environments local to the sources. Future high-cadence polarimetric observations, particularly following the discovery of RM excursions, will be essential for further evaluating these candidates and constraining their physical origin.

items.title: Constraining Galaxy Cluster Triaxiality via Weak Lensing. I. Preparation for the Rubin Data beyond Leading Order
items.abstract: Abstract The 3D mass distributions of galaxy clusters are generally triaxial, a geometry that is difficult to constrain from projected observations. In this work, we measure the projected halo shapes of clusters from weak-lensing (WL) signatures using the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling software, a tool developed by the Dark Energy Science Collaboration to analyze data from NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We measure ensemble halo ellipticity on the plane of the sky via axis-aligned stacking and multipole expansion of WL signatures. We study a precursor dataset: the redMaPPer cluster catalog, the metacalibration shape catalog, and the Directional Neighborhood Fitting photometric redshift catalog from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 public data release. We select clusters that have a high centering probability (>90%) of the identified central galaxy, and use the satellite galaxy distribution to determine the major-axis orientation for stacking. We extend the analysis to the second order of ellipticity in monopole and quadrupole measurements. The projected ellipticity of the cluster sample is found to be 0.307 − 0.014 + 0.013 (axis ratio 0.530 − 0.015 + 0.016 ), with extra percent-level systematics introduced mainly by miscentering. The projected cluster ellipticity shows no statistically significant dependence on redshift or richness (mass proxy). We further verify the accuracy of the cluster shape measurement using mock catalogs. This analysis is applicable to datasets from wide-area cosmic surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope, where larger sample sizes will lead to tighter constraints on cluster shapes.

items.title: Bouncing singularities in Schwarzschild geometry: A geometric origin of the quasinormal mode convergence region
items.abstract: We show analytically that the convergence of the QNM expansion of the retarded Green's function of the Schwarzschild spacetime is set by a singularity in the complex time plane. The singularity has a simple geometric origin: it is an example of a `bouncing singularity' in the language of AdS/CFT literature, caused by a null geodesic which bounces from the black hole singularity. Our work explains why the QNM convergence region at real times is bounded by null ray which scatters from the gravitational potential at a seemingly unremarkable point ($r_* = 0$ in the conventions of previous work) -- this ray is the same distance from the origin as the bouncing singularity in the relevant complex plane. The same set of singularities are responsible for an annular region of convergence for the Matsubara mode sum which describes the early time behaviour of the Schwarzschild Green's function for perturbations close to the horizon.

items.title: (LRDs) 2 : The Low-ReDshift Little Red Dots Survey. II. DESI DR1 Sample
items.abstract: Abstract JWST has revealed a substantial population of “Little Red Dots” (LRDs) at z > 4, challenging conventional active galactic muclei (AGN) frameworks. However, the low-redshift regime remains largely unexplored. In the second paper of the (LRDs) 2 series, we present a systematic selection from DESI DR1 and identify 27 LRDs at z = 0.2–0.9, yielding a number density lower limit of 7.5 × 10 −10 cMpc −3 . We conducted near-IR spectroscopic follow-up observations for 21 of them, revealing their full spectral energy distribution (SED) shapes and emission lines. These low- z LRDs share the hallmark properties of their high- z counterparts: compact morphology, V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme decrements (median H α /H β ∼ 15), frequent Balmer absorption (70%), and blackbody-like optical-to-near-IR continua. All have low metallicity, occupy the same regions in the BPT diagram as high- z LRDs, and have softer ionizing spectra than typical AGNs. The consistency between low- z and high- z LRD properties indicates the same physical processes at work. The correlation between broad-line Balmer luminosity and L 5100 deviates from that of local type-1 AGNs, limiting the direct application of local BH mass calibrations. Ionized [O iii ] outflows are ubiquitous (78%). One LRD at z = 0.196, J1717+3807, shows robust long-term variability in the i and Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) bands. The optical-to-near-IR continua of LRDs reveal a wide range of temperatures ∼2000–4700 K (peak 0.6–1.4 μ m), with a subset showing cooler and larger envelopes than those at high z . Low- z LRDs serve not only as proximate laboratories for probing the nature of LRDs, but also trace the cosmic evolution of this population from the cosmic dawn to the present day.

items.title: Revealing a multi-zone circumnuclear dust response in UGC 11487 through phase-resolved WISE W1--W2 diagnostics
items.abstract: Mid-infrared (MIR) flares trace dust reprocessing in obscured tidal disruption event (TDE) candidates, especially when the primary optical or ultraviolet flare is weak, missed, or strongly obscured. We investigate the phase-dependent W1--W2 evolution of the MIR-selected TDE candidate UGC 11487 (WTP14adeqka) and test whether its infrared behavior can be described by a single self-similar MIR response or requires a structured circumnuclear dust response. For the first time, we performed a phase-resolved analysis of the WISE/NEOWISE W1--W2 evolution of UGC 11487 (WTP14adeqka) over 2014--2024. We combined empirical W1--W2 timing, color, and flux diagnostics with phenomenological modeling and axisymmetric dust radiative-transfer calculations driven by hydrodynamically motivated fallback histories. We also constructed an aperture-matched ultraviolet-to-radio spectral energy distribution of the host galaxy. UGC 11487 exhibits a decade-long MIR flare characterized by a delayed and broader W2 response, color hysteresis, and systematic cooling from sim900 K to sim500--600 K. Observed-window positive-fluence centroids give a W2--W1 centroid offset of Δ t_ ̊m cent =224 d, corresponding to an effective differential response scale of 0.188 $, and the integrated IR energy is $(2.9--3.8) pc. The effective infrared luminosity reaches erg s -1 erg. A single fixed-color phenomenological component is strongly disfavored ( =281.7$); the preferred compact description is a two-component phenomenological model. Two physical dust-echo solutions with different fallback histories reproduce the broad W1 and $W2 light-curve evolution through compact and extended dust populations. The host is a moderately star-forming isolated barred disk, modeled under an absent or weak persistent active galactic nucleus assumption. ̊m BIC The MIR evolution suggests an obscured TDE-like accretion transient reprocessed by a spatially and thermally distributed dust population. Phase-resolved WISE diagnostics constrain differential interband response scales, while radiative-transfer modeling connects the observed evolution to the source history and dust geometry. The two-band data admit multiple physical solutions.

items.title: Probing the baryonic--dark matter connection in galaxy clusters using X-rays with gated recurrent unit neural networks
items.abstract: Precise mass measurements are essential for cosmology, but traditional hydrostatic equilibrium (HSE) methods are prone to bias, particularly in dynamically disturbed systems. In this work, we introduce a deep learning approach based on a novel gated recurrent unit (GRU) that predicts the total three-dimensional mass profiles of galaxy clusters directly from the spherically symmetric radial profiles of the intracluster medium (ICM), including temperature, density, pressure, and enclosed gas mass. Treating these radial profiles as sequential data allows the GRU to capture physically motivated dependencies across radii while naturally handling profiles with different numbers of radial bins. We trained and validated our model on high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations from þethree, achieving a 1σ scatter of sim5% in cluster mass predictions from idealised three-dimensional profiles over most of the cluster region, which is substantially lower than what would be obtained with conventional HSE mass estimates. The model also provides robust radius-dependent uncertainty estimates, while observational uncertainties can be incorporated through a Monte Carlo approach. Our algorithm demonstrates robustness against variations in data quality and cluster morphology. We further demonstrate that the model generalises well across independent hydrodynamical simulation suites (GIZMO-SIMBA and GADGET-X) when trained jointly, recovering unbiased mass profiles in both cases. Feature importance analysis shows that enclosed gas mass dominates the predictions, with pressure and temperature shaping the radial structure, reflecting physically meaningful mass assembly. To examine mass estimates for observational data, we applied the GRU approach to the REXCESS and X-COP galaxy cluster samples observed with XMM-Newton. The GRU and HSE mass estimates show close agreement for the lower-mass REXCESS sample, while HSE masses are systematically lower than the GRU predictions for the higher-mass X-COP sample, an offset consistent with hydrostatic mass bias. This approach provides a powerful data-driven framework for precise and unbiased cluster mass estimation, bridging simulations and observations to improve the accuracy of cluster-based cosmological studies. Moreover, it can be readily extended to Sunyaev–Zel'dovich and optical datasets, making it a versatile tool for multi-wavelength cluster mass inference.

items.title: Time-Reversal Invariant Topological Photonic Alloy
items.abstract: Abstract Conventional approaches generate quantum spin Hall (QSH) and quantum valley Hall (QVH) effects by breaking spatial inversion symmetry across the entire photonic crystal. Modulating the bulk transmission gaps within such periodic frameworks has traditionally relied on the global modification of structural parameters throughout the lattice, which often presents substantial challenges for device reconfigurability and postfabrication adaptability. While recent advances have begun to explore localized tuning mechanisms to overcome these limitations, in this work, we demonstrate a fundamentally distinct mechanism for generating topology: the random, local breaking of crystalline spatial symmetries in a reciprocal photonic alloy. Using a photonic alloy platform based on random substitutional disorder in a parallel-plate metal waveguide, we show that disorder-driven local breaking of z-direction mirror and in-plane symmetries can open topological gaps to trigger QSH and QVH phase transitions, respectively. Importantly, this symmetry-engineered disorder manifests exclusively as diagonal perturbations, inherently suppressing backscattering in interspin/valley channels and thereby supporting robust helical edge states and valley kink states. Rigorous topological characterization via an improved, mode-mixing-free reflection-phase winding method reveals a striking size-dependent scaling behavior in both configurations, where the threshold doping concentration required to trigger the topological phase transition asymptotically vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. By enabling flexible, on-demand bulk gap engineering simply through random doping tuning─rather than relying on magnetic constituents or global structural reconfigurations─this photonic alloy platform not only deepens understanding of disorder-induced topological physics but also offers a scalable, highly efficient design strategy for integrated topological optical communications.

items.title: Tidal deformation of an accreting compact object
items.abstract: Tidal deformation of a compact object serves as a sensitive probe of the strong-gravity regime and nature of the compact object. It captures how a compact object responds to the external perturbing field of a companion. In realistic astrophysical settings, compact objects are typically immersed in matter-rich environments, which can significantly alter the response. In this work, we investigate the static deformability of Schwarzschild-like exotic compact objects (ECOs) embedded in a quasi-stationary, self-gravitating thin accretion disk. By modelling the external spacetime with a relativistic thin-disk solution, we isolate environmental contributions to the scalar and spin-1 response while maintaining analytical control. We show that, for perfectly reflecting ECOs, the characteristic logarithmic dependence of the scalar and spin-1 response on compactness, set by near-horizon physics, remains intact even in the presence of accretion. The disk primarily amplifies the overall magnitude of the response significantly. These findings highlight that environmental effects can seriously impact tidal signatures, while still permitting, under suitable conditions, the distinguishability of horizonless compact objects from black holes in gravitational-wave observations.

items.title: First Fast Radio Burst Search Campaign at the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy
items.abstract: Abstract Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are intense millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin whose physical nature remains under investigation, and which also probe the intergalactic medium. We report on the first FRB search campaign carried out at the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy (IAR), between 2024 December and 2026 March, targeting nearby galaxy superclusters in the southern sky. We observed fields in the Ophiuchus, Shapley, and Sculptor/Phoenix supercluster regions with one of the two 30 m antennas of the IAR, using a ROACH-based backend with 400 MHz of bandwidth centered at 1400 MHz and a time resolution of 41–82 μ s, for a total net observing time of 212 hr. The data were searched for dispersed single pulses with PRESTO in the dispersion measure (DM) range of 100 ≤ DM ≤ 500 pc cm −3 , and candidates were classified with the FETCH machine learning classifier, validated on archival Parkes data containing known FRBs and on synthetic bursts injected into IAR observations. One FRB candidate, FRB 20251018, was identified on 2025 October 18 in an observation pointed toward the galaxy cluster A2870, in the Phoenix supercluster, with a DM of 243 ± 20 pc cm −3 , a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.2, and a FETCH score of p = 0.99. To the best of our knowledge, it would, if confirmed, be the first FRB detected from South America. A set of more marginal candidates is also presented. These results demonstrate the capability of the IAR antennas to detect FRBs and support extending the monitoring campaign to coincident dual-antenna observations and crossmatches with gravitational-wave events and electromagnetic transients.

items.title: A unified modeling of X-ray and gamma-ray spectro-polarimetric data: The case of Cygnus X-1
items.abstract: With the advent of new instrumentation, the available spectro-polarimetric measurements in the X-ray and gamma-ray domains have increased significantly. For black-hole X-ray binaries such as Cygnus X-1, a clear discrepancy between the independent measurements of X-ray and soft-γ-ray polarization has emerged. This discrepancy challenges our understanding of the accretion process and emission mechanisms, including acceleration processes at play and the geometry of the system. We thus aim to develop a general-purpose method to model the broadband, high-energy spectro-polarimetric data. Our novel approach makes it possible to simultaneously fit the spectral and polarization data from independent instruments in different energy bands. Measurements with widely different energy bin sizes and statistical significances are combined in a robust and statistically sound way in a single fit, taking into account energy-dependent polarization mixing from different model components. We applied our method to the spectro-polarimetric data of the black-hole X-ray binary Cygnus X-1 in the 2,keV--2,MeV range and show that it enables us to describe the shape of the elusive soft γ-rays' hard tail with unprecedented quality and in exceptional detail. We constrained the photon cutoff energy from optically thin synchrotron emission at $( _ + - ) $. Using this value, we discuss the origin of the nonthermal electrons in the context of Bohm diffusion and synchrotron cooling. We further provide a new explanation for the misalignment of the polarization of the synchrotron hard tail compared to the jet axis based on magnetic-field helicity and Doppler boosting. Overall, our new approach offers a simple and straightforward way to apply models to diverse spectro-polarimetric data for the broader community. 10^ 2 keV

items.title: Schwarzschild perturbations in Lorenz gauge via elliptic differential equations
items.abstract: Accurate predictions of gravitational wave signals from asymmetric compact binaries are accessible through black hole perturbation theory and self-force calculations. Faithful waveform models will require contributions from first- and second-order terms in the small mass-ratio expansion. The problem of second-order Kerr perturbations is exacerbated by non-separability of the metric perturbation equations and non-linear mode coupling, which motivates this $m$-mode approach. This work moves towards the eventual goal of second-order Kerr perturbations by calculating first-order Schwarzschild metric perturbations via $m$-modes in the frequency domain for the first time. We solve the Lorenz gauge field equations as a system of coupled elliptic partial differential equations that govern each $m$-mode. Our Mathematica code implements a second-order finite difference representation of the field equations, which we solve as a sparse linear algebra problem. Regularization near the small body is achieved through the effective source method, and our presentation introduces a new puncture expansion of the singular field for a point mass in Kerr spacetime. Issues related to problematic near-horizon behavior are explored and then mitigated by applying sophisticated near-horizon boundary conditions. Our results illustrate the features of each component and $m$-mode of the metric perturbation, and we are able to calculate gravitational wave energy fluxes with sufficient accuracy to enable future second-order self-force calculations.

items.title: Two-fluid Schwarzschild solution
items.abstract: Abstract We consider the interior two-fluid Schwarzschild solution. That is a model of compact (neutron) stars with admixed dark matter. The two constant energy densities generalize the interior Schwarschild solution to the case of two fluids (representing standard model matter and dark matter, for instance), interacting mutually solely by the common gravitational field. In general, the two-fluid core is surrounded by a one-fluid corona (envelope). Only for special parameters (the model depends on energy densities $$e_1,e_2$$ e 1 , e 2 and central pressures $$p_{\textrm{c}1},p_{\textrm{c}2}$$ p c 1 , p c 2 of the fluids), both fluids occupy the same region. Despite the sum of two energy densities in that region, the compactness bound of 4/9 is not exceeded. Therefore, a Buchdahl limit for two fluids holds. A conceivable object is one with a stark leakage of one fluid (e.g. dark matter) beyond the two-fluid core.

items.title: Stellar Flares Rather than High T int as Possible Cause for the Missing Methane in Young Exoplanets: The Case Study of V1298 Tau b
items.abstract: Abstract Recent observations of V1298 Tau b, a warm sub-Neptune ( R = 9.85 ± 0.3 R ⊕ , M = 13.1 ± 5.3 M ⊕ , T eq = 670 K) orbiting a young (10–30 Myr) K star, show depleted methane and surprising abundances of CO 2 in its atmosphere. This makes the planet an interesting target to study the “missing methane problem,” where Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer, and JWST have revealed many sub-Jovian planets with effective temperatures cooler than 800 K to be depleted in methane compared to equilibrium chemistry predictions. On V1298 Tau b, an intrinsic temperature ( T int ) of 500 K is required to explain the methane depletion if strong mixing from a warm interior is the reason for the missing methane, but this T int is too large for a planet of its age and size according to standard interior structure evolution theories. Here, we show that stellar flares can result in methane depletion in a warm planet’s atmosphere with nominal T int ∼ 100 K. During a stellar flare, fast methane photolysis rates cannot be balanced by diffusion from below into the upper atmospheric layers probed by observations. Young active stars flare frequently, and we show that the timescale of diffusion for the methane to recover from a flare-induced depletion can be slow compared to the flare frequency. Over time, the atmosphere reaches a new steady state set by the average flare frequency and energy. This new steady state shows depleted methane in the 2 mbar region, and abundant CO, CO 2 , and HCN, which results in synthetic transmission spectra that reproduce the main features of the recent JWST observations of V1298 Tau b.

items.title: Distinguishing lensing and precessional modulation in binary black-hole inspiral waveforms
items.abstract: Binary black holes (BBHs) emit gravitational waves (GWs) as they inspiral towards merger. These GWs can be gravitationally lensed by large-scale structure along the line of sight, potentially creating multiple images of the same source with fixed time delays determined by the lensing geometry. As the BBHs inspiral, the GW frequency increases, leading to successive constructive and destructive interference between the multiple images. BBHs also have spins $\mathbf{S}_i$ that may be misaligned with their orbital angular momentum $\mathbf{L}$. As the BBHs inspiral, these misaligned spins cause $\mathbf{L}$ to precess about the total angular momentum $\mathbf{J}$, modulating the GW emission similar to pulsar emission resulting from a misaligned jet rotating in and out of the line of sight. We investigate the ability of a single L-shaped GW detector to distinguish between these two sources of modulation. We find that precessional modulation can mimic the lensing modulation between two images with comparable magnifications when the time delay between the images is short enough that fewer than three interference fringes occur during the time the GW signal spends in the sensitivity band of the detector. As strong lensing is rare for GW sources at moderate redshift while misaligned spins are common for BBHs produced in certain formation channels, ruling out precessional modulation is essential to identifying genuinely lensed systems.

items.title: A Very Fast Symplectic Integrator for Planetary Systems: WHFast512 in x86 Assembly
items.abstract: Abstract Long-term integrations of planetary systems are used in a variety of astrophysical applications, for example, to determine a system’s stability. In this paper, we describe significant speed and accuracy improvements to the WHFast512 integrator. By completely rewriting WHFast512 in x86 assembly, we gain fine-grained control over CPU instructions and are able to keep the entire simulation state in CPU registers, only writing to memory when an output is required. We also reduce the number of branches in the code, improve the Kepler solver’s speed and accuracy with a convergence check, switch the Hamiltonian splitting to Jacobi coordinates, implement symplectic correctors, and add support for ejection and collision detection. As a benchmark, we run simulations of the solar system with all eight planets and general relativistic corrections for 5 Gyr. With our improvements, we can integrate this system in 9 hr, more than 8× faster than the standard version of WHFast . This makes WHFast512 by far the fastest N -body integrator for this kind of simulation. We run extensive tests to verify the integrator’s accuracy, with a particular focus on removing any long-term bias, and show that the accuracy is now 5 orders of magnitude better for typical setups compared to the earlier version of WHFast512 . The new WHFast512 integrator is freely available in the REBOUND integrator package.

items.title: Fast and Furious—High-velocity Features of Ca and Si in the Spectra of Type Ia Supernovae*
items.abstract: Abstract High-velocity absorption lines of Ca II and Si II (high-velocity features (HVFs)) are common in the early spectra of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), but their physical origin is still poorly understood. We used 181 optical spectra of 56 SNe Ia that show HVFs in at least the Ca II near-infrared (NIR) triplet to better understand the nature of HVFs. To model the profiles of HVFs we applied Gaussian fitting as well as spectrum synthesis modeling with the SYNOW code. We found that Gaussian fitting usually underestimates the velocity of HVFs compared to SYNOW, and derived a linear formula for correction. In accord with many previous studies, the observed properties of HVFs (velocity, strength, and duration) were found to correlate with the general observables of SNe Ia (decline rate and spectral subtype). Brighter, slow-declining supernovae usually exhibit stronger, higher-velocity HVFs, while fainter objects typically show weak, low-velocity HVFs. SNe Ia in early-type galaxies showed weaker and slower HVFs compared to events in late-type galaxies in our sample. Comparing these observational findings with theoretical predictions, we conclude that the overall physical picture of HVFs is quite complex, and could be explained by multiple models. A double-detonation explosion model is promising as it is inherently capable of explaining the creation of high-velocity shells that may produce HVFs, but an asymmetric delayed detonation model or interaction with circumstellar material cannot be ruled out.
