items.title: The 200–300 GHz Survey for 18 Class II Disks in the Ophiuchus Star-forming Complex
items.abstract: Abstract We measured the 198–310 GHz flux densities of 18 Class II protoplanetary disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming complex using the Submillimeter Array (SMA). The ∼200–300 GHz spectral indices ( α 200−300 ) of these disks are 2.3 − 0.5 + 0.2 . In this observed frequency range, emission properties of the Ophiuchus disks are very similar to the 48 spatially compact Class II disks in the Taurus-Auriga region observed in a previous SMA survey. Combining the Ophiuchus and Taurus-Auriga samples, the Pearson correlation coefficient between α 200−300 and the flux density at 250 GHz ( F 250GHz ) is 0.27 ( p = 0.02). We do not find a convincing correlation between α 200−300 and the R 95% radius of the disks. Our interpretation for the α 200−300 values being close to 2 in the spatially compact disks is that at ≳200 GHz frequencies, the continuum emission in these disks is dominated by optically thick dust thermal emission, independent of F 250GHz and R 95% . As a result, the (sub)millimeter luminosity and the apparent disk size are positively correlated, which has been found in numerous resolved emission surveys of Class II disks. In young clusters with ages of ∼1–2 Myr, Class II disks with smaller radii or lower (sub)millimeter luminosities are not necessarily those in which the dust mass budget has been consumed or dispersed.

items.title: Wind-Fed Magnetic Flux and the Emergence of X-ray Coronae in Active Galactic Nuclei
items.abstract: Abstract We propose a scenario for the onset of radiatively efficient Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) in which circumnuclear stellar and supernova-driven winds supply mass and partially ordered magnetic flux to a compact disk reservoir around a supermassive black hole. A coherent poloidal component surviving advection to small radii strengthens inward, lowering the gas plasma beta until mean Maxwell stresses overtake MRI turbulence, compress the disk vertically, and open a magnetically dominated wedge above it. Within a quasi-force-free description of this wedge, the field self-organizes toward a critical twist at which the net radial transport changes sign, defining a magnetic saturation radius rc ∼ 10 rg. The magnetic squeezing of the disk fixes the pressure balance at the interface between the disk and wedge, confining the accumulated flux at rc: flux advected toward this boundary is preferentially shed, fixing Br∝r−2 in the interior. From the field topology alone we then derive a normalized saturation flux φ ∼ 50, consistent with the MAD plateau of GRMHD simulations. The resulting compact, time-dependent saturation region is a natural candidate for the AGN X-ray corona, being collisionless, magnetized, and, at high compactness, plausibly pair-rich, with hadronic pair injection providing a conditional additional channel. Its size, variability, and spectral hardness are controlled by rc, the compactness, and the magnetization. We connect these scalings to observed coronal sizes, variability, and the power partition between the corona and jet. We further propose that Little Red and Blue Dots could represent a disk-reservoir phase preceding luminous AGN activity.

items.title: Understanding How Coronal Heating and Magnetic Field Scaling Affect Global Properties of the Low and Middle Corona
items.abstract: Abstract The magnetic field of the Sun is a key driver of coronal heating and solar wind acceleration. In tandem, these influence the observable morphology of the corona, along with defining the magnetic connectivity and magnitude of open magnetic flux. Here, we investigate how coronal heating affects the magnetothermal state of the 3D global corona by analyzing a series of data-constrained, thermodynamic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations for solar minimum conditions. We vary the overall heat deposited in the corona via modifying the input Poynting flux of a wave-turbulence-driven (WTD) model for coronal heating and by scaling the inner boundary magnetic field. We quantify the magnetic, thermodynamic, and combined magnetothermal effects on our simulations. We find that increasing the overall amount of heat leads to a higher magnitude of open flux and a more visibly open white-light morphology in the K-Corona between 1.5 and 6 R ⊙ . We quantify how plasma β evolves and drives morphological differences between simulations. We also compare these runs to an extremely high-resolution reference solution that includes small-scale magnetic information in the surface boundary condition. This latter comparison provides insight into the further development of “subgrid” corrections for low(er) resolution models to best represent the structure and observables of the corona and inner heliosphere.

items.title: Ultraviolet instruments on the Habitable Worlds Observatory: considerations and capability trades on the multi-object, integral-field, and high-resolution modes of a potential ultraviolet instrument
items.abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is NASA’s next-generation astrophysics platform, delivering transformative capability in the search for life and study of the origins of the universe. Among the instruments under consideration for HWO is a multipurpose ultraviolet spectrograph and imager that provides a deep toolbox for some of the most pressing science investigations of the next several decades. We present a basic draft model of a potential UVI, including a multi-object spectrograph, far ultraviolet imager, high-resolution spectrograph, and integral-field spectrograph. The draft designs for these channels of the UV instrument serve as a basis for a general discussion of the instrument architecture and design challenges while also identifying potential trades, enhancements, and other considerations that the HWO project will need to address as it moves into the formulation phase. We conclude with a presentation of several scientific simulations that have helped guide the capabilities of the draft design. We intended to serve as a summary of UV instrument modes, technology, and potential design ahead of planned instrument studies in the late 2020s and then phase A in the early 2030s.

items.title: Tracing the Influence of Distant companions on Exoplanetary Systems (TIDES). I. Highly Eccentric and Misaligned Binary Companions to Hot Jupiters
items.abstract: Abstract The origin of hot Jupiters remains an open question. A significant fraction reside in binary or multiple star systems, suggesting that stellar companions may play an important role in shaping their present-day architectures. However, the orbits of the vast majority of these stellar companions remain poorly constrained, leaving their role in hot Jupiter evolution an open question. We present the Tracing the Influence of Distant companions on Exoplanetary Systems (TIDES) survey, a campaign to map the orbits of stellar companions in systems hosting hot Jupiters to assess the extent to which binaries play a role in hot Jupiter formation and migration. Here, we introduce our survey design and new orbital fits for the first six systems in our sample— τ Boo, WASP-2, WASP-11, WASP-76, HAT-P-14, and HAT-P-16—by combining previous observations of the stellar companions together with new Keck/NIRC2 imaging and Keck Planet Imager and Characterizer (KPIC) relative radial velocities. Among these six systems, the four with the most precisely constrained orbits exhibit high eccentricities ( e ≥ 0.8), and three of these systems also display significant planet–binary misalignments (Δ i ≥ 20°). This suggests the orbital properties of stellar companions to hot Jupiter host stars are qualitatively different than field binaries and binaries hosting inner transiting small planets. These orbital architectures are consistent with stellar companions shaping the evolution of hot Jupiters, either through high-eccentricity migration or by participating in an earlier episode of dynamical evolution that ultimately led to hot-Jupiter formation. Continued orbital monitoring of the full sample will reveal whether outer stellar companions play a causal role in the evolution of hot Jupiters.

items.title: First L-type Substellar Object Discovered in the Vicinity of the Embedded Cluster NGC 2023
items.abstract: Abstract We present the first substellar object in a star-forming region spectroscopically confirmed with Euclid, namely J054158.70-021031.4. This young and faint source is located close to the embedded open cluster NGC 2023. It has a spectral type of L3, a reddening of A V = 3 mag, proper motion consistent with the nearby cluster NGC 2024, and a magnitude of ∼24.5 in the Euclid optical band. At the distance of 403 pc, its inferred mass lies close to the planetary-mass boundary. We discovered the object by searching for ultracool dwarf candidates in the Euclid Early Release Observations. The search was based on photometric criteria, followed by the analysis of slitless 2D spectroimages in order to distinguish features that indicate the nature of these objects. This work demonstrates the potential of Euclid to unveil previously hidden populations of very low-mass objects, located in obscured regions where star formation is ongoing.

items.title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-Ray Weakness
items.abstract: Abstract A major question about JWST’s little red dots (LRDs) at z ∼ 4−8 is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broadband limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At z ∼ 0.3, similarly luminous sources require ∼10 3−4 less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six “local little red dots” (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: “X-normal” LLRDs resemble type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas “X-weak” stack lies ∼0.5–0.7 dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at ∼3.3 σ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame ∼2−3 keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona (Δ α ox ∼ −0.1 to −0.2) with Compton-thin absorption ( N H ∼ 10 22−23 cm −2 ), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

items.title: PeV Diffuse Neutrinos from Magnetically Arrested Disks in Low-luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei
items.abstract: Abstract Radiatively inefficient accretion flows (RIAFs) in low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) are promising candidates for the PeV astrophysical diffuse neutrino background (DNB), but how the magnetically arrested disk (MAD) state affects their neutrino output and what fraction of LLAGNs are in this state remain unclear. We present a comprehensive study of diffuse neutrino emission from the inner accretion flows of LLAGNs in the MAD state, including all three flavors and both hadronuclear ( pp ) and photohadronic ( pγ ) production channels. Assuming that ∼5% of the accretion power is transferred to nonthermal protons, current IceCube data allow at most 2.3 × 10 −3 of LLAGNs to have their inner accretion flows in an MAD state that can produce high-energy neutrinos. A lower fraction of the accretion power transferred to nonthermal protons would allow a proportionally larger fraction of such LLAGNs. Assuming that the comoving number density of low-excitation radio galaxies (LERGs) approximately matches that of LLAGNs in the MAD state, we also estimate an MAD fraction of ≃1.6 × 10 −3 . The corresponding diffuse intensity is compatible with current IceCube data and testable by IceCube-Gen2. For this MAD fraction, the all-flavor diffuse intensity peaks at E ν ≃ 1.5 PeV, with E ν 2 Φ ν ≃ 2.6 × 1 0 − 9 GeV cm − 2 s − 1 sr − 1 . Current IceCube data are beginning to challenge several predictions from previous LLAGN RIAF models, and the MAD component can become the dominant contribution from LLAGN accretion flows beyond the cutoffs of most earlier RIAF spectra considered here.

items.title: NOEMA Observations of the Center of M33: A Parsec-scale Molecular Filament and an Ordered Gas–Star Formation Sequence
items.abstract: Abstract We present NOEMA CO(1–0) observations of the inner ∼500 pc of M33 at a resolution of 0 . ″ 91 × 0 . ″ 37 (3.7 × 1.5 pc), resolving the compact molecular gas structures and revealing their relation to recent massive star formation. The most prominent structure is a southeastern (SE) molecular filament that extends 76 pc along its principal axis, is 23 pc wide, and contains three CO-bright knots. Across eight independent transverse cuts, the adjacent H α ridge is displaced preferentially to one side of the principal CO ridge by a median of 10 . 0 − 1.4 + 0.9 pc. Young OB candidates are more closely associated with H α than with compact CO. The filament shows little velocity change along its length but a resolved gradient across its minor axis. Its elongated morphology, transverse kinematics, and ordered CO–H α distribution are consistent with locally asymmetric molecular-gas compression and subsequent massive star formation. Across the wider field, 23 well-measured compact clumps have a median radius of 2.67 pc and a median velocity dispersion of 2.15 km s −1 . Their line width and apparent virial-parameter distributions show no clear difference between the SE filament and the rest of the field. Although the local spiral potential and pattern speed remain unconstrained, the observations provide a resolved view of a compression-compatible molecular-to-ionized-gas sequence in the center of M33.

items.title: Status and prospects of the TAMBO project and the TAMBITO R&D prototype
items.abstract: The detection of astrophysical PeV-scale neutrinos by IceCube and KM3NeT observatories has opened the window to probe new phenomena in the universe. However, a deeper study of the sources remains limited by the small astrophysical flux and the sizable atmospheric neutrino background. The Tau Air-Shower Mountain-Based Observatory (TAMBO) aims to overcome these limitations by detecting tau neutrinos from 1 PeV to 1 000 PeV, an energy range in which backgrounds are largely suppressed and which lies between the reach of optical-Cherenkov observatories and that of radio-based experiments. TAMBO will employ up to 5,000 particle detectors installed on the face of a steep hill in the Colca Valley (Perú) to detect tau neutrinos interacting with the face of the canyon in front via the decay products of the associated tau leptons. In this contribution, we will describe the current status of the project and its R&D, focusing on the 100-unit array TAMBITO prototype, the projected timeline, and the physics potential that this unique detector brings to the field.

items.title: Mean-element Parareal: Parallel-in-Time Integration of the Solar System
items.abstract: Abstract Long-term integrations of planetary systems have long been considered inherently sequential: each time step must start from the \emph{exact} state at the end of the previous one, because any error in that state, however small, is amplified by orbital shear and chaos and alters the trajectory. Because a single step of a modern Wisdom--Holman integrator takes only $\sim$100\,ns---too short to split across cores---additional cores have previously only been used to run multiple simulations in parallel. We introduce mean-element parareal (MEP), a parallel-in-time scheme that accelerates a single Solar System integration (eight planets, general relativity) at the same accuracy as the serial integrator. Combined with a latency-optimized C kernel that integrates 5\,Gyr on one core in 5.8\,h, MEP completes a 5\,Gyr integration in 52\,min on 64 cores (a parallel speed-up of $6.7\times$, and $10.4\times$ faster than the previous 9.0\,h single-core record) or in 1.8\,h on 16 cores ($3.3\times$ parallel speed-up, $5.0\times$ faster than the previous record). MEP succeeds because its coarse propagator uses a numerical first-order mean-element theory to remove the short-period oscillations from the semi-major axes, preventing Keplerian shear from amplifying them into growing phase errors. Standard parareal with a coarse Wisdom--Holman integrator fails for planetary orbits because no inexpensive coarse integrator can resolve these oscillations. To our knowledge, this is the first measured multicore speed-up of a single long-term planetary integration and opens a pathway towards larger-scale parallelization. MEP is freely available in Parachron, a modified version of \rebound{}, at \url{https://github.com/hippke/parachron}.

items.title: Naturalization of Vinti’s intermediary orbit—or how to get rid of small divisors in Brouwer’s satellite solution
items.abstract: Abstract A naturalization, in the sense of Deprit, of Vinti’s dynamical system makes the construction of a first order analytical satellite perturbation solution without critical divisors possible. The process gives hints on how to recast Brouwer’s classical solution in a form that is free from small divisors too. The functionality of classical perturbation solutions is in this way extended to the close vicinity of the critical inclination. The new analytical solution bears terms that may grow unbounded, but their negative effects do not disclose in time intervals in which this kind of solution may be useful in practice.

items.title: Jets and winds from the most powerful compact object in NGC 5408
items.abstract: Super-critical accretion onto stellar-mass compact objects is sometimes revealed by ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs). In other cases, X-rays are heavily obscured along our line of sight, but a super-Eddington accretion power can be indirectly revealed by multi-band studies. We have identified a candidate super-critical source in NGC,5408 (labelled X-2). We argue that it is powered by accretion; it is among the most powerful in the local Universe, despite its apparent X-ray faintness; and it has exceptional optical properties (both in the continuum and in the lines). We carried out a multi-band imaging and spectral study with the Australia Telescope Compact Array, the Very Large Array, the Space Telescope, the Very Large Telescope, and the X-ray Observatory. Hubble Chandra We found an unresolved source with variable radio emission (5 GHz luminosity of a few times 10^ 35 erg s -1 $); red optical continuum with absolute magnitudes M_ V,0 ≈ -9.1, M_ I,0 II łambda4686; point-like hard X-ray emission; and marginally resolved soft X-ray emission. We also found an ≈20-pc He^++ nebula near X-2 associated with candidate Wolf-Rayet stars. The optical continuum declined by 2 mag between 2010 and 2024 as did the intensity of the broad and narrow lines. We argue that the system is powered by the radiative and mechanical output of a super-Eddington stellar mass black hole and estimate an accretion power of ≳10^40 erg s$^ -1 . We propose that X-2 is a Compton-thick ULX seen at high inclination with a flaring jet and X-ray emission emerging from the polar funnel. We argue that the optical continuum and the broad emission lines are signatures of an optically thick outflow launched either from the accretion disk or from an luminous blue variable-like donor star, but more speculatively, we posit that it was caused by the long sought-for, elusive phase of common envelope ejection. We suggest that X-2 is undergoing a short-lived phase of hyper-Eddington accretion.

items.title: Sex differences in fibrillar collagen composition are linked to subcutaneous adipose tissue expandability and adipocyte precursor proliferation.
items.abstract: Background Physiological expansion of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) protects against harmful lipid deposition and metabolic disease and is generally greater in women than men. We hypothesised that sex differences in fibrillar collagen composition and remodelling contribute to differences in SAT expansion and function. Methods SAT from age- and BMI-matched men and women, SAT from male and female mice exposed to a high-fat diet to induce adipose tissue expansion and obesity, and publicly available human SAT and VAT RNA sequencing data sets were analysed. SAT was assessed by proteomics, histology, Western blot, qRT-PCR and flow cytometry. The 3T3-L1 preadipocyte cell line was used to test the effect of altered collagen type 1-to-3 ratio. Results Men showed greater SAT fibrosis than women. Fibrillar collagen levels correlated negatively with BMI in women but positively with cholesterol and liver enzyme levels in men. Despite similar adiposity, HFD-induced obese female mice had healthier metabolic profiles and fewer fibroinflammatory SAT changes than males. HFD preferentially induced Col1a1 in males and Col3a1 in females. Unchallenged male mice had a higher collagen type 1-to-3 ratio than females, and a similar sex difference was observed in humans. A lower, female-like collagen type 1-to-3 ratio increased preadipocyte proliferation. Consistently, acute HFD increased proliferation of SAT PDGFRβ + adipogenic stem cells in females only. Conclusions Sex differences in fibrillar collagen composition and remodelling may promote greater SAT expansion in females by facilitating adipogenic precursor proliferation and limiting fibroinflammatory changes during obesity.

items.title: Neural mechanisms of information sharing intention under known and unknown veracity: A dual-process model incorporating impression management.
items.abstract: Existing research has primarily focused on information judgments, with relatively little attention paid to the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying information sharing. The dual-process model has mainly been applied to explain information judgment processes, and its applicability to information sharing intention remains to be systematically examined. To address this gap, the present study employed functional magnetic resonance imaging to investigate information sharing intentions and neural mechanisms under unknown and known veracity knowledge states (N = 43). The results showed that veracity knowledge states significantly influenced information sharing intentions, which is moderated by information valence and morality rating. In the unknown veracity condition, neural activity more strongly consistent with heuristic and affective processing, with significant activation in the temporal pole (TP), fusiform gyrus (FG), and lingual gyrus (LG). In the known veracity condition, neural activity more strongly consistent with analytical and social cognitive processing, with significant activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), temporoparietal junction (TPJ), and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Furthermore, the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) was considered the core brain region involved in information sharing intention. Together, this study contributes to extending dual-process models to the domain of information sharing from the impression management perspective.

items.title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders.
items.abstract: Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood-brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental-immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

items.title: "Everyone Has Complex Trauma": New Alliances, Rising Markets, and Emerging Therapeutic Challenges in the Treatment of Young Offenders in Chile.
items.abstract: This article examines the growing centrality of the clinical category of complex trauma within the Chilean juvenile justice system, analyzing its reception, dissemination, and effects on professional practice. Drawing on twelve months of ethnographic fieldwork in a Juvenile Probation Service in Santiago de Chile, the study shows how the discourse of complex trauma has fostered new institutional alliances, shaped an emerging educational market for professional training, and generated therapeutic challenges in interventions with young offenders. Despite the growing traction of developmental neuroscience as a principal explanation for the sequelae of childhood adversities, practitioners pragmatically combine neurobiological, psychological, psychodynamic, and moral reasoning in their daily work to address offenders' suffering. In doing so, they continuously place notions of guilt, culpability, responsibility, and agency into tension, redefining them. The findings suggest that the expansion of complex trauma transcends the clinical domain, engaging political, economic, and cultural dimensions that reconfigure the relationships between victimization, delinquency, and social reintegration. The article concludes that complex trauma has not only redefined the etiology of juvenile delinquency but also reshaped the criteria through which culpability and the potential for redemption are determined, thereby redrawing the boundaries of institutional interventions.

items.title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction.
items.abstract: Delirium is a frequent and distressing neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by acute disturbances of attention, awareness and cognition. Delirium emerges in response to diverse medical insults, particularly in hospitalized patients. Despite its high prevalence and association with accelerated cognitive decline, dementia and mortality, the neurobiology of delirium remains incompletely understood, and there are no treatments for delirium. Evidence from electrophysiology, neuroimaging, biomarkers and emerging animal models has begun to clarify the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying delirium. Delirium can be conceptualized as the interaction of acute systemic or cerebral stressors with pre-existing vulnerabilities, creating a 'perfect storm' for brain dysfunction. Generalized electroencephalographic slowing and network disintegration are convergent signatures across diverse types of delirium. Disruptions in neuromodulatory systems, energy metabolism and neuroimmune signalling may underlie impairment of large-scale brain function. The mechanisms that drive acute delirium may also contribute to subsequent brain injury and long-term decline, compounding its broad personal and societal impact.

items.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
items.abstract: Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

items.title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: 2-AG as a potential biomarker for predicting response to short-term fluoxetine treatment in a mouse model of depression.
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex psychiatric condition with significant individual and social impact and marked variability in treatment response. Identifying biomarkers that predict antidepressant efficacy remains a major challenge, and metabolomic approaches offer a powerful tool to uncover biochemical changes associated with depression and treatment outcome. The prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus are key brain regions involved in the pathophysiology of MDD and antidepressant response. Fluoxetine, one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressants, influences not only serotonergic signaling but also the endocannabinoid system. Accordingly, evaluating endocannabinoid levels might provide critical insight into their contribution and the effect of fluoxetine. To identify biomarkers associated with early antidepressant response, male mice were exposed for 5 weeks to the chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) protocol, with fluoxetine treatment administered during the final week. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analyses of hippocampal and prefrontal cortex samples revealed that behavioral improvement following short-term fluoxetine treatment was accompanied by increased hippocampal 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), along with reduced GABA and glutamate levels in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that increased 2-AG levels may predict early response to fluoxetine.

items.title: Contextualizing biological heterogeneity in brain structural normativity assessments across the aging continuum with the nearest neighbor normativity framework.
items.abstract: Background Despite established consensus about the individuality of brain physiology and structural changes, current neuroimaging biomarker paradigms heavily rely on population averages. Here, we define normativity not as a single reference point but as a landscape of permissible configurations arising from diverse physiological manifestations. Methods We introduce the Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N 3 ) framework, designed to parse the natural heterogeneity in brain structural measurements into a diversity-aware biomarker of brain structural decline. Through repeated comparisons within different demographic subgroups, N 3 contextualizes an individual's measurements from several viewpoints along the aging continuum. Relying on local density estimation, it accommodates multiple, shared normative configurations within and across age groups. We use T1-weighted MRI data from 29,883 individuals for training and 7,013 individuals for validation, and benchmark our framework against Brain Age models and Normative Modeling. We evaluate each biomarker's ability to detect neurodegenerative diseases, using them as representative models of atypical brain structural decline. Results In group-level analyses, the N 3 biomarker shows the largest effect sizes in the detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer's Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. Similarly, the N 3 biomarker achieves the highest predictive performance in the classification of neurodegenerative diseases on a single subject level. Notably, the N 3 estimates remain stable across age and robust to compositional changes in the reference sample. Finally, correlation analyses indicate that it captures distinct and complementary aspects of brain structural variation compared to existing approaches. Conclusions Our findings underscore that rethinking normativity assessments to explicitly accommodate natural inter-individual variability can advance our collective efforts toward truly personalized patient care.

items.title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons.
items.abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population. Significance Statement Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11's role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.

items.title: Ventromedial hypothalamic output to the anterior hypothalamic area evokes complex escape behavior.
items.abstract: The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) and anterior hypothalamic area (AHA) contribute to the orchestration of defensive responses to threat. We set out to test the effects of VMH to AHA (VMH→AHA) stimulation on behavior, organ-systems physiology, circulating pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, and brain activity patterns that support escape behavior. We used optogenetics in male and female SF1-Cre mice for behavioral assays, physiological measurements, and brain activity pattern mapping. For the first time, we demonstrate that VMH SF1 →AHA photostimulation increases complex escape behavior that requires three-dimensional navigation. Even in anesthetized mice, VMH→AHA photostimulation increases fractional shortening of the heart consistent with sympathetic arousal. In addition, we demonstrate that VMH→AHA photostimulation increases levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6. In the brain, we find significant elevations of activity in the lateral habenula, anterior hypothalamic area, ventral premammillary nucleus, ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, and locus coeruleus. Significance statement We demonstrate that VMH→AHA photostimulation increases escape behavior that depends on a three dimensional route of navigation, increases levels of the cytokine IL-6, as well as increases activity in the lateral habenula, ventral premammillary nucleus, ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, and locus coeruleus. This work informs how hypothalamic circuitry drives behavioral and physiological responses that facilitate escape from threats in the environment.

items.title: Carotid near-occlusion pathophysiology: A narrative review and expanded cerebrovascular theory.
items.abstract: The purposes of this review are to summarize the pathophysiology of carotid near-occlusion (CNO) and formulate how known hemodynamic theory can be expanded to specifically address CNO. A systematic search revealed 51 articles addressing CNO pathophysiology. ICA flow reduction and collateral pathway activation are hallmarks of CNO. While CNO is associated with a high prevalence of reduced cerebrovascular reserve (CVR), severely impaired CVR was uncommon. Hence, hypoperfusion stroke mechanism is uncommon. Embolic mechanism studies are few and with mixed results. In hemodynamic theory variant, we propose that good collateral capacity results in CNO early during stenosis severity progression and no hemodynamic stroke/TIA. Conversely, we propose that poor collateral capacity results in more severe stenosis for CNO to develop and hemodynamic stroke/TIA will occur when the stenosis is sufficiently severe. This suggested theory predicts that a mismatch between too little distal collapse given a certain stenosis severity might indicate hypoperfusion. In conclusion, CNOs are flow-reducing stenoses associated with collateral use and unclear stroke mechanism. We propose an expansion of known hemodynamic theory to specifically address CNO where collateral capacity is the key factor that determines what stenosis severity is required for CNO to form and for hypoperfusion occur (if it occurs at all).

items.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
items.abstract: Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

items.title: Management of suspected infectious and autoimmune encephalitis in children - National Guidelines from the United Kingdom Joint Societies.
items.abstract: Encephalitis is a rare but often devastating clinical syndrome resulting from inflammation of the brain parenchyma. Encephalitis is a neurological emergency with diverse infectious, autoimmune and inflammatory causes. It can be recognised late or missed, especially as mimics of encephalitis can make the diagnosis and appropriate treatment challenging. Delays in the recognition and treatment of encephalitis carry significant risks of morbidity and mortality. Since the first UK guideline for the management of suspected viral encephalitis in children was published in 2012, there have been substantial developments in the field. Advances in molecular diagnostics and antibody testing, alongside improved access to neuroimaging and electrophysiology have broadened the capacity to identify underlying aetiologies. The recognised spectrum of infectious and immune-mediated causes of encephalitis has expanded, and clinical experience with immunomodulatory therapies has grown considerably. A multidisciplinary national working group, representing neurology, infectious diseases, microbiology, virology, neuroimmunology and acute medicine, alongside national professional and third-sector organisations, was convened in Liverpool in 2023 to develop updated UK Joint Societies guidelines for the management of suspected infectious and autoimmune encephalitis in children. This guideline provides pragmatic, evidence-informed recommendations on the clinical recognition, investigation, diagnosis, acute management and rehabilitation of children with suspected encephalitis. It emphasises early identification and parallel consideration of infectious and immune-mediated causes, with particular attention to decision-making during the critical first 24-72hours of presentation. Standardised diagnostic and therapeutic pathways are presented to support consistent care across healthcare settings. Where the evidence base, including of diagnosis, remains limited, the need for early specialist and multidisciplinary input is emphasised. These recommendations aim to reduce mortality, limit long-term neurological morbidity, and improve outcomes for children with encephalitis across the UK.

items.title: Cerebellar Mutism Syndrome After Brain Tumor Surgery in Adults: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis.
items.abstract: Cerebellar mutism syndrome (CMS) is well characterized after pediatric posterior fossa surgery, but its presentation in adults is poorly defined, and inconsistent use of the term posterior fossa syndrome (PFS) complicates interpretation. We systematically reviewed new CMS in adults after brain tumor surgery. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched in September 2026 for English-language original articles published from 2000 onward, supplemented by reference-list, citation, and full-text searching. Eligible reports described patients aged ≥18 years with new mutism, marked speech reduction, or posterior fossa syndrome affecting speech after tumor surgery. Patients were classified as having alert CMS (A), an akinetic variant (B), or a broader or uncertain phenotype not establishing CMS (C). Reports were JBI-appraised and synthesized narratively. Twenty-three reports describing 29 adults were included. Eighteen had documented postoperative mutism (alert CMS, 10; akinetic variant, 8); the other 11, including 4 with PFS reported in aggregate, had a broader or uncertain phenotype. Patients were aged 18-81 years (median, 37.5); tumors included medulloblastoma, glial, glioneuronal, ependymal, metastatic, and benign lesions. Alert CMS began on postoperative days 1-4, whereas the akinetic variant often began later, frequently with hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or other complications. Speech usually returned within weeks, but residual dysarthria, ataxia, or cognitive deficits were reported in 10 of the 18 patients with documented mutism. Only 18 of the 29 adults had documented postoperative mutism. Alert, akinetic, and broader presentations should be distinguished, and return of speech does not signify complete recovery. Prospective adult cohorts with standardized phenotyping are needed.

items.title: SUMO-2/3 modification of PINK1 restrains basal mitophagy through MAPL-dependent regulation of mitochondrial surveillance.

items.title: The functional significance of human macular pigment: Optical, visual and neural effects.
items.abstract: The foveal region of primates is specialized to accumulate dietary yellow carotenoids, lutein (L) and zeaxanthin (Z) which collectively form the macular pigment (MP). These pigments selectively attenuate short-wave visible light. Although MP is often regarded mostly for its protective role in reducing photo-oxidative damage to the retina, its functional significance to everyday vision is becoming increasingly apparent. Psychophysical methods have been used for decades to measure the pigments showing direct connections to visual function. Evidence is accumulating, however, that the optical effects of MP alter perception under natural viewing conditions. For instance, increasing MP density through intervention enhances chromatic contrast, improves target visibility through simulated atmospheric blue haze, reduces glare disability and discomfort, and speeds recovery from photostress. Conversely, evidence that these optical filtering properties improve conventional visual acuity or contrast sensitivity by reducing chromatic aberration remains limited. Beyond these optical mechanisms, L and Z may also exert biochemical and cellular effects. L and Z accumulate in central nervous system tissue, where intervention studies suggest potential effects on visual processing speed, attention, memory, and neural efficiency. Emerging evidence also supports localized and systemic roles for these carotenoids in retinal development and structure and metabolic regulation. MP density varies by more than an order of magnitude among healthy individuals; while this implies corresponding individual variation in optical filtering, further research is required to determine if this variation extends proportionally to the wider structural, functional, and metabolic effects of these carotenoids.

items.title: Predicted condensation-related signatures localize to two C-terminal regions of the prion protein across cervid PRNP variants associated with chronic wasting disease.
items.abstract: Genetic variation in cervid PRNP influences chronic wasting disease (CWD) susceptibility and progression, but it remains unclear whether disease-associated substitutions produce localized differences in sequence-derived properties relevant to prion protein (PrPC) condensation. We compared a white-tailed deer (WTD) reference sequence with 10 modeled variants on the same mature PrP scaffold (residues 24-233). For each sequence, we calculated intrinsic disorder, FuzDrop per-residue droplet-promoting propensity (pDP) and binding-mode entropy (Sbind), predicted residue-level pKa values, and a discrete-charge summary at pH 7.0. The overall profiles preserve a long N-terminal droplet-promoting region, whereas variant-associated differences are concentrated in selected intervals. In the FuzDrop outputs, residues 126-140 show allele-dependent changes in pDP near the droplet-promoting threshold, and residues 220-230 show variant-specific changes in Sbind, including lower Sbind for S225F/Y and higher Sbind for elk-like Q226E. These differences occur without large changes in overall intrinsic disorder. KaML pKa predictions identify near-neutral titratable sites that provide electrostatic context for these local predictor differences. Independent atomistic simulations of monomeric PrP further detected variant-sensitive backbone behavior and intramolecular contacts involving these intervals. Together, the analysis identifies residues 126-140 and 220-230 as computationally defined candidate intervals that overlap regions implicated independently in prion conversion or CWD fibril structure, motivating direct tests of cervid PrP condensation and maturation.

items.title: Mesoscale connectivity of substructures within the human amygdaloid complex.
items.abstract: The amygdala operates as an integrative network hub, participating in emotional, cognitive, and distributed neural circuit functions. Though once thought of as a single anatomical entity, the amygdala is increasingly being recognized as a complex network of functionally and anatomically distinct nuclei and substructures. Mesoscale diffusion MR images (250 μm isotropic acquisition, upsampled to 125 μm) of the post-mortem human temporal lobe were acquired to allow the identification of the structural components of the amygdaloid complex, which includes the amygdala, as well as the surrounding transitional areas. Amygdala nuclei, including their 13 subnuclei and related substructures were defined, delineated and segmented to generate a unique 3-dimensional visualization of the amygdaloid complex in its anatomical context. Volumetric analyses and scalar indices revealed its morphological and microstructural composition, whereas tractography exposed the intra-amygdala connectome. Both canonical and non-canonical pathways were identified and quantified for a more in-depth network analysis. A virtual dissection of pathways involving the lateral nucleus, which is the largest nucleus (33% of the amygdala), for instance, showed numerous extra-amygdala pathways, as well as intra-amygdala pathways, consistent with its well-established role as the primary input site to the amygdala. A majority of connections are localized in the dorsal lateral subnucleus, which can be conceived of as the dominant gateway for afferent integration. In contrast, the central nucleus, emerged as the primary output hub from the amygdala. This intra-amygdala connectome framework establishes a structural roadmap that advances a mechanistic understanding and informs future network-based therapeutic strategies for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

items.title: Caregiver Perceptions of Compassionate Extubations in a Neuroscience ICU versus Hospice.
items.abstract: Compassionate extubation may be performed in inpatient hospice facilities; however, how this experience compares to the hospital setting is unknown. This study explored caregiver perceptions of care and outcomes for patients who transferred to an inpatient hospice facility for compassionate extubation, compared to those for patients compassionately extubated in a hospital neurosciences intensive care unit (NSICU). Investigators identified patients with severe acute brain injury who underwent compassionate extubation in the University of North Carolina Medical Center (UNCMC) NSICU or a UNC inpatient hospice facility between January 2021 and July 2023. A research assistant audio-recorded semi-structured interviews with patient caregivers who were English-speaking and present for care with compassionate extubation. Interview transcripts were coded using a combination of deductive and inductive coding, and investigators conducted a thematic analysis. Of 39 caregivers contacted, 9 from the hospital and 10 from the hospice completed interviews. Themes emerging from transcripts were environment, emotional support, and provider communications. Most caregivers were satisfied with the care delivered, but there were differences between settings and groups. Caregivers in both groups noted shortcomings in the hospital of convenience, tense environment, and bereavement services. The hospice group praised the physical and peaceful environment and compassionate care delivery. There was variability within both groups for how supportive they perceived communication. Inpatient hospice may improve the experience for caregivers of neurologic patients undergoing compassionate extubation and allow access to increased bereavement support. Innovation in models of care for compassionate extubation, including transition to hospice, has the potential to improve patient and caregiver outcomes.

items.title: Impact of Biannual Community-Directed Treatment with Ivermectin on Onchocerciasis Transmission in Rural Tanzania: A Parasitological and Entomological Survey.
items.abstract: High prevalence of onchocerciasis and epilepsy prompted a shift from annual to biannual community-directed treatment with ivermectin (CDTI). We assessed the effect of biannual CDTI on onchocerciasis transmission and progress towards WHO elimination targets. Cross-sectional parasitological and entomological surveys were conducted. Ov16 serology among children aged 6-10 years was conducted in 2017/18, 2021, and 2024 and ivermectin uptake was assessed. Blackflies were collected in 2024 and analysed in pools for Onchocerca volvulus infection. The prevalence declined from 17.2% (95% CI: 14.7-19.9) after two decades of annual CDTI in 2017 to 13.3% (95%CI: 11.6-15.1) after four rounds of biannual CDTI in 2021 and further to 10.7% (95%CI: 9.1-12.5) after eight rounds of biannual CDTI in 2024. Non-uptake of ivermectin by children rose to 21.6% in 2024 compared to 15.8% in 2021 and 20.3% in 2017/18. Anti-Ov16 seropositivity was significantly lower in 2024 (OR=0.61, 95%CI: 0.45-0.82) compared to 2017/18 and was associated with age and residence in middle-altitude villages. Among 20,321 Simulium damnosum s.l flies analysed, 43.7% of the pools tested positive for Onchocerca volvulus, with an infectivity rate of 0.58% (95%CI: 0.47-0.71). Biannual CDTI reduced transmission; however, high Ov16 seroprevalence among children and Simulium infectivity above WHO elimination thresholds indicate ongoing transmission, highlighting the need to strengthen CDTI and complementary vector control interventions.

items.title: Beyond conventional neurodiagnostic: quantum-enabled mapping of AGE-RAGE dynamics in type 3 diabetes.
items.abstract: Type 3 Diabetes (T3D) is a conceptual framework used to describe the association between cerebral insulin resistance, metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative processes, particularly those associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). The advanced glycation end products (AGEs)-receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) axis has been implicated in oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling and neuronal dysfunction. However, conventional biochemical approaches often provide endpoint measurements and may not fully resolve the spatial and temporal dynamics of these processes. Advances in quantum sensing and nanotechnology offer potential tools for detecting selected physicochemical signals in biological systems, although their demonstrated capabilities vary substantially across platforms. This review examines the biological relevance of the AGE-RAGE axis in neurodegeneration and discusses the principles and types of quantum sensing technologies, including nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and quantum dots, alongside other nanomaterial-based sensing approaches. Particular attention is given to probe functionalization, bioconjugation, signal transduction and experimental platforms that could support future investigations of AGE-RAGE-associated processes. Importantly, direct, real-time quantum sensing of AGE-RAGE interactions in living neuronal systems remain to be experimentally established. Accordingly, proposed applications involving receptor activation, downstream signaling, brain organoids, brain-on-chip systems and in vivo imaging are considered in terms of their potential, limitations and validation requirements. Challenges relating to target specificity, biological interference, biocompatibility, spatial and temporal resolution and translational feasibility are also discussed. This review outlines a prospective framework for investigating AGE-RAGE-associated signaling dynamics while distinguishing established sensing capabilities from applications that require further experimental validation.

items.title: Neuroprotective actions of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Neurodegeneration: From mechanisms to clinical translation.
items.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been explored as potential therapeutics for neurodegenerative disorders, yet a comprehensive integration of their neuroprotective mechanisms across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and related conditions remains to be consolidated. This review examines the multimodal effects of GLP-1RAs on neuroinflammation, autophagy, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation, with a focus on translational relevance and alignment between preclinical findings and clinical evidence. A systematic synthesis of preclinical and clinical studies investigating GLP-1RA administration in neurodegenerative disease models and populations was conducted. Studies reporting neuroprotective outcomes and mechanistic pathways were included, and clinical trial data and real-world evidence for AD, PD, Huntington's disease, stroke, diabetic encephalopathy, and peripheral neuropathy were systematically evaluated. Preclinical evidence revealed that GLP-1RAs modulate key pathogenic processes, including amyloid-β and tau pathology, α-synuclein accumulation, neuroinflammatory cascades, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Clinical data provided variable support, with emerging real-world evidence suggesting potential benefits. Novel strategies-such as dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, enhanced blood-brain barrier penetration, and sustained-release formulations-were identified as promising approaches to improve efficacy, although significant gaps remain between preclinical promise and clinical outcomes. This review consolidates evidence that GLP-1RAs exert broad neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms, but clinical translation is still evolving. The potential of GLP-1-based therapies as disease-modifying interventions for neurodegeneration warrants further investigation, with particular attention to bridging preclinical and clinical findings and optimizing drug delivery strategies.

items.title: The role of protein lactylation in spinal cord injury: metabolic and epigenetic remodeling and regulation of the immune microenvironment.
items.abstract: Secondary injury after spinal cord injury (SCI) is triggered by a complex pathological cascade, including ischemia-hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, inflammation and cell death, and serves as a decisive factor for the prognosis of neurological function. Accumulating evidence indicates that lactate is not merely a by-product of anaerobic metabolism; it also acts as a substrate for protein lactylation, linking cellular metabolic status to gene transcription. This narrative review summarizes the mechanisms underlying lactylation in SCI: post-injury ischemia and hypoxia drive glycolytic reprogramming, leading to lactate accumulation and subsequently triggering a global upregulation of lactylation. Lactylation exerts distinct, cell-type-specific functions: in microglia/macrophages, it simultaneously promotes repair and exacerbates injury; in astrocytes, it primarily facilitates metabolic support and protective polarization, and in oligodendrocytes, it drives remyelination. Additionally, it mediates signal transmission from innate to adaptive immunity via the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis. Site-specific patterns of lactylation help explain these opposing biological outcomes and inform precision-oriented therapeutic strategies aimed at lactylation. We also highlight unresolved challenges and promising research avenues for this field.

items.title: Association of midbrain IL-6 with impaired nest-building behavior and therapeutic effect of Ninjin'yoeito in old hindlimb-unloading mice.
items.abstract: Psychiatric symptoms can substantially impact rehabilitation outcomes in older patients with disuse syndrome. However, the mechanisms underlying these psychiatric symptoms remain poorly understood, and no established treatment is currently available. This study used hindlimb unloading (HU) as a model of disuse syndrome in old male mice to evaluate the effects of Ninjin'yoeito (NYT), a traditional Japanese herbal medicine. After 2 weeks of HU, old mice underwent the nest building test to evaluate goal-directed behavior, and the open field and elevated plus maze tests to assess anxiety-like behavior. Compared to age-matched sham mice, HU-subjected mice showed declines in nest building and locomotor activity but no appreciable anxiety-like behavior during reloading period. Seven days after HU, IL-6 expression was elevated in the midbrain and was co-expressed with microglia in the ventral tegmental area (VTA). In young mice, intra-VTA injection of IL-6 impaired nest building behavior. In activated primary microglial cultures, NYT reduced IL-6 mRNA expression. During recovery from HU, repeated NYT administration improved nest building and motor function while reducing midbrain IL-6 protein levels in old mice. These findings suggest that elevated IL-6 expression in midbrain/VTA is associated with the impairment of goal-directed behavior after HU and that this impairment can be attenuated by NYT. Collectively, these preclinical findings suggest that pharmacological intervention may provide a therapeutic approach for psychiatric-like behavioral changes associated with disuse syndrome.

items.title: A meta-analytic comparison of eye movement subtypes as potential biomarkers of schizophrenia.
items.abstract: Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder characterized by significant cognitive and perceptual dysfunctions, including disturbances in eye movements such as saccades, smooth pursuit, and fixations. These oculomotor abnormalities have been increasingly studied as potential biomarkers for schizophrenia. However, previous studies have been limited by inconsistent findings and methodological variability. More specifically, to date, literature lacks a direct comparison of the main types of eye movements and their relative metrics (e.g., number of fixations) with respect to the main brain function involved in each one (e.g., attention, memory). The present pre-registered meta-analysis overcomes these limitations by using data from 211 studies, comprising 539 samples, for a total of 9675 schizophrenia patients and 12086 healthy controls. Results highlighted antisaccades error rate, indexing inhibitory control capacity, as the most effective and precise for distinguishing schizophrenia patients from controls, thus indicating this eye movement as a putative biomarker for schizophrenia. Scanpath length during free-viewing tasks, indexing global visual scanning ability, was identified as the second-best candidate. By providing a comprehensive, quantitative evaluation, this study advances understanding of eye movement dysfunction in schizophrenia and aids the development of more objective diagnostic tools and treatment strategies. Data and other relevant materials are available at https://osf.io/jr9qs/.

items.title: Comparing behavioral outputs across automated tracking software reveals platform-dependent variability in zebrafish neurobehavioral analysis.
items.abstract: The zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a prominent model in behavioral neuroscience, with the novel tank diving test (NTT) representing one of the most validated paradigms for assessing anxiety-like responses and vertical exploration. Although automated video-tracking software are widely used to quantify behaviors, the results obtained from different programs are rarely equivalent, representing a critical challenge for data comparability. Variations in detection algorithms and coordinate processing may compromise the interpretation of behavioral outcomes and reproducibility across studies. Here, we aimed to systematically assess the agreement, accuracy, and reproducibility of behavioral metrics across different video-tracking platforms, and to determine whether a standardized post-analysis approach could improve cross-system comparability. To achieve our goal, we compared four well-established systems: ANY-maze and EthoVision (closed-source software), and TrackR and ToxTrac (open-source software), using the zebrafish NTT paradigm. To enable comparison across platforms, an independent post-analysis approach was applied using the CartesianBehaviour package, which utilizes spatial coordinates to calculate movement patterns and minimize biases introduced by software-specific data processing. Our results revealed differences in tracking accuracy and intra- and inter-software data variability, demonstrating systematic discrepancies in behavioral parameters such as total distance traveled and time spent in the top area. Despite these differences, the use of a common post-analysis framework showed strong positive correlations across systems. Finally, our findings demonstrate the lack of direct equivalence between behavioral metrics obtained from different tracking platforms and reinforce the importance of standardizing post-analysis to ensure data reproducibility in neurobehavioral research.

items.title: A neural circuit mediating altitude control in Drosophila.
items.abstract: Flight is a remarkably efficient mode of locomotion that is largely responsible for the extraordinary evolutionary radiations of birds, bats, pterosaurs, and insects. Whereas walking animals need only control locomotion on a two-dimensional surface, flight requires active altitude regulation, a process by which the brain transforms self-motion cues into motor patterns that regulate lift. Using an integrative approach combining optogenetics, high-speed videography, two-photon imaging, robotics, and connectomics, we identified a single pair of descending neurons in Drosophila that control altitude. To search for candidate cells, we performed an optogenetic screen of sparse driver lines targeting descending neurons that project to the flight neuropil of the ventral nerve cord and identified one bilaterally paired neuron, DNa10, whose activation elicits changes in wing kinematics consistent with descent. A replay of the kinematics on a dynamically scaled robot confirmed that the wing motion elicited by DNa10 activation generates a reduction in upward force. Optogenetic activation of this neuron causes free-flying animals to descend, whereas ablation or silencing of the cell in tethered flies elicits fictive ascent. Functional imaging reveals that DNa10 is activated by downward visual motion and inhibited by upward motion. These results are consistent with a connectomic analysis showing that DNa10 receives monosynaptic input from large-field visual interneurons sensitive to vertical body motion and provides direct output to three wing motor neurons that regulate the lift. Collectively, these results identify core components of a circuit for altitude control that links the detection of visual motion to the alteration of aerodynamic forces.

items.title: Effectiveness of an early reading intervention for young children with intellectual disabilities who need or use augmentative and alternative communication on trajectories of decoding and sight word recognition: Study protocol for a cluster-randomized controlled factorial trial.
items.abstract: Children with intellectual disabilities who need or use augmentative and alternative communication are often excluded from early reading instruction in both kindergarten and school. Behavioral challenges, lack of functional speech, and low expectations regarding reading acquisition may be contributing factors. Reading ability has a significant impact on the self-expression and social life of individuals who need or use augmentative and alternative communication. These individuals can acquire reading skills with a tailored curriculum designed to meet their needs. Research shows that phonological-based reading instruction can be beneficial for this population; however, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated early reading instructions both in kindergarten and first grade on developmental trajectories for these individuals. This study will examine the effect of an early reading intervention on trajectories of decoding and sight word recognition for children with intellectual disabilities who need or use augmentative and alternative communication. The intervention will be implemented in kindergarten and first grade using a two-by-two factorial, randomized controlled trial. Kindergartens are randomized into one of four groups: (1) intervention in kindergarten and first grade, (2) intervention in kindergarten only, (3) intervention in first grade only, or (4) training-as-usual in both years. Each intervention lasts 37 weeks over the course of one academic year, with children aged 4-8 years receiving reading instruction delivered by special education teachers. The intervention uses Reading for All material, which is a phonological-based instruction targeting skills such as letter-sound knowledge, first-sound recognition, sound blending, shared reading, sight word recognition, and decoding. Outcomes will be assessed at multiple time points during each intervention year. The results of this RCT bring evidence of effectiveness of phonological reading instruction among children with intellectual disabilities who need or use augmentative and alternative communication on trajectories of decoding and sight word recognition from kindergarten to first grade. Moreover, our design tests the indirect effect of phonological awareness (formed by sound blending and first-sound recognition) and letter-sound knowledge on trajectories of decoding. Because the use of a control group that does not receive any intervention raises ethical concerns, all participants in the control group will be offered access to the reading material in second grade, outside the study context.

items.title: Altered task-evoked sensorimotor cortical hemodynamic responses in degenerative cervical myelopathy: an fNIRS pilot study.
items.abstract: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) commonly impairs hand function. fMRI studies have demonstrated supraspinal sensorimotor alterations in DCM. However, cortical responses during clinically relevant fine motor tasks remain incompletely characterized. We hypothesized that sensorimotor cortical hemodynamic responses would be attenuated in DCM compared with healthy controls while performing fine motor hand tasks. Patients with DCM and healthy controls underwent functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) while performing hand closing and pegboard tasks. Left and right sensorimotor cortices were predefined as regions of interest. Oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbR) responses were quantified. Seven DCM patients and eight healthy controls were analyzed. Contralateral sensorimotor HbO responses were lower in DCM during left hand closing (p = 0.01) and right hand dexterity (p = 0.03). An HbR group difference was present only during the right-hand dexterity task (p = 0.046). DCM patients required longer to complete the pegboard task with both dominant (32.3 ± 4.2 s vs. 23.5 ± 2.0 s; p < 0.01) and non-dominant hands (31.9 ± 4.7 s vs. 25.6 ± 1.1 s; p < 0.01). DCM was associated with task dependent attenuation of sensorimotor cortical hemodynamic responses and impaired hand dexterity. These preliminary findings suggest altered task-evoked sensorimotor cortical hemodynamics in DCM and warrant confirmation in larger studies. fNIRS is a portable neuroimaging tool suitable for studying cortical motor physiology in ecologically valid outpatient and bedside settings and may facilitate the design and evaluation of future interventions.

items.title: Predicting outcomes in microdiscectomy surgery with applied machine learning.
items.abstract: Microdiscectomy surgery is a common procedure used to treat lumbar disc herniation (LDH), a condition causing significant lower back pain and sciatica. Despite its widespread use, outcomes vary, with some patients experiencing re herniation. Accurate prediction of postoperative outcomes could improve patient counselling and treatment planning. This study explores the application of machine learning models to predict re-herniation at 12 months using preoperative clinical and demographic data. This multi-centered study used data from a randomised controlled trial involving 211 patients who underwent microdiscectomy. After addressing missing data, 152 cases were analysed. Logistic regression was first applied to determine significant covariates, followed by the development of supervised learning classifiers, including Random Forest, AdaBoost, and Neural Networks. Model performance was evaluated using metrics such as the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (ROC-AUC). Significant predictors of re-herniation included smoking status and emergency department presentations. Smokers were 11 times more likely to experience re herniation, and those with frequent ED visits were 19 times more likely to do so. The Random Forest model achieved the highest predictive performance, with an MCC of 0.47 and an AUC of 0.69. Application of SMOTE improved sensitivity but decreased specificity in most models. Machine learning models, particularly Random Forest, demonstrated moderate predictive ability for re-herniation following microdiscectomy. Significant preoperative factors like smoking and ED visits were strongly associated with poor outcomes. These findings suggest that machine learning can enhance clinical decision-making by identifying high-risk patients, allowing for more personalised treatment strategies.

items.title: Longitudinal hemodynamic trajectories in severe symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis under endovascular versus medical management.
items.abstract: Hemodynamic compromise plays an important role in stroke recurrence in patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (sICAS). We aimed to characterize longitudinal CT perfusion (CTP) changes in patients with severe sICAS managed with endovascular treatment (EVT) or medical management (MM). This retrospective cohort study included patients with severe sICAS (70%-99% stenosis) and recent ischemic stroke (<3 months) identified from a CTP database. Patients were grouped according to treatment received: MM alone or EVT plus MM. Baseline and follow-up CTP examinations were obtained at least 5 months apart. Changes in perfusion deficit volumes defined by relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF) and time-to-maximum (Tmax) thresholds were evaluated using adjusted longitudinal models. Propensity score overlap-weighted generalized estimating equation models were used for sensitivity analyses. Clinical events were recorded descriptively. Among 102 patients (44 MM; 58 EVT), perfusion deficit volumes defined by rCBF < 38% and < 34% significantly expanded in the MM group (both P = 0.018), whereas the EVT group showed no significant change. Primary adjusted analyses showed significant treatment-by-time interactions for rCBF < 38% and < 34% (both interaction P = 0.021). Overlap-weighted estimates remained directionally consistent but were not statistically significant (P = 0.162 and P = 0.160, respectively). The 1-year rates of target-territory recurrent ischemic stroke were 9.1% with MM and 8.6% with EVT. Primary adjusted analyses suggested different longitudinal rCBF trajectories between groups, but these differences were not statistically significant after overlap weighting. These findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: From potential to practice: An International survey on technology adoption and needs in epilepsy neuropsychology.
items.abstract: Technological integration offers opportunities to improve neuropsychological practice in epilepsy care. Compared to other healthcare fields, neuropsychology has been relatively slow to incorporate these advancements into clinical practice. To describe the use of technology in epilepsy neuropsychology and identify priorities for technological development. An online survey of multiple choice and open-ended questions was developed in English and translated into Spanish, then sent to practicing neuropsychologists working in epilepsy care across all six International League Against Epilepsy world regions. The survey collected data on the settings in which neuropsychological services are provided to people with epilepsy, the technologies currently in use, the barriers to technological adoption, and desired future developments. 179 neuropsychologists from 39 countries participated in the survey. The majority of respondents were women (69 %), aged 30-49 (60 %), and held a PhD (60 %). Key barriers to technological adoption included concerns around tool validation, financial limitations to purchase existing tools, and a lack of culturally and linguistically relevant normative data. Priorities for future development included predictive algorithms, automating psychometric aspects of clinical practice, and better leveraging of functional neuroimaging technologies. This international survey highlights that while epilepsy neuropsychologists are open to adopting new technologies in their clinical practice, there are several barriers hampering uptake across the field. Survey responses highlighted that technological developments that are practical, accessible, evidence-based, and suitable for culturally and linguistically diverse populations are required to meet the needs of the epilepsy neuropsychology workforce.
