items.title: Global Prevalence and Risk Factors of Digital Eye Strain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Comprehensive data on the global prevalence of digital eye strain and its associated risk factors remain scarce. This study aimed to estimate the global prevalence of digital eye strain and its associated risk factors. CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, CBM, PubMed, Embase, WoS, and Cochrane were searched through July 2026 for studies on digital eye strain prevalence and risk factors. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed bias, and pooled estimates were calculated using fixed- and random-effects models. A total of 11,254 individuals with digital eye strain were included. The meta-analysis revealed a global prevalence of digital eye strain of 63%. The prevalence of digital eye strain was relatively high in the African Region (AFR) and in low-income countries (LICs), reaching 73% in both. Among these factors, being female (OR = 2.18, 95% CI: 1.82-2.62), near-viewing of digital screens (OR = 2.71, 95% CI: 2.09-3.51), wearing optical correction (OR = 2.40, 95% CI: 1.85-3.13), using video display terminals for 2-4 h per day (OR = 2.77, 95% CI: 1.78-4.31), >4 h per day (OR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.86-3.52) or >6 h per day (OR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.56-2.30), exposure to poor lighting (OR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.24-2.10), inadequate ergonomic design (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.19-2.49), excessive screen brightness (OR = 2.99, 95% CI: 1.72-5.19), failure to follow the 20-20-20 rule (OR = 3.04, 95% CI: 2.30-4.01) and extra-work electronic device use (OR = 1.95, 95% CI: 1.29-2.96) were identified as risk factors for digital eye strain. Digital eye strain imposes a higher disease burden in the AFR, LICs and among university students. More representative regional and population studies are needed to guide targeted prevention and interventions for high-risk groups.

items.title: Lived experiences of type 1 diabetes and disordered eating: Insights for prevention and early intervention in Paediatric care.
items.abstract: The high prevalence and risks of eating disorders and disordered eating in type 1 diabetes (T1D) are well recognised, yet the aetiology is poorly understood. Current understanding draws on established eating disorder models, complemented by an emerging lived experience evidence base. This study aimed to retrospectively explore how disordered eating develops whilst growing up with T1D using lived experience in order to inform future prevention strategies within clinical practice. A qualitative design underpinned by an interpretivist approach was used to explore the lived experiences of adults diagnosed with T1D in childhood who self-identified as having experienced disordered eating. Eleven participants (aged 18-61; 10 females, 1 male) were recruited via social media and advocacy networks between January and October 2023. Semi-structured interviews were conducted remotely. Data were analysed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework, with attention to researcher positionality and context. Analysis generated five themes that highlight how disordered eating develops and is maintained in paediatric diabetes care: Connection with others: Relationship dynamics shaped early food and diabetes behaviours; Shame and secrecy: Stigma related to weight, diabetes, and eating behaviours reinforced secrecy Identity and self-view: Identity within the healthcare system and feelings of inadequacy and control-based behaviours as well as neurodiversity and mortality. Feeling held back: Emotional and social limitations of diabetes including trauma, contributed to disordered eating; Change and transitions: Shifts in care, technology, and independence influenced disordered eating behaviours. These findings highlight illness and care-specific drivers that extend beyond body image concerns. This study challenges dominant, weight-focused frameworks by revealing how disordered eating in T1D is shaped during paediatric diabetes care. Prevention must be embedded within routine paediatric diabetes care. Findings offer a lived-experience framework to inform more inclusive, psychologically informed paediatric diabetes services.

items.title: Slow- Versus Normal-Paced Breathing During an Emotional Task: Limited Evidence for Greater RMSSD Change or State-Affect Benefits.
items.abstract: Slow-paced breathing (SPB) is widely promoted for stress regulation, but its incremental benefit over an active paced-breathing control across age groups remains uncertain. We compared SPB (prescribed 6 cycles/min) with normal-paced breathing (NPB; prescribed 12 cycles/min) during an emotional picture-rating task in 82 younger and 84 older adults. Outcomes were baseline-to-task changes in heart rate variability indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) and mean heart rate, and pre-post changes in state anxiety and affect. The primary RMSSD analysis included 162 participants after the ± 3 median absolute deviation exclusion rule. RMSSD was higher during the task than during the preceding baseline in both protocols. The primary Time × Breathing condition interaction did not establish a larger change under SPB, β = 0.090, 95% CI [- 0.022, 0.203], p = .116, and was sensitive to outlier handling. A secondary task-period contrast showed higher RMSSD under SPB than NPB (ratio = 1.23, p = .009). Mean heart rate decreased without a reliable protocol difference in change. State anxiety and affect showed no robust advantage of SPB. Mixed-model sensitivity analyses likewise did not establish overall protocol differences in change. No reliable age moderation was detected. Respiration was not recorded directly, and adherence to 6 cycles/min or comparable respiratory exposure across ages could not be verified. Overall, the primary analyses provided no reliable evidence of a greater RMSSD change or of an acute state-affect benefit under SPB in this task context; they neither establish equivalence nor isolate the effect of breathing frequency.

items.title: Cluster analysis based on alexithymia in young women: exploring addictions, psychological symptoms and relational vulnerability factors.
items.abstract: Alexithymia has been identified as a transdiagnostic risk factor for addictive behaviours. It has also been widely linked to various psychological risk factors related to addictions. (I) to explore clusters of young women based on alexithymia and; (II) to examine differences between clusters in terms of addictive behaviours (gambling, alcohol, drugs and compulsive buying) and associated psychological symptoms. The sample consisted of 239 women aged between 18 and 35 years. Three clusters were found based on the three subscales of alexithymia (TAS-20). Cluster 1 was characterised by lower scores on alexithymia and low scores on all variables. Cluster 2 was characterised by intermediate levels of identifying and describing emotions and high scores on hopelessness. Cluster 3 showed the highest levels of alexithymia, addictive behaviours and all other study variables except for hopelessness. Young women with addiction risk or problems may benefit from different preventive and therapeutic approaches depending on the alexithymia subscales.

items.title: A century of mosquito diversity and distribution in Haiti and the Dominican Republic (1905-2024).
items.abstract: Mosquito-borne diseases represent a major public health threat, particularly on islands and in resource-limited settings. Hispaniola, the second-largest island in the Caribbean, shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, is highly vulnerable to such diseases due to recurrent extreme climatic events, endemic diseases such as malaria, filariasis and dengue, and challenging socio-economic and political conditions that hinder effective vector control. Moreover, knowledge of mosquito (Diptera: Culicidae) biodiversity and distribution on the island is outdated and fragmented. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of mosquito species diversity and associated vector-borne diseases in both countries, covering the period 1905-2024, using the Web of Science and PubMed databases, as well as grey literature and entomological collections. The data were synthesised into an updated checklist and historical distribution maps. A total of 1604 occurrence observations were extracted from 82 studies, of which 1369 unique occurrence observations were retained after deduplication. Our review identified 13 genera and 62 mosquito species on the island, of which 12 species are exclusive to the Dominican Republic, one is exclusive to Haiti and 49 species are shared by both countries. There was greater species richness in the Dominican Republic, with 61 species, compared with Haiti, with 50 species, likely reflecting differences in topography, land use and research efforts. The most frequently reported species were Aedes aegypti, Anopheles albimanus, Ae. albopictus, Culex quinquefasciatus, Cx. nigripalpus and Psorophora jamaicensis. This updated checklist and distribution analysis covers the last 120 years and is the first harmonised, comprehensive long-term synthesis of culicid biodiversity in Haiti and the Dominican Republic to date. It provides a critical foundation for risk assessment and the design of integrated vector management and surveillance strategies to address future mosquito-borne disease threats in the region.

items.title: Risk Factor Profiles May Differ Between Younger-Onset and Late-Onset Colorectal Cancer: An Exploratory Analysis of Individual and Cumulative Risk Factors Among the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cohort.
items.abstract: Rates of young-onset colorectal cancer (CRC) are on the rise globally. Despite this growing burden, the drivers of young-onset adult CRC remain largely unknown. This study aimed to compare risk factor profiles between younger-onset and late-onset CRC to evaluate differences in their risk factor profiles. The Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial dataset, comprising ∼155,000 US participants including 1219 CRC cases, was analysed. Participants were stratified by age (≤59 vs. ≥60 years). Associations of demographic, clinical and behavioural risk factors with CRC were computed using multivariable Cox regression with the multiplicative interaction of exposures. Reduced rank regression was used to derive dietary patterns (DPs). Among the ≤59-year cohort, no individual risk factor (excluding age) was independently associated with the risk of CRC. However, the multiplicative effect of hypertension and smoking had a nominal association with younger-onset CRC (p = 0.047). In contrast, in the ≥60-year cohort, individual (sex, body mass index, diabetes and alcohol) as well as combinations of risk factors were associated with CRC. Significant DPs appeared exclusively to impact the risk of CRC in the ≥60-year cohort. However, no interactions remained significant following correction for multiple testing; findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. These findings suggest that the drivers of CRC in younger individuals may be different from their older counterparts. These exploratory findings offer novel insight into CRC risk in the young and highlight the need to reconsider interactions between CRC risk factors.

items.title: Biomimetic Optically Encoded Hydrogel Fiber Enables Simultaneous Olfactory-Mechanosensory Perception for Robotic Plume Tracing.
items.abstract: Dynamic odor plumes encode gas identity and airflow transport as coupled spatiotemporal cues, requiring olfactory-mechanosensory fusion perception for intelligent robotic navigation in vision-denied environments. Yet current olfactory-mechanosensory systems typically rely on separated sensing units, limiting co-localized mechanochemical discrimination. Here, we report a biomimetic flexible optical fiber (BFOF) comprising a coaxial hydrogel fiber with distributed, self-assembled odor-sensitive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) on its exterior, enabling simultaneous decoding of wind vectors and olfactory cues within a single compact optical architecture. Inspired by the spatially integrated mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors in ant antennae, the BFOF employs conformal MOF-hydrogel interfaces to enhance evanescent-field coupling without compromising receptor activity or waveguiding, partitioning multidimensional airflow attenuation and odor fluorescence into separable optical channels for low-crosstalk olfactory-mechanosensory fusion. Therefore, it achieves high sensitivity, fine directional selectivity, and fast temporal response across a wide range of airflow conditions. It identifies 16 individual gases, 96 mixtures, and the physiological states (unripe, ripe, overripe, and rotten) of 8 fruits with high accuracy. Coupled with a lightweight machine-learning framework, this work establishes rapid, precise, and closed-loop anemotactic navigation and multi-target odor tracing in complex three-dimensional (3D) spaces, offering a compact optical sensing platform for embodied robotic olfaction beyond static gas classification.

items.title: Contribution of the srtBCD pilus cluster genes sbp1 and sbp3 to the virulence of Streptococcus suis serotype 2 sequence type 1.
items.abstract: Streptococcus suis is an important zoonotic bacterial pathogen that causes substantial economic losses to the porcine industry and serious invasive infection in humans. Many virulence factors have been characterized as being involved in S. suis virulence and pathogenesis. Among these, the srtBCD pilus cluster gene, which encodes three type C sortases (srtB, srtC, and srtD) and four pilin subunit proteins, sbp1-sbp4, is associated with disease-causing S. suis isolates. In this study, we constructed mutant strains devoid of sbp1 and sbp3 in a virulent S. suis serotype 2 sequence type 1 strain, and evaluated the impact on virulence using both in vitro and in vivo models of infection. This study identifies sbp1 and sbp3 contribute to host-pathogen interactions. Inactivation of either gene reduced the bacterium's ability to damage epithelial cells, attach to host cells, and invade them, demonstrating their role in the early stages of infection. In addition, inactivation of sbp1 or sbp3 decreased the expression of the sortase-associated gene cluster (SSU1889, SSU1886, srtB, srtC, srtD) and several virulence-related genes, including the adhesin gene ssfsb, eno and the cytolysin gene sly, suggesting that these proteins influence a broader network. Among the two proteins, sbp1 appeared to have a greater impact on virulence, as the Δsbp1 mutant showed stronger reductions in virulence gene expression and caused lower mortality in mice, although statistical does not significant, suggesting that sbp1 plays a more prominent role than sbp3 in pathogenicity.

items.title: UL45-46 as the preferred insertion site for herpesvirus-of-turkeys-vectored H9N2 avian influenza vaccines: comparative analysis of immunogenicity and protection.
items.abstract: H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) has evolved into a threat to the global poultry industry, causing huge economic losses and persistent public health risks. Due to inadequate cellular and mucosal immunity, current inactivated vaccines fail to prevent infection and block virus transmission. The recombinant herpesvirus-of-turkeys (HVT)-vectored vaccine is a promising control strategy, but the insertion site with the higher immunogenicity of the hemagglutinin (HA) gene is still unclear. This study compared the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of recombinant HVT vaccines expressing the H9N2 HA gene at the unique long (UL)45-46 and unique short (US)2 sites. The HVT-HAUL45-46 virus maintained replication kinetics consistent with the parental HVT and demonstrated genetic stability through 20 consecutive passages. Compared with HVT-HAUS2, HVT-HAUL45-46 induced significantly higher hemagglutination inhibition (HI) antibody titers and stronger HA-specific cellular immunity. Following the H9N2 challenge, the UL45-46 vaccine completely prevented intestinal viral shedding and significantly reduced lung viral loads and histopathological lesions. These findings establish UL45-46 as a better insertion site for HVT-based H9N2 vaccines.

items.title: The social gradient in adolescent unintentional injuries demands policy attention.
items.abstract: Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in adolescence, yet they remain underprioritised within adolescent health and equity agendas. Recent Danish studies reveal substantial socioeconomic inequalities in unintentional injuries. Injury risk and injury-related mortality follow a clear social gradient, with adolescents from less advantaged backgrounds experiencing higher rates of both outcomes. Despite these disparities, evidence on effective and equitable prevention strategies remains limited, and current policy efforts largely focus on road traffic injuries while overlooking other important causes. Furthermore, existing injury surveillance systems inadequately capture adolescent-specific contexts and activities, limiting opportunities for targeted prevention. Unintentional injuries are an important but overlooked source of health inequality in adolescence. Reducing the burden of injury requires greater policy attention, stronger research and surveillance, and a focus on the social determinants that drive injury risk. Addressing these upstream factors may improve both injury outcomes and adolescent health more broadly.

items.title: The role of sigmoidoscopy in colorectal cancer screening - public preferences and predicted uptake.
items.abstract: Participation in cancer screening is crucial to maximise its benefit. In colorectal cancer (CRC) screening, stool tests or colonoscopies are commonly offered worldwide screening tests. In the German CRC screening programme, the insured can primarily choose between stool test and colonoscopy. However, sigmoidoscopy is also an evidence-based procedure to reduce CRC mortality and even prevent CRC. Based on individual preferences, we aim to estimate the uptake for either colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, or stool test in CRC screening. In 2020, statutory insured individuals aged 50, 55, and 60 in Germany, Lower Saxony, were invited to participate in a discrete choice experiment (DCE). Each participant received 8 choice tasks, each of which presented two unlabelled (procedure A and B) screening alternatives defined by 6 attributes (CRC incidence and mortality, complications, preprocedural bowel preparation, need for transportation home, colonoscopy following a positive test result). Each attribute had 3 levels. To calculate the indirect utility and probability of uptake of stool testing, sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, and 'no screening', the preference weights of the attribute levels used to define the 4 alternatives were summed. Estimates were compared between standard screening (stool test or colonoscopy) and extended screening (+ sigmoidoscopy). External validity of the DCE was checked by comparing predicted and intended (2 items in the questionnaire) participation. From n = 666 valid respondents, a greater proportion of women (22.5%; 95%CI 16.2-28.9%) than men (13.4%; 95%CI 9.6-17.2%) preferred sigmoidoscopy in an extended screening scenario. Compared with standard screening, the predicted uptake for colonoscopy and the stool test as well as for 'no screening' was slightly lower when sigmoidoscopy was offered as an additional option. The extended screening could yield a slightly higher non-significant total participation in CRC screening in both women (+ 5.8%; 95%CI -0.4-12.0%) and men (+ 3.1; 95%CI -3.4-9.6%) than standard screening. Intended and preferred uptake did not differ substantially. A relevant proportion of the eligible population, more women than men, appears to prefer sigmoidoscopy for CRC screening when given the option. This additional option tends to increase overall predicted participation in CRC screening. Future studies are needed to evaluate the acceptance and feasibility of the additionally offered sigmoidoscopy in today's CRC screening. DRKS00019010, 2019-11-18.

items.title: Mind the uncertainties - a cross-sectional study on perceptions of cancer risks for factors with inconclusive or limited evidence among the Swedish general public.
items.abstract: Identifying environmental and lifestyle factors that increase the risk of cancer is a complex scientific endeavour, with the degree of certainty regarding carcinogenicity existing along a continuum. To make informed health decisions, the general public must be well informed, both about factors that increase and decrease cancer risk. However, misconceptions can easily gain a foothold in the public consciousness. This study aimed to examine perceptions of carcinogenicity in Sweden regarding factors where the scientific evidence is inconclusive or limited, in relation to demographic strata. This cross-sectional study used a pre-existing data set with a randomly selected sample of 1520 participants (18-84 years old) recruited from a Swedish online panel. Statistical analyses utilized post-stratification weights to make the results representative for the general Swedish population. Weighted univariate tests and logistic regression models were used for examining associations between demographic groups and perceptions of carcinogenicity for twelve factors with inconclusive or limited evidence. Most participants perceived snus (76%), E-cigarettes (67.1%), food additives (63.0%), stress (50.7%), and burnt food (50.4%) as carcinogenic. Whilst no significant differences were observed regarding E-cigarettes, snus was more likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by older (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.01; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00-1.02 per year older) and college/university educated (1.47; 1.09-2.00) participants, while it was less likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by males (0.66; 0.48-0.90) and high-income earners (0.62; 0.40-0.95 compared to low-income earners). Food additives were more often perceived as carcinogenic by older participants (AOR 1.02; 95% CI 1.01-1.03 per year older) and middle-income earners (1.47; 1.03-2.08 compared to low-income earners), while stress and burnt food were more likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by college/university educated (1.49; 1.15-1.91 and 1.54; 1.20-1.98, respectively) participants. A large proportion of the Swedish general public endorses several unestablished cancer risk factors as carcinogenic. The heterogeneous awareness regarding different factors observed in this study illustrates how challenging it is for individuals to navigate the complex and nuanced scientific evidence regarding cancer risk factors. This highlights the importance of clear and transparent public health messaging.

items.title: Extreme Heat Events and Increased Risk of Motor Vehicle Crashes, Injuries, and Fatalities: Exploring Differential Impacts across California Census Tracts.
items.abstract: Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death in the USA, killing approximately 120 people daily. California led the nation in motor vehicle deaths for seven consecutive years (2016-2022), with fatalities climbing overall. Extreme heat events (EHEs) have intensified with climate change, potentially increasing crash risk and severity, but this link remains understudied. This study assessed the relationship between different EHE definitions and the risk of crashes, and the associated number of injuries and fatalities in California census tracts across May-October of 2010-2020. Twelve EHE definitions were calculated using high-resolution gridded daily temperature data based on various metrics, thresholds, and duration. A time-stratified case-crossover approach quantified EHE impacts on property-damage-only (PDO) crashes, non-PDO crashes, injuries, and fatalities. Effect modification was explored by climate type, crash-related factors, traffic exposure, road network design, and urbanicity. Compared to non-EHE days, EHE exposure increased crash risk across all outcomes for same-day and 2-day durations and for most 3-day definitions. The largest effects were generally observed for the most extreme EHE threshold (99th percentile maximum temperature), where PDO crashes showed the largest increase for 2-day exposure (OR = 1.07, 95% CI 1.05-1.09). At the same threshold, we estimate a statewide average of 115 excess PDO crashes, 66 excess non-PDO crashes, and 102 excess injuries annually, while the corresponding fatality estimate (3 excess fatalities annually, 95% CI -1-7) was imprecise. Heterogeneity was observed across climates, crash-related factors, traffic volumes, and urbanicity. This study provides insight into the increased risk of crashes due to heat and the magnitude of impact across EHE definitions in California, supporting the need for heat-responsive traffic-safety measures.

items.title: High Per-capita Area of Accessible Urban Green Space and Lower Self-reported Anxiety/Depression Problems among Older Adults in Korea: A Nationwide Multilevel Study ​.
items.abstract: Although a growing body of literature has linked urban green space to better mental health, less is known about population-normalized area-level green-space provision intended for everyday use, particularly among older adults. This study examined the association between district-level per-capita living-area urban forest area and self-reported anxiety/depression problems among older adults in South Korea. We analyzed data from 79,931 participants aged 65 years or older in the 2024 Korea Community Health Survey. Anxiety/depression problems were assessed using the anxiety/depression dimension of the EQ-5D-3L. Exposure was measured using the 2023 Korea Forest Service per-capita living-area urban forest indicator, assigned to each participant's district of residence, and categorized into quartiles. Associations were examined using two-level random-intercept logistic regression models accounting for clustering within public health center areas and adjusting for individual-level covariates, including the urban-rural residential classification. Overall, 17.5% of participants reported anxiety/depression problems. Compared with the lowest exposure quartile (< 9.7 m2/person), the highest quartile (≥ 31.8 m2/person) was associated with lower odds of anxiety/depression problems (adjusted odds ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval, 0.63-0.87), whereas no statistically significant associations were observed for the intermediate quartiles. These findings suggest that a high level of district-level living-area urban forest provision may be associated with lower odds of anxiety/depression problems among older adults, with potential implications for age-friendly urban planning.

items.title: Greenness, Air Pollution, and Insulin Resistance in a Latin American Megacity: A Longitudinal Mediation Analysis of the ELSA‑Brasil Cohort ​.
items.abstract: Studies examining the relationship between greenness and insulin resistance may elucidate the distal association between greenness and type 2 diabetes. The role of air pollution on this association remains unclear. We investigated whether air pollution mediated the association between greenness and insulin resistance, among non-diabetic participants (N = 2715) from the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Adult Health (ELSA-Brasil) in São Paulo megacity, Brazil, followed-up for approximately 8 years (2008-2010, 2012-2014, 2017-2019). Neighborhood greenness (NDVI, in quartiles), air pollution (PM2.5 and PM10), and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) were examined using mediation analysis, allowing for exposure-mediator interaction. Total, natural direct, and natural indirect effects were estimated, using mixed-effects models, stratified by the neighborhood socioeconomic status (NSES) and adjusted for individual age, sex, education and income. In PM10 analysis for participants from low NSES, higher neighborhood greenness was associated with lower insulin resistance, in a dose-response pattern, as indicated by the total (β = -0.49, 95% CI -0.91, -0.05; β = -0.20, 95% CI -0.54, 0.16; and β = -0.07, 95% CI -0.38, 0.27, for the 4th, 3rd, and 2nd NDVI quartile vs 1st quartile, respectively) and natural direct effects (β = -0.59, 95% CI -1.06, -0.09; β = -0.32, 95% CI -0.67, 0.03; and β = -0.05, 95% CI -0.37, 0.27, for the 4th, 3rd, and 2nd NDVI quartile vs 1st quartile, respectively). The natural indirect effect indicated no mediation by PM10. Similar results were found for the PM2.5 analysis. Greenness was associated with lower insulin resistance among adults living in low NSES areas. However, no evidence of air pollution mediation was found. These results suggest that greater neighborhood greenness may be associated with better cardiometabolic health in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas.

items.title: Untargeted serum and cerebrospinal fluid metabolomics of apparently healthy rabies virus-positive dogs in Nigeria.
items.abstract: Rabies remains a neglected zoonotic disease of global public health importance because of its near-universal fatality, limited reliable antemortem diagnostic options, and absence of effective treatment following the onset of clinical signs. However, metabolic alterations in dogs that are rabies-positive but show no observable clinical signs remain poorly characterized. Therefore, this study aimed to identify differentially abundant metabolites in apparently clinically healthy, direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)-positive dogs compared with DFA-negative dogs. Samples comprising brain tissue, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were collected from 231 apparently clinically healthy dogs. Rabies virus antigen was detected in brain tissue using the direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, and dogs were classified as rabies-positive or negative based on the results. Metabolites were extracted from serum and CSF using a validated sample preparation procedure for untargeted metabolomics. Metabolomic profiling was performed using comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography coupled with time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC-TOFMS) under optimized analytical conditions. Rabies virus antigen was detected in 20 of 231 brain tissue samples (8.7%). Corresponding serum and CSF samples were classified as rabies (DFA)-positive, while 20 negative samples were selected for comparison. After quality control, 868 serum and 300 CSF compounds were retained. Neither principal component analysis nor partial least squares discriminant analysis separated the groups in either matrix. Four serum features remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction: Analyte 634, glyceric acid and Analyte 706 were lower, and benzoic acid was higher, in DFA-positive dogs. Analyte 634 gave the highest discovery-set area under the curve (AUC = 0.9575). In CSF, one unannotated feature (Analyte 369) was lower in DFA-positive dogs after FDR correction. Serum Analyte 634 and CSF Analyte 369 share retention times and mass spectra and may be the same compound. The serum pathways with the lowest enrichment p-values were mapped mainly by glyceric acid alone, and no CSF pathway remained significant after FDR correction. Indolelactic acid was higher in DFA-positive dogs in both matrices at the nominal level only. Four serum features and one CSF feature differed between apparently healthy DFA-positive and DFA-negative dogs after FDR correction. These are discovery-stage candidate features that require structural confirmation, targeted quantification and validation in an independent cohort before any diagnostic claim can be made.

items.title: Perception of Dental Students on a Remote and Asynchronous Course on Evidence-Based Practice. A Qualitative Study.
items.abstract: Considering the influence of the public health context on current teaching modalities and the importance of teaching Evidence-Based Dentistry (EBD) to undergraduates. This study aimed to qualitatively assess the perceptions and opinions of dental students enrolled in a remote and asynchronous EBD course at the School of Dentistry of Ribeirão Preto, University of São Paulo, Brazil. Individual remote interviews were conducted and analysed using the Framework Analysis method. Six major themes emerged: motivations for enrolling, expectations regarding professional impact, perceived gains in knowledge and skills, impressions of the remote format, barriers to learning and suggestions for improvement. Based on students' reports, the course was perceived to expand their understanding of EBD concepts, encourage critical thinking and promote greater autonomy and proactivity in learning. Although they valued the flexibility and technical advantages of the asynchronous format, they also highlighted reduced interaction with instructors and peers as a limitation. The course appeared to achieve its intended goals, as students noted the development of both theoretical knowledge and practical EBD skills. The participants identified the emergence of a self-reported autonomous and critical attitude toward scientific evidence, even though it was not objectively tested. It is therefore suggested that future editions of the course adopt a hybrid or integrated format, combining flexibility with opportunities for in-person discussion and collaboration, in order to maximise engagement and learning outcomes.

items.title: A unified framework for defining and analyzing spatial niches in spatial omics data analysis.
items.abstract: The term 'spatial niche' is widely used in spatial omics analyses but is inconsistently defined across studies. We survey the literature and find that it most commonly refers to the following three distinct concepts: (1) a proximity-based neighborhood around an anchor cell or spatial spot; (2) a computationally derived spatial domain comprising spatially proximal spots or cells with shared molecular features; and (3) a biologically grounded ecosystem comprising cellular and noncellular components that support resident cells. We organize existing studies under this taxonomy and distinguish two main analytical roles-niches as spot-level covariates for modeling local context, and niches as spot clusters for within-niche and between-niche compositional and molecular analyses. To reduce ambiguity, we recommend reserving 'niche' for biological ecosystems while using 'spatial neighborhood' and 'spatial domain' for the corresponding computational constructs. We also provide a practical decision framework to help researchers align niche definitions and analytical strategies with the biological questions at hand.

items.title: From penicillin to precision: reframing AMR in dentistry through time - past lessons, present risks, and future solutions.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a public health global threat projected to cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050 and a major health protection issue. Dentistry contributes approximately 10% of antibiotic prescriptions worldwide, often for conditions where antibiotics offer limited benefit. This article reframes AMR in dentistry through a historical, current, and future lens, integrating risk assessment principles, empirical prescribing trends, and precision strategies. We trace the trajectory from the penicillin era to modern stewardship challenges, examine the dental AMR burden and prescribing patterns using English Surveillance Programme for Antimicrobial Utilisation and Resistance 2023-2024 data, and explore innovative solutions including rapid diagnostics, microbiome restoration, and non-antibiotic therapies. Drawing on evolutionary insights from ancient microbiomes, we argue that AMR is not merely a clinical phenomenon, but a microbial ecological imbalance driven by industrialisation and antibiotic overuse. Future health protection strategies involving interdisciplinary working must combine stewardship with precision dentistry and microbial ecosystem restoration in a one-world setting to mitigate AMR risk while preserving microbial and host resilience. Public health plays an important role working with a range of other stakeholders/agencies in a multidisciplinary approach.

items.title: Health systems and dental services across the four nations of the UK.
items.abstract: Following the devolution of health policy in the late 1990s, England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland have developed increasingly divergent approaches to the planning, commissioning, and delivery of National Health Service (NHS) dental services. This paper provides a comparative analysis of how these four systems now differ, focusing on governance structures, primary care contracting models, and national oral health improvement strategies. Three distinct contractual models have emerged: England has a target-driven system, Scotland and Northern Ireland have fee-per-item arrangements, and Wales is transitioning toward a needs-based care-package model. Scotland and Wales maintain strong national programmes to improve oral health, while England relies on locally commissioned initiatives and Northern Ireland faces capacity constraints within dental public health. These structural differences have implications for prevention, access, and workforce sustainability. Workforce pressures are evident across all nations but are shaped by the financial and operational incentives embedded within each contract model. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that dental policy in the UK has become increasingly divergent post-devolution and policy choices made by each nation have produced distinct systems that continue to evolve independently. These findings highlight ongoing challenges in delivering equitable, prevention-focused NHS dental care and offer insight for future policy development across the four nations.

items.title: Community-based (midstream) approaches to improving child oral health across the UK.
items.abstract: As health is a devolved matter in the UK, each of the four countries has developed a unique approach to improving the oral health of children in order to meet the needs of their population. Public health interventions can be classed into three main categories: national level (upstream) policy initiatives, community-based (midstream) interventions, and individual level (downstream) interventions. Midstream interventions aimed at improving child oral health have been implemented to varying degrees across all four countries of the UK. This article presents a descriptive overview of the main midstream child oral health improvement programmes in each of these four countries, identifying key challenges and opportunities presented around each approach and the policy framework in which they are operating. Common facilitators across all four countries included cross-party political support and integration with early years services, while sustainability of funding and workforce capacity were identified as challenges to implementation. Robust long-term monitoring and evaluation frameworks are needed to inform effective resource allocation and sustain the improvements achieved.

items.title: The role of dental public health in patient, public and the professions' safety: insights and case studies from England.
items.abstract: Introduction Dental public health (DPH) is a clinical dental specialty that works across six domains and the three pillars of public health, including health protection. Across the UK, the DPH speciality workforce plays a vital role in the management of dental health protection cases, utilising their system-level knowledge and clinical leadership to address complex health protection incidents in dental setting. This paper is one of two papers dealing with health protection as part of this Themed Issue on the speciality and aims to provide insights to the systems leadership role it plays within health protection across the UK. The second paper is focussed on antimicrobial resistance, which is another key element of protecting the health of our population.Methods This paper provides a narrative overview of the role of dental public health and includes case studies focussed on the contribution of specialist leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic response and the management of a dental case involving a practice with infection prevention control concerns.Case studies Through these case studies, the proactive and wide impact the speciality has in the protection of patients, the public and the dental workforce is highlighted.Conclusions The management of complex dental incidents, with health protection concerns requires robust, timely, and evidence-informed system response. Specialists in DPH provide critical clinical and system leadership, enabling partnership working and influencing coordinated actions across organisational boundaries. Their specialist understanding of the unique combination of dentistry and public health is crucial for patients, public, and healthcare workforce protection.

items.title: No oral health without a workforce? A public health perspective on the UK oral health workforce.
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide a public health perspective on achieving a sustainable oral health workforce in the UK. This involves taking a strategic perspective on need, demand and supply, drawing on contemporary sociological theory on professions and workforce governance.Despite having more dental professionals than ever before and a diverse skill mix, people living in the UK are challenged to access to dental care, and disease levels are rising among adults. New models of professionalism and workforce governance are emerging, all of which are impacting what it means to be a health professional in a higher income country at this point in the 21st century. Multiple pressures, including demographic, political, economic, technological, and environmental drivers, necessitate strategic transformation while also shaping professions.A future sustainable workforce will require systems redesign, organisational and workforce development to align with population and professional need. A renewed focus on innovation embracing prevention, equity, humanity, professional engagement, and effective leadership will enable the dental workforce to be reshaped over time to serve current and future generations more effectively. There is indeed no oral health without a workforce but there is also no sustainable workforce without systemic reform.

items.title: Embracing health in older age: older people matter.
items.abstract: Introduction The proportion of older adults over 65 years of age is increasing across the UK and Republic of Ireland and projected to reach 25% of the population by 2050. There is a high prevalence of dental disease in older adults, and this is complicated by medical and social circumstances.Aim The aim of this paper is to describe the oral health challenges that older people present and provide an overview of recent studies that have sought to promote oral health in older adults.Discussion The oral health needs of older people have changed considerably over the last 20 years, with most now dentate or partially dentate with a high burden of repair and replacement of restored and missing teeth. This presents an unprecedented burden to the health system, and continued reliance on the existing curative model of oral healthcare is not realistic. There is an urgent need to shift the focus away from treatment to prevention of disease across the life course. Barriers to care for older adults, particularly those who are medically compromised or living in care homes, include mode of remuneration and lack of confidence among primary care dentists to provide domiciliary care to older patients. There is a need for more inter-professional care for older adults, which requires an integrated effort between the stakeholders, including healthcare funders, professionals and patient advocacy groups as we prepare to meet these challenges. Recently developed training initiatives to upskill the dental workforce and develop evidence for care in nursing homes are presented in this paper.Conclusion There is an urgent imperative to educate and empower the population to further reduce the prevalence of dental disease across the life course. More work is needed to develop the future workforce to manage care needs of an increasingly diverse older adult population.

items.title: Dental public health in action: driving change in complex systems.
items.abstract: Consultants in dental public health (CsDPH) translate national policy and evidence-based guidance into local action to improve oral health and reduce inequalities. This article presents three case studies from across England: dental services equity audits in the West Midlands, oral cancer prevention in the North West, and water fluoridation expansion in the North East, illustrating how CsDPH drive change within complex and evolving health and care systems. Beyond generic leadership skills, CsDPH bring a distinctive combination of clinical dental credibility and population health expertise. This enables them to interpret dental evidence and service realities for wider system leaders, align National Health Service dental commissioning and local authority prevention programmes with broader priorities, and connect agendas across primary care, public health, cancer pathways, and wider determinants of health. Their dual training supports the use of local intelligence to target prevention, equity, and fairness, particularly where oral health inequalities exist, working with partners and communities around shared goals. The case studies demonstrate how CsDPH adapt national frameworks to local contexts and embed oral health within integrated care, strengthening prevention and improving access for those with greatest need.

items.title: A life course approach to population oral health.
items.abstract: Oral health inequalities are caused by social, commercial, and political determinants, and remain a persistent national and global challenge. This paper presents an overview of the social determinants of health and highlights the importance of a life course perspective to examine and understand how health inequalities are produced and perpetuated. We discuss how life course theory is linked to wider public health strategies such as the Common Risk Factor Approach and population (or upstream) approaches to prevention, and how it applies to oral health promotion. We emphasise the relevance of a life course approach for dental professionals and policymakers concerned with reducing oral health inequalities and propose how such an approach can be translated into evidence-based oral health policy and practice.

items.title: Dental public health: a trainee perspective from England.
items.abstract: Dental public health (DPH) specialty trainees are dentally qualified and focus on improving oral health at a population level in addition to individual patients. DPH trainees enter training with a broad range of dental career experiences. To attain specialist registration, DPH trainees undertake a 3-4-year programme which develops both technical and strategic leadership skills. DPH training includes activities such as advocating for oral health within the general health context, developing and applying evidence-based guidelines to support health improvement initiatives and addressing oral health inequalities amongst vulnerable and disadvantaged groups. Experiential learning is a key component of DPH training, delivered through projects and placements across a range of health and social care organisations. This trainee-authored paper provides an overview of the possible motivation for entering DPH specialty training, examples of the training experiences involved and consideration of how the wider dental workforce benefit from engaging with DPH teams.

items.title: Evolution of UK dental public health education: current perspectives and future directions.
items.abstract: Dental public health is one of 13 recognised dental specialities in the UK and is a discipline focused on improving oral health and reducing health inequalities, optimising the benefits of healthcare, ensuring services are equitable, efficient and effective, and providing health protection to safeguard members of the dental team, patients and the public. Learning outcomes relevant to dental public health feature in undergraduate dental curricula and the importance of dental public health knowledge, skills and understanding is becoming increasingly important due to the recognition of oral health as a core component of general health, greater integration of oral healthcare services in primary care and increasing skill mix in the oral health workforce.Dental education has advanced significantly in recent years to embrace more primary care-based training, where students are exposed to patient care earlier in their training and often in underserved communities that are more diverse and challenging for the delivery of dental care. This modernisation of dental curricula has also occurred in dental public health where traditional approaches are being replaced with more experiential learning opportunities outside of the dental school and undertaken by direct engagement with communities and the organisations that support members of the community who are more vulnerable and disadvantaged. These new innovative approaches contextualise dental public health in a way that is difficult to replicate in a lecture and situate learning in real-world environments such as schools, community spaces, workplaces and civic and religious institutions.The aim of the article is to provide an overview of dental public health education at undergraduate level, and to place this in the context of wider dental education frameworks such as the UK General Dental Council Safe practitioner framework and workforce development.

items.title: Modelling future dental workforce need for adults with special care needs within the UK.
items.abstract: Aims Special care dentistry (SCD) in the United Kingdom (UK) provides care for a range of adults with complex needs, including physically and mentally disabled people, older adults with dementia, adults with medical, emotional, sensory, mental or social impairment, or a combination of these factors, who require care in a range of settings. The aim of this research was to establish a needs-based workforce planning model and tool that focuses on assessing SCD's workforce capacity and capability to deliver tailored dental services for the UK's disabled populace.Methods A predictive analytics tool using Python and HTML was developed to integrate multiple large national datasets to identify key variables for long-term workforce planning and model future SCD demand through 2050. There are currently 13 million disabled adults, 5.9 million of whom are 'disabled; limited a lot'. National and regional population demand projections for SCD were calculated until 2050 using data mainly from the Office for National Statistics and the 2021-2022 Family Resources Survey. National data on the specialty were obtained from registration and survey data. National and regional resource supply projections for SCD were calculated until at least 2040 recursively from 2018 taking into consideration multiple factors.Results A detailed analysis highlighted several key findings. Under the present scenario, supply aligns with demand only when 5-8% of the 'disabled; limited a lot' category require complex dental care, suggesting that only a small proportion of needs is currently met by specialists. Planning for the future, for the baseline scenario, where 50% of the 'disabled; limited a lot' population is considered to have complex needs, even adding 150 specialty trainees per year will not meet projected need until 2040 due to the length of training. If the other half of the 'disabled; limited a lot' population is assumed to have moderate needs, then upskilling and adding 0.2% of the primary care dentists' pool, or about 80 primary care dentists to the dentists with extended skills (DES) pool per year, would allow this level of moderate need to be met as early as 2034. Strategic workforce redirections, such as even transitioning just 0.1% or 40 primary care dentists into the DES pool per year, could begin to significantly alter the supply-demand dynamics, together with a modest increase in specialty training numbers.Conclusions This study highlights the immense and growing need for SCD and the upskilling of frontline practitioners in caring for adults with additional needs. In essence, while the challenge before us is monumental, it is not insurmountable. Strategic planning, focused training initiatives, and nimble workforce reallocation are pivotal to ensuring that the UK's vulnerable populations receive the specialised dental care they deserve.

items.title: How commerce influences health and oral health.
items.abstract: There is increasing recognition that commercial factors can influence health and oral health both negatively and positively. This narrative review summarises the tactics used to market sugar, tobacco and alcohol, products that can be harmful to oral health. This article considers options open to governments and official agencies to combat the adverse influence of commerce on oral health. It also examines the role of the dental care system itself as a commercial determinant. Finally, it also reviews how commercial determinants can positively influence oral health.Dental professionals need to be aware of the influence of commercial actors on oral health. Such knowledge can enable them to act as advocates for health and oral health improvement and to engage meaningfully in wider societal debates.

items.title: Dental public health: past, present and a future?
items.abstract: This paper explores the development of dental public health from two perspectives: that of a discipline and that as a specialist area of activity within the National Health Service. It argues that dental public health as a discipline has grown in importance, not least since its inclusion by the General Dental Council within the undergraduate curricula for both dental and dental care professionals but also by recognition as one of the 13 dental specialties. However, as a speciality, it has been challenged by repeated re-structuring of the health service resulting in fragmented leadership and reduced capacity. While similar issues have impacted on public health, the decline has been compounded by the decline of state-funded dental care as a share of all dental care provision. While the academic discipline continues to have influence on policy at various levels, the speciality finds itself at a crossroads. Going forward, the speciality needs to ensure that it demonstrates its value within the wider healthcare system. This can be achieved by articulating its role in contributing to oral health improvements aligned with public health principles and, where system shortcomings exist, challenging those in power.

items.title: MRI measures of oxygen extraction fraction in the subacute phase of mild neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
items.abstract: Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of clinical progression is critical. Our group has previously demonstrated regional quantification of oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), a noninvasive MRI-derived measure of cerebral oxygen utilization in newborns with encephalopathy receiving therapeutic hypothermia (TH). This study evaluates whether regional OEF measured between 2 and 7 days of life distinguishes newborns with mild encephalopathy who are not treated with TH and subsequently exhibit clinical progression within the first day of life from those who remain clinically stable. Vessel-specific OEF maps of the brain were obtained using the accelerated T2-relaxation-under-phase-contrast (aTRUPC) MRI technique from full-term newborns with mild encephalopathy and healthy controls. OEF was quantified across six predefined venous drainage regions. Fifty-three full-term newborns (28 with mild encephalopathy, 25 healthy controls) were enrolled. Seven newborns with mild encephalopathy showed clinical progression on the first day of life and received TH (TH group); the remaining did not receive TH (non-TH group). OEF was significantly lower in cortical regions in the TH group compared with healthy controls and the non-TH group. Cortical OEF represents an innovative imaging biomarker. Prospective studies are needed to determine its value for risk stratification during the therapeutic window. Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of progression remains challenging during the therapeutic window. Cortical oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) measured between 2 and 7 days of life was significantly lower in newborns who progressed within the first day of life than in newborns with mild encephalopathy who did not progress and healthy controls. Regional OEF may provide a noninvasive biomarker for early risk stratification and treatment decision-making in newborns with mild encephalopathy.

items.title: Measuring Quality in Assisted Living: The Oregon Way.
items.abstract: Assisted living (AL) is the largest residential long-term care provider for dementia specific services in the United States (US), but no nationally accepted standards exist for measuring AL quality in the US Oregon's legislatively mandated Quality Measurement Program (QMP) requires all licensed AL communities to report five quality indicators annually: direct care staff retention, training compliance, falls with injury, prescriptions for nonstandard antipsychotic medication use, and resident satisfaction scores as measured by CoreQ. We linked the 2024 QMP quality measure data to administrative data for all licensed Oregon AL communities with 25 or more beds (n = 450). We examined whether these indicators differ by organizational characteristics. We used ordinary least squares regression models to examine the associations between these quality metrics and memory care (MC) endorsement, profit status, Medicaid contract, size, and rural location. MC communities reported a higher rate of falls with injury (11.6% vs. 7.3%) and double the rate of nonstandard antipsychotic prescriptions (18.6% vs. 9.1%) compared to standalone AL, with no statistically significant differences in staff retention, training compliance, or overall resident satisfaction scores. Nonprofit communities had higher staff retention (+11.5 percentage points) and higher resident satisfaction scores across all CoreQ domains compared to their for-profit counterparts. Finally, communities with a Medicaid contract reported higher nonstandard antipsychotic prescription rates (+4.7 percentage points) and lower overall CoreQ scores compared to non-Medicaid communities. Performance on some QMP measures differed by MC endorsement, ownership structure, and Medicaid contract. Because QMP does not capture measures of resident acuity, these differences should not be read as differences in overall care quality. Future work should examine whether and how contextual information such as payer-mix and case-mix adjustment and ownership data could make public reporting more informative.

items.title: Evolutionary Emergence of HIV-1 Subtype G and Subtype-Linked Transmitted NNRTI Resistance Among HIV Patients in Oman.
items.abstract: This study aimed to characterize HIV-1 subtype distribution and transmitted drug resistance (TDR) patterns among treatment-naïve individuals in Oman to inform evidence-based treatment guidelines and molecular surveillance strategies. A nationwide retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted to analyse HIV-1 pol gene sequences from all newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve individuals in Oman over a nine-year period. A total of 963 treatment-naïve individuals diagnosed with HIV-1 infection between 2016 and 2024 were included in this nationwide retrospective analysis. Partial pol gene sequences encompassing protease and reverse transcriptase regions were amplified and sequenced. Subtyping was performed using multiple computational tools (COMET, RIP and jpHMM) with phylogenetic confirmation using maximum-likelihood methods. Drug resistance mutations were interpreted using the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (version 9.5). Subtype G was the predominant lineage (38.2%, n = 368), followed by subtype A1 (28.0%, n = 270), CRF01_AE (11.7%, n = 113), and subtype C (7.4%, n = 71). Sixty-four other recombinant strains were identified, including three novel CRFs candidates. Subtype A1 exhibited the highest resistance burden (21.1%, n = 57), primarily associated with the K103N substitution, whereas subtype G remained largely susceptible (96.2%, n = 354). Overall, 13.0% (n = 125) harboured at least one NNRTI resistance mutation under the ≥ 15 threshold. No major resistance mutations were detected against nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), including tenofovir, emtricitabine, and lamivudine. The Omani HIV-1 epidemic is characterized by subtype G dominance, subtype-specific resistance patterns, and identification of putative novel circulating recombinant forms (CRFs). The high NNRTI resistance burden (13.0%) supports prioritizing INSTI-based regimens. Continuous molecular surveillance is essential for monitoring emerging resistance.

items.title: Making patient-reported outcomes reusable at scale.
items.abstract: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are essential to understanding how people live with illness, treatment, and care, and are increasingly promoted for routine use in clinical practice, quality improvement, and value-based health care. PROs are also increasingly relevant in digital health and artificial intelligence applications, both as inputs to predictive models and as outputs reflecting patient-centred aspects of health. Yet, PROs remain difficult to reuse at scale: their implementation is inconsistent across health-care settings, measurement approaches are highly heterogeneous, and PROs are rarely available as large, standardised, analysable datasets suitable for multisite analyses and advanced analytics, including artificial intelligence models. In this Viewpoint, we argue that the central challenge is not a lack of initiatives, but the absence of a coherent, end-to-end approach that connects measurement, routine capture, data standards, and analytic reuse. We propose a practical four-step pathway towards Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) PROs. This pathway focuses on (1) defining the outcome domains that matter and selecting high-quality questionnaires; (2) capturing PROs consistently at the point of care in structured, computable formats; (3) storing them in analysable, shareable data models; and (4) establishing transparent cross-questionnaire linking to enable comparable scores. None of these steps poses major technical challenges in isolation; the primary difficulty is that these efforts are often developed in silos, with minimal coordination across disciplines, from questionnaire development and validation to clinical workflows, informatics standards, analytic infrastructures, and governance. A shared FAIR-PROs approach would allow PROs to become a routine, reusable component of learning health systems and a driver of both person-centred care and data-driven innovation.

items.title: Clade I and Clade II monkeypox virus in Barcelona, 2025-2026: More similarities than differences in a case-case study.
items.abstract: Clade I is becoming more predominant in Europe and may differ epidemiologically from Clade II. This case-case study (N=100) compared Clades I and II detected in Barcelona between September 2025 and June 2026. Crude and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) were estimated using logistic regression models. While the overall epidemiological profile and clinical severity were similar, Clade I cases were more likely to reside in lower-income districts, less likely to be migrants (aOR=0.34, 95%CI 0.25;0.47), and more frequently reported sexual activity during leisure activities(aOR=7.55, 95%CI 3.93;14.53), attendance at large-scale events(aOR=18.78, 95%CI 7.40;47.67). Clinically, Clade I cases showed higher odds of fever (aOR=1.55, 95%CI 1.05;2.28), odynophagia (aOR=5.13, 95%CI 2.98;8.85), oral rash (aOR=42.60, 95%CI 12.11;149.88) and generalized rash, whereas generalized lymphadenopathy (aOR=0.33, 95%CI 0.15;0.71) and anogenital rash (aOR=0.55, 95%CI 0.36;0.83) were less frequent. These findings suggest that Clade Ib circulation in urban settings currently mirrors the epidemiological patterns established by Clade IIb.

items.title: Acute Care Utilization and Cost Outcomes of Home-Based Palliative Care for Persons Living with Dementia in the United States: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Given the shift toward value-based payment models, which reward high-quality and cost-effective care, an increasing number of palliative care programs are being integrated across care settings in health systems and organizations in the United States to reduce patient use of more costly services such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits. Home-based palliative care (HBPalC) is one community-based palliative care delivery model that may help delay facility and nursing home placement and reduce hospital use and costs. This review synthesized evidence on hospital utilization and cost outcomes associated with HBPalC among people living with dementia (PLWD) in the United States. PubMed, Embase, and Cumulated Index in Nursing and Allied Health Literature were searched from inception through October 2025. All U.S.-based studies were included if samples included PLWD and the study examined the impact of HBPalC on hospital utilization (i.e., hospitalization and ED use) or health care costs. A total of eight studies were included. Overall, HBPalC provided core services such as symptom management and advanced care planning. PLWD-specific HBPalC focused on addressing neurobehavioral symptoms and supporting caregivers. HBPalC was consistently associated with reductions in hospitalization and associated costs, although evidence for changes in ED utilization was not available, with no studies reporting ED outcomes for PLWD specifically. HBPalC was associated with reduced hospitalization, but its impact on ED use was inconclusive for PLWD. Most studies had heterogeneous patient samples and did not report PLWD-specific outcomes. There is a lack of HBPalC specifically designed for PLWD, and more studies are needed to evaluate HBPalC's impact on ED use among PLWD.

items.title: Preventive Home Visits for Older People: The Effect of Continuity on Mobility, Nursing Home Admission and Mortality.
items.abstract: To investigate how preventive home visits, and return visits by the same healthcare worker, were associated with mobility, nursing home admission, and mortality among older adults. Observational cohort study. Self-report of preventive home visits and mobility. Nursing home admission and mortality were register-based. Multivariable logistic regression models with generalized estimating equations. The Danish Intervention Study on Preventive Home Visits. About half received one or more preventive home visits. The majority had return visits from the same healthcare worker. There were no significant associations between number of visits and return visits, and nursing home admission and mortality, respectively. Compared to receiving multiple preventive home visits by different healthcare workers, receiving no visits was significantly associated with lower odds of mobility limitations. A tendency to better mobility was observed when receiving return visits by the same healthcare worker, but statistically insignificant. While a continuous relation to the healthcare worker did not show a significant advantage over intermittent relation, the other results are consistent with healthy user-bias, suggesting that pre-existing health drives the observed pattern of receiving preventive home visits. A continuous relation to the healthcare worker may potentially benefit those at risk of functional limitations. Heterogeneous findings in previous studies may stem from variations in frequency and content of visits, which are rarely studied. Multi-disciplinary studies on organization, frequency, and evaluation of preventive home visits are needed. This study was reported in accordance with STROBE guidelines for cohort studies. No patient of public contribution.

items.title: Digital Tools for the Detection of Dermatitis: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Contact dermatitis (CD) plays a significant role in occupational health due to its frequent occurrence and environmental triggers and is among the most common occupational diseases in Western countries. Despite its prevalence, occupational contact dermatitis (OCD) is often overlooked by occupational physicians, largely due to limited knowledge and a lack of validated detection tools. Advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising opportunities for improving early detection, yet an overview of available digital tools and their effectiveness in dermatitis detection is lacking. A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cinahl, and Scopus. The search focused on original studies published in peer-reviewed journals between 2014 and 2024. Forty-three studies evaluating digital tools for dermatitis detection were included, categorized as models (n = 31) or devices (n = 12). Models represent AI algorithms not yet in practical use, while devices are tools already implemented. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were the most commonly used computational technique. Median sensitivity and specificity were 0.84 and 0.97 for all tools, 0.85 and 0.97 for models, and 0.78 and 0.97 for devices. The results provided in this review will serve as valuable input for the development of new tools to enhance early OCD detection.

items.title: From Diagnosis to Adaptation: Meaning-Making Throughout the Illness Experience of Patients With Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension-A Hermeneutic Phenomenological Study.
items.abstract: To explore the illness experience and meaning-making of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension from diagnosis to adaptation. A qualitative study using a Heideggerian hermeneutic phenomenological design. From July to December 2025, purposive sampling recruited 12 adults with PAH from a teaching hospital in northern Taiwan. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, with data collection and analysis occurring concurrently. Transcripts were read, compared, and interpreted through the hermeneutic circle, supported by field notes and reflexive notes. Six interrelated themes and 15 categories were identified: (1) Cycles of hope and disappointment; (2) Physical decline and disruption to daily life after disease onset; (3) Waiting on the edge of collapse; (4) Information gaps and unmet information needs; (5) Rediscovering possibilities for living; and (6) Finding a place in life within the limits of the disease. Patients experienced diagnostic delays, physical decline, treatment waiting, and information gaps. As treatment stabilised, they shifted from hoping to return to pre-illness lives to adjusting expectations, roles, and attitudes and engaging in disease management. Adaptation was an ongoing process. Participants' retrospective accounts suggest that adaptation to PAH involves more than accepting the illness. Patients continuously reinterpret the illness, themselves, and their future amid physical and daily-life changes. Family, peers, and healthcare professionals support hope and adaptation. Care for pulmonary arterial hypertension should extend beyond disease control and symptom management. Nurses can support patients through case management, information, and family and peer support across illness stages. This study highlights illness adaptation as a continuous process of adjusting perspectives on illness, self, and future, suggesting that care for PHA should address patients' long-term lives alongside disease management. This study was reported in accordance with the COREQ guidelines. No patient or public contribution.

items.title: Effects of plastic exposure on human health.
items.abstract: Plastic pollution is a critical environmental and public health challenge, with growing evidence linking human exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics, and associated chemicals to adverse health outcomes. This review summarises current knowledge on the health effects of plastic exposure, addressing both established findings and critical knowledge gaps. We examine human exposure to plastics and associated health risks based on available clinical and epidemiological evidence. Additionally, we explore chemicals associated with plastic, including their potential as carcinogens and disruptors of endocrine and immune function. Recognising the urgent need for preventive measures, we examine emerging strategies for reducing plastic burdens, including global regulatory efforts like the United Nations Plastics Treaty and proposed public health guidelines. By integrating current evidence, this review aims to provide a foundation for advancing research and informing strategies to mitigate health risks associated with plastic.

items.title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Body Donation Research (2006-2025): Perspectives From Medical Education, Ethics, and Policy.
items.abstract: Body donation is fundamental to anatomical education and biomedical research. The field has expanded from technical dissection to include ethical, regulatory, and educational dimensions, yet a systematic bibliometric analysis of its evolution is lacking. This study maps the knowledge structure, collaboration patterns, and research frontiers of the English-language body donation literature (2006-2025), focusing on the interplay among anatomical education, cultural ethics, and institutional governance. Publications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on August 5, 2026; 419 English-language articles met the eligibility criteria. CiteSpace (v6.2.R3) and VOSviewer (v1.6.18) were used to analyze collaboration networks, cocitation structures, citation bursts, and keyword co-occurence. Annual output increased steadily across three phases. The retrieved literature is concentrated in a small number of countries and institutions, a pattern inseparable from the language and database boundaries of the corpus, and collaboration is denser within regions than between them. Keyword co-occurence produced five clusters, mapped onto three analytical domains: anatomical education, cultural ethics, and institutional governance, the last with no cluster of its own. Organ donation concepts are still frequently conflated with body donation, and research frontiers have shifted from gross anatomy pedagogy toward legal regulation and public willingness. Body donation research has evolved from a technique-driven paradigm into a multidisciplinary field integrating humanistic care, legal frameworks, and educational innovation. Remaining gaps include the uneven representation of world regions in the indexed literature and the conflation of body and organ donation; both constrain culturally adaptable governance and anatomical education.

items.title: Genome-wide DNA methylation study uncovers epigenetic markers associated with early life stress in individuals with major depressive disorder.
items.abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is a significant risk factor for major depressive disorder (MDD); however, the epigenetic mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly characterized, partly due to the lack of trauma-stratified control groups in previous studies. We performed genome-wide DNA methylation profiling using Reduced-Representative Bisulfite Sequencing (RRBS) on whole blood samples from 90 adults divided into four groups: MDD with ELS (n = 30), MDD without ELS (n = 30), controls with ELS (n = 15), and controls without ELS (n = 15). Differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified employing MethylKit and DMRcate (≥5 CpGs, FDR < 0.05) and annotated via FUMA GENE2FUNC and clusterProfiler. Our analysis revealed 551, 581, and 479 DMRs in comparisons of MDD vs. control, MDD + ELS vs. control + ELS, and MDD non-ELS vs. control non-ELS, respectively. Core genes SELENOO, FASN, and THOC7 were consistently differentially methylated across all groups, reflecting shared mitochondrial, metabolic, and RNA-processing mechanisms. The MDD + ELS group demonstrated a higher DMR burden, particularly in regions associated with active promoter chromatin, with ELS-specific genes HIVEP3 and NRL exhibiting GWAS evidence linked to treatment-resistant depression and ADHD. Conversely, DMRs in MDD non-ELS were enriched in repressed chromatin states, with hypermethylation in loci within CAMK4 and CALM1 suggesting constitutive silencing of calcium-dependent neuronal signaling pathways. Our findings underscore the significant contribution of ELS to specific epigenetic changes associated with MDD, particularly in neurodevelopmental and stress-response pathways. In contrast, MDD without ELS exhibited a distinct methylation profile that affected synapses and synaptic plasticity. Our study, therefore, emphasizes the necessity of trauma-informed approaches in psychiatric research.

items.title: Chronic Endometritis: Does the Current Evidence Justify Routine Diagnosis and Treatment?
items.abstract: Chronic endometritis (CE) has become a widely investigated and increasingly treated condition in reproductive medicine, despite persistent uncertainty regarding its biological and clinical validity. In this review, we critically examine whether CE, as currently defined by endometrial CD138-positive plasma cells, constitutes a clinically meaningful pathology that justifies routine screening and management. Current diagnostic criteria are heterogeneous and unvalidated; CD138-positive plasma cells vary across the menstrual cycle and are also found in fertile women, while evidence for a consistent infectious or inflammatory phenotype remains lacking. Although an association between CE and reproductive failure has been reported in several observational studies vulnerable to confounding, large euploid embryo transfer studies challenge the existence of a prevalent endometrial factor that substantially impairs implantation. Most importantly, while antibiotics reduce CD138 positivity, controlled studies have not shown any impact of treatment on reproductive outcomes, and apparent benefits largely arise from methodologically weaker comparisons. Until biological validity and clinical benefit are established, routine screening and treatment for CE in reproductive medicine cannot be justified.
