items.title: Assessors' Perspectives on the Failure to Fail Underperforming Nursing Students: A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Aims The aim of this narrative review is to explore reasons for the failure to fail of underperforming, nursing students, from the assessor perspective. Background When assessing student nurses on practice placements, assessors often have difficulty assigning a failing grade to students who fail to demonstrate competence in accordance with practice standards. Failure to fail is the act of passing nursing students on their clinical placement who do not display acceptable clinical performance. This issue can have considerable consequences for patient and staff safety, as well as legal implications for the workplace and the nursing profession. Design A mixed-methods narrative review utilises thematic synthesis, following Thomas and Harden's (2008) three-stage approach of coding, development of descriptive themes and generation of analytical themes. Methods A search of CINAHL, Emcare, Ovid and ProQuest-British Nursing Index and Google Scholar was conducted, and hand-searching techniques were utilised. All data were sourced between November 2023 and January 2024. English-language literature published since 2019, focusing on the assessment of underperforming students from the assessor's perspective, was reviewed. Results Eleven papers were included in the review, nine of which were qualitative and two quantitative papers. Thematic synthesis was used to identify four main themes: educational assessment and feedback, student assessment, practical constraints and educational psychology. Conclusion Failure to fail is an ongoing issue and was evidenced in the literature from a variety of high-income countries. Assessors experienced various challenges in failing underperforming students. It is essential for assessors to have the support of practice educators and university faculties, to have protected time to complete assessments and associated documentation and to have access to further education and training.

items.title: Action Control as a Moderator of Automatic-Reflective Processes on Physical Activity.
items.abstract: Dual-process theories have demonstrated considerable utility in predicting physical activity behavior, yet mechanisms capable of simultaneously targeting reflective and automatic processes remain underexplored. This study examined whether action control strengthens the association between reflective processes (i.e., intention) and physical activity while attenuating the effect of goal-conflicting automatic processes (i.e., implicit attitude). A two-wave prospective design was employed, with assessments administered 1 week apart to 529 undergraduate students from Australia (n = 259) and the United States (n = 270). Path analysis indicated that, contrary to expectations, action control strengthened the association between goal-conflicting implicit attitude and physical activity behavior. Action control also partially mediated the relationship between intention and physical activity. These findings provide empirical support for a moderative perspective on dual-process theory and position action control as a volitional mechanism that facilitates the translation of intentions into behavior while shaping the behavioral influence of automatic processes.

items.title: Associations of short and long sleep duration with multiple adverse health outcomes among ageing adults in South Africa.
items.abstract: Background The aim of this study was to assess the longitudinal associations between short and long sleep duration with multiple adverse health outcomes (mortality, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, functional limitations, depressive symptoms, loneliness, posttraumatic stress (PTSD) symptoms, impaired cognition, dynapenia, addominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity, and general obesity) among community-residents 40 years and older, also broken down by sex. Methods Data from three waves of the "Health and Ageing in Africa: A Longitudinal Study of an INDEPTH Community in South Africa (HAALSI)" (2015-2022) were utilized. There were 10483 observations of people who were 40 years of age or older. The American National Sleep Foundation was used to measure self-reported sleep duration. The association between sleep duration and 7-year mortality was assessed using hazard ratios. The longitudinal relationships between short and long sleep duration (using normal or recommended sleep length as a reference) and unfavorable health outcomes were estimated using linear, conditional, and multinomial logistic fixed effects (FE) regressions. Results This study showed an association between short sleep duration and mortality, hypertension, depressive symptoms, and cardiovascular disease, while there were no significant associations between short sleep duration and diabetes, functional limitations, loneliness, PTSD symptoms, impaired cognition, dynapenia, abdominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity and general obesity. Furthermore, this study found an association between long sleep duration and functional limitations, depressive symptoms, loneliness, PTSD symptoms, impaired or lower cognition, dynapenia, abdominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity and general obesity, while there were no significant associations between long sleep duration and mortality, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and diabetes. Conclusions Short sleep duration was associated with four and long sleep duration with nine adverse health outcomes. The results can be applied to health literacy and education initiatives to promote getting adequate sleep, which is a crucial aspect of total sleep health. Future studies from other countries are recommended.

items.title: The impact of positive experiences in childhood and adolescence on later mental health: A systematic review of longitudinal cohort studies.
items.abstract: Background Positive experiences in early life are increasingly recognised as important contributors to mental health across the lifespan. While adverse childhood experiences have been extensively studied, the role of singular and cumulative positive experiences remains less well understood. This systematic review synthesises longitudinal evidence on associations between empirically measured positive experiences in childhood or adolescence and adult mental health outcomes. Methods Four databases (APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, and Scopus) were searched from inception to January 2024 and updated in May 2026. Eligible studies were longitudinal cohort studies examining associations between exposure to singular or cumulative positive experiences from birth to age 18 and adult outcomes of depression, anxiety, psychosis, or bipolar disorder, measured through clinical diagnoses, symptom-level assessments, or broader psychopathology indices. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist, and findings were narratively synthesised. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023482969). Results 20 studies ( N = 63,271) were included. Physical activity, engaged parenting, peer social support, school belonging, school connectedness, religious service attendance, and cumulative positive experiences were associated with a reduced risk of adult depression. School belonging, school connectedness, perceived support from family and friends, and a greater number of positive relative to adverse experiences were associated with lower levels of anxiety. A positive home atmosphere, greater social cohesion, higher levels of physical and leisure-time activity, and participation in sports competitions were linked to fewer psychotic symptoms. No studies examined bipolar disorder. All studies were of moderate to high quality, although definitions and measurement of positive experiences varied. Conclusion Positive experiences in childhood and adolescence may contribute to better mental health outcomes in adulthood. However, further longitudinal research is needed to clarify mechanisms, timing, and cumulative effects, and to standardise measurement across diverse populations.

items.title: What's the Goal? Reconsidering the Importance of Higher-Order Cognition in Internalizing Psychopathology.
items.abstract: To date, the field of computational psychiatry has largely focused on testing for dysfunction within lower-level cognitive processes in psychopathology, such as biases related to attention, reinforcement learning and memory. While this work has yielded important insights, there is clear evidence from empirically validated psychotherapeutic interventions to suggest that these lower-level cognitive processes are often intact. Here, we argue that etiological and maintaining factors for internalizing disorders may be more appropriately situated in higher level cognitive processes such as goal-selection. We further suggest that future research should incorporate behavioral tasks and models that allow for participant-defined goals to reveal higher-level mechanistic targets. We believe that considering these higher-level deficits in goal-selection, possibly in tandem with low-level impairments, may augment ecological validity and clinical relevance.

items.title: Beyond Restriction: Physical Activity as Part of Eating Disorder Treatment and the Factors Influencing Its Implementation. A Mixed-Method Study.
items.abstract: Objective Although there is growing consensus in the literature that physical activity (PA) can be a beneficial component of eating disorder (ED) treatment, it is less clear whether this shift is reflected in clinical practice. This study explored current practice and clinicians' experiences with implementing PA in ED treatment in Norway, including barriers and facilitators. Method This mixed-methods study includes a national survey of clinicians and unit managers in Norwegian ED services (N = 27), supplemented by interviews with seven clinicians from the sample. Data were analyzed using descriptive data and reflexive thematic analysis. Results PA was offered in 14 of 27 participating units (52%), mainly in inpatient services. Quantitative findings indicated that implementation varied with local competence, leadership, resources, and clinical frameworks. Main barriers were identified to be limited resources, a need for competence development, lack of professional networks, and need for clinical guidelines. The interviews identified four overarching themes related to experiences with PA, which largely supported the quantitative findings. Interview findings highlighted how therapists used therapeutic alliance-building to motivate and educate patients. Barriers identified were lack of national guidelines and a reliance on local champions contributing to the fragility of PA services. Conclusions PA provision in Norwegian ED services varies considerably, with 52% of the survey-responding units providing PA in treatment. Clinicians highlighted both the therapeutic potential of PA and challenges related to implementation, suggesting a need for greater organizational support and competence development. The low response rate may introduce non-response bias, potentially affecting validity.

items.title: Longitudinal attendance trajectories across three academic years in English secondary schools: Putative predictors and associations with emotional difficulties.
items.abstract: Objective To identify longitudinal attendance trajectories across secondary education, examine factors associated with trajectory class membership and assess associations with emotional difficulties. Method Three years of linked #BeeWell survey and administrative data were analysed for 28,736 pupils aged 12-13 in 2021/2022 across 156 secondary schools in Greater Manchester, England. Piecewise latent growth mixture modelling identified attendance trajectories across nine consecutive terms. Multinomial logistic regression examined putative predictors of class membership across individual, family, school, peer and community domains. Emotional difficulties were modelled as a latent growth process. Results Consistently High (92.4%), Progressive Decline (5.1%) and Decline and Partial Recovery (2.5%) trajectories emerged. Socio-economic disadvantage was strongly associated with both sub-optimal (persistently absent) trajectories (ORs = 2.94-4.97), with dose-response effects for neighbourhood deprivation. Special educational needs were associated with greater odds while sufficient sleep, school belonging and minoritized ethnic group membership was associated with lower odds of both sub-optimal classes; good physical health was associated with reduced odds of Progressive Decline only. LGBTQ+ identity was not independently associated in fully adjusted models. Pupils following sub-optimal trajectories reported higher emotional difficulties at study outset (d ≈ .34-.41), with no differences in rates of change over time. Conclusion Attendance trajectories are socially patterned and associated with multiple co-occurring vulnerabilities. Emotional difficulties differences existed at outset but did not widen, inferring underlying vulnerability rather than a cumulative process across the observation window. Evidence of partial recovery indicates improvement is possible. Putative predictors tested herein offer promising candidates for research into causal mechanisms.

items.title: How Do Exhausted Adolescents Become Ready for Activation? A Developmental Recovery Framework for School Refusal and Youth Social Withdrawal.
items.abstract: School refusal and youth social withdrawal are commonly addressed by restoring participation, yet some adolescents appear too exhausted to use otherwise appropriate opportunities for activity. This integrative narrative review synthesises school-refusal research, behavioural activation, developmental psychology, stress recovery, self-determination, and self-efficacy theory to examine how readiness for engagement returns. It proposes a Developmental Recovery Framework in which declining recovery capacity may progress towards exhaustion, while relational and environmental support creates an assisted recovery period. Recovery Quality is described across four overlapping domains-thinking, self-regulation, creativity, and social connection-that may recover unevenly and indicate when support is becoming psychologically usable. The framework can be entered before persistent absence or during recovery from established withdrawal. Assessment emphasises school-home differences, repeated multi-informant observation, and the quality rather than duration of digital activity. Practical implications are to build from capacities already returning, maintain a usable relationship without coercion, and define recovery beyond school attendance. The framework is a conceptual synthesis requiring longitudinal testing and should complement, not replace, diagnostic assessment and established interventions.

items.title: Clinical Profiles Among Adolescents Referred for Suspected Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: an Exploratory Retrospective Study.
items.abstract: IntroductionThe Clinical High Risk of psychosis (CHRp) concept is widely used to identify adolescents at risk of psychotic disorder. However, current tools lack specificity regarding actual transition, as they struggle to distinguish developmental vulnerabilities from true prodromal psychotic states.MethodsThis retrospective monocentric study included 26 French adolescents aged 11-18 referred between 2021 and 2023 to a specialized CHRp consultation. The multidisciplinary evaluation, involving involving child and adolescent and adult psychiatry professionals, combined the CAARMS, developmental and attachment-based interviews, and final synthesis considering differential diagnoses.ResultsNine adolescents were classified as CHRp, and 5 of them transitioned to psychosis. CHRp adolescents were significantly younger and more often referred through emergency department. An exploratory multidimensional analysis identified two clinical profiles: a psychosis-spectrum profile and a broader psychological and environmental vulnerability profile characterized by attachment-related difficulties, child welfare placement, and self-harm behaviors, without transition to psychosis.ConclusionA diagnostic approach grounded in developmental and environmental specificities may enhance the predictive specificity of CHRp status in adolescents. Differentiating psychotic vulnerability from alternative psychopathological trajectories-particularly attachment-related and intrafamilial relational difficulties-may appear crucial for tailoring early interventions. It may help identify a more homogeneous and genuinely at-risk population.

items.title: Cue-Induced Craving Predicts Momentary Risk for Binge Eating in BED: An EMA Study.
items.abstract: Objective Food craving is a central feature of binge-eating disorder (BED) and may be a proximal mechanism linking environmental food cues to binge eating. Although laboratory studies show that food cues elicit craving and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies show that craving predicts binge eating, no study has tested whether craving is the momentary mechanism linking naturalistic food-cue exposure to binge eating. We tested this prospective within-person mediational model in daily life among individuals with BED. Method Adults with BED (N = 43) completed a 10-day EMA protocol. Multilevel structural equation modelling tested the within-person pathway from momentary food-cue exposure to craving to subsequent binge eating, controlling for prior craving and prior binge eating. Results At the within-person level, food-cue exposure predicted increased craving, which in turn predicted a greater likelihood of subsequent binge eating, supporting a significant mediation effect. Conclusions These findings provide the first EMA-based evidence that food-cue exposure increases binge-eating risk in BED through momentary increases in craving. Results highlight cue-induced craving as a potential key mechanism underlying binge eating and suggest that interventions targeting craving regulation and cue reactivity may improve treatment outcomes.

items.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
items.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.

items.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

items.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
items.abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

items.title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
items.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.

items.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

items.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
items.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

items.title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
items.abstract: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.

items.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
items.abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

items.title: ARCHER: From Rationale Imitation to Executable Reasoning in Small Language Models
items.abstract: Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce \textbf{ARCHER}: \textbf{A}ction-trace \textbf{R}einforcement for \textbf{C}alculator-grounded \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{R}easoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five standard sub-10B backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average across benchmark accuracies, including gains of 8.95 points on MATH-500 and 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. Evaluations on two additional reasoning-specialized 7B backbones further show that executable grounding remains beneficial after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation. These results demonstrate that executable supervision and reward-guided behavioral refinement provide a general and effective training paradigm for compact mathematical reasoners.

items.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

items.title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
items.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}γ\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

items.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
items.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

items.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
items.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

items.title: Typing Matters: Muscle, Language and Typing Behaviour in Live Keystroke Decoding from sEMG
items.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) from the wrists can recover typed text without a keyboard. It is usually posed as a signal-inference problem: characters are read out of the muscle signal and character error rate is reported offline. We argue that this framing removes most of the problem. The decoder is constrained simultaneously by the muscles, by the language being typed, and by typing behaviour such as typos, corrections, backspaces and line breaks, and a usable system must predict keys live while the hand keeps moving. Existing systems fall short on two counts: (1) they process sEMG in fixed windows and carry nothing from one window to the next, discarding context accumulated over a session, and (2) they lack any understanding of the linguistic structure that drives typing, so every keystroke is inferred from the muscle signal alone. We propose a fully causal, zero-lookahead sEMG typing decoder built on a state space model (SSM), in which a single model decodes a whole session without windowed partitions, conditioned on what has already been typed. We achieve this by fusing a traditional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model, instilling both sEMG and linguistic understanding in one model. To train such a model for per-character typing rather than whole-word text, we introduce a retokenization method that rewrites ordinary prose as human-like typing, with keystrokes, typos, backspaces and line breaks included, converting WikiText into a large typing corpus where none existed. Our model, having never seen a single sEMG-to-character transcript in typing, achieves a state-of-the-art character error rate of 25.13% on emg2qwerty's cross-user benchmark, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters, while running strictly causally with no future context.

items.title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
items.abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

items.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
items.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

items.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
items.abstract: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

items.title: Toward On-Device Markerless 6DoF Tracking of a Physical Manipulative on a Mixed-Reality Headset: A Preliminary Study
items.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.

items.title: Towards Explainable Sleep Stage Classification using Single-Channel Electroencephalogram
items.abstract: Automated sleep staging has achieved strong bench- mark accuracy; however, clinical adoption remains limited due to a lack of interpretability. In this work, we fill the research gap by extending the SleepXAI sleep staging framework to systematically compare five different XAI methods. Further, attribution fidelity is evaluated using Spearman rank correlation with AASM-defined EEG frequency bands, serving as clinically grounded reference signals. In this paper, we focus on single- channel Electroencephalogram (EEG), which is more amenable to practical clinical deployment compared to full polysomnography setups. Experiments are conducted on the Sleep-EDF benchmark dataset and the DREAMT dataset. In DREAMT, we stratified subjects based on OSA into four Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) severity groups. We observed that the SleepXAI model achieves strong classification performance on both datasets. Among the evaluated methods, Integrated Gradients (IG) consistently achieves the highest mean attribution fidelity across all five sleep stages on Sleep-EDF and across all AHI groups on DREAMT, outperforming all other evaluated methods under the Spearman rank correlation metric. These findings highlight the importance of attribution method selection as a key factor for ensuring reliable and clinically interpretable automated sleep staging systems.

items.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
items.abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.

items.title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
items.abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.

items.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
items.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

items.title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators
items.abstract: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.

items.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
items.abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care
items.abstract: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering evidence-based interventions, and how to manage personal-data use and sharing across AI and care stakeholders. We designed and evaluated ARC, a voice-based conversational agent that operationalizes multidomain lifestyle intervention through sessions with predefined goals, participant context, and evidence-based components. In a 3-day remote study, 80 older adults completed 473 sessions across six session types (9,183 turns; averaging 19.4 turns and 6 minutes per session). Participants reported favorable usability, acceptability, and use intentions. System-level analyses showed strong domain-level but modest participant-specific contextual reuse, no significant personalization-fidelity association, and fidelity limitations centered on incomplete delivery of intervention components rather than off-protocol drift. Within care relationships, expectations for personal-data use and sharing varied by data type and recipient. Our findings support feasibility of conversational delivery of multidomain lifestyle intervention, offer methods and system-design insights for longitudinal evaluation, and motivate an evaluation agenda for generative AI health interventions: user-experience and outcome measures should be complemented by evidence of whether intended intervention processes were delivered as designed.

items.title: AI-Based Multi-View Echocardiographic Image Synthesis using Dynamic Shape Control
items.abstract: Although automated methods have improved echocardiographic workflows, progress remains constrained by the need for large, well-annotated datasets. As the development of clinical databases is often limited by ethical and logistical challenges, synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising alternative. However, existing approaches commonly rely on left ventricle shape-based supervision or are tailored to specific cardiac views, limiting the generation of additional standard and unconventional imaging planes and the preservation of multi-view consistency across cardiac chambers. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework for shape-controlled synthesis of multi-view echocardiographic sequences. First, multi-view cross-sections are extracted from dynamic whole-heart meshes. Ultrasound-like appearance is then introduced through a two-stage AI-based pipeline. In Stage 1, an unpaired GAN-diffusion model translates these cross-sections into realistic echocardiographic frames. As this translation is performed independently at the frame level, Stage 2 employs masked video reconstruction to improve temporal coherence and cardiac motion. Evaluation demonstrated high frame-level realism for both stages, while the integration of Stage 2 substantially improved video-level motion quality and temporal consistency. Overall, the proposed framework enables the generation of realistic multi-view echocardiographic sequences from diverse cardiac models, providing a scalable source of annotated data for dataset augmentation and the development of multi-view cardiac assessment methods.

items.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
items.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

items.title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
items.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

items.title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
items.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.

items.title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders
items.abstract: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the DL classifier. To mitigate adversarial attacks, we introduce a defensive variational autoencoder (DVAE) that maps potentially perturbed inputs back to their clean versions. End-to-end fine-tuning of the downstream beam classifier on the DVAE-reconstructed RSSI representations further boosts prediction accuracy. Simulation results show that causal beam selection achieves accuracy comparable to conventional methods while providing an \(\mathbf{829\times}\) lower per-sample computational cost than SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), a widely used explainable AI (XAI)-based feature selection method. It further reduces beam-sweeping overhead by \(\mathbf{59.4\%}\) and \(\mathbf{89.8\%}\), compared to conventional DL-based beam selection and exhaustive search, respectively. The DVAE-based defense effectively denoises adversarial inputs, sustaining 85\% accuracy across different perturbation bounds, retains baseline performance on unperturbed RSSI inputs and surpasses defensive distillation defense scheme by 15--20\% on average under different attack scenarios.

items.title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization
items.abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent complements the model: it reads the target database's schema and column statistics and adds validated single-row derived columns, without access to labels or model scores. On 21 RelBench tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, the MoREGT backbone improves on the Relational Transformer pretrained on the same databases by 2.25 points of mean AUROC and 5.83 points of mean nMAE. The agent's columns raise mean AUROC from 78.45 to 79.63 and lower mean nMAE from 27.91 to 26.98, the highest means on both metrics among the compared methods, including RT-J, which pretrains on about 400 times as many databases.

items.title: AI for Parameter Selection in Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization
items.abstract: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods provide a way to compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend sensitively on configuration choices such as the subspace dimension, propagation timestep, and the allocation of a fixed sampling budget across circuits, for which no formal selection method exists. In this work, we explore whether oracle models can predict the quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and the candidate configuration. Using synthetic Hamiltonians with controllable spectral properties, we show that machine-learned models can map a Hamiltonian directly to the best-ranked configuration within a predefined grid for the SKQD algorithm, validated against classical Krylov propagation, achieving strong rank correlations between true and predicted error and runtime, Spearman $ρ= 0.969$ and $ρ= 0.905$, respectively. Extending the approach to 50 molecular Hamiltonians (20-50 qubits), with reference ground-state energies from classical calculations, we train regressors that predict the simulation error and runtime for a given molecule--configuration pair ahead of execution, and classifiers to distinguish, from 600 SqDRIFT quantum-hardware runs, whether a configuration achieves a ground-state energy within chemical accuracy ($1.6\times10^{-3}$ Ha $\approx 1$ kcal/mol). For the molecular Hamiltonians, the models additionally provide an a priori feasibility and resource estimate, predicting whether a molecule can reach chemical accuracy on current hardware and at what runtime, thus correctly classifying held-out molecules at the molecule level, achieving balanced accuracy 61.8% in-distribution and 100% for five larger held-out molecules.

items.title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
items.abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

items.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
items.abstract: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.

items.title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
items.abstract: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. items.title: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering
items.abstract: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning. Yet, standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, displacing representations from the distribution the model was trained on and eroding generation quality. We show that \emph{when} along a generation the intervention is applied is a decisive axis of control. We cast steering as a per-token allocation problem under a fixed budget of steerable tokens, so that methods differ only in which tokens they select, making allocation the sole variable. Within this framework we introduce two gates. The first, Contrastive Feature Projection (CFP), is memoryless and selects the tokens least aligned with the target behavior through a sparse, interpretable feature projection. The second, Closed-Loop Adaptive Bernoulli Steering (CLABS), is trajectory aware. It treats allocation as closed-loop feedback control, tracking the alignment a generation has accumulated so far and spending budget where the trajectory falls behind. On a linear steering-response model we derive an explicit gain region that guarantees closed-loop stability of CLABS and show that its integral term reduces the steady-state tracking offset. Empirically, CFP and CLABS achieve the largest behavioral shift among budgeted gates at matched budgets, with CLABS strongest under the tight budgets where allocation matters most, while best preserving fluency.

items.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
items.abstract: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. We validate this acquisition on 33 open-source decoder-only models across nine architecture classes, demonstrating that the recovered bytes are byte-exact and usable for downstream analysis. As a use case, we apply linear probes trained on standard framework activations to the recovered states, successfully distinguishing refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88 on held-out prompts. This work establishes that live, observational access to intermediate hidden states is feasible on named inference platforms, providing a new source of evidence for examining the operational behavior of deployed AI systems.

items.title: ParetoM$^3$: Learning on the Pareto Set under Preference Guidance via Min-Max-Min Optimization
items.abstract: Learning across multiple inherently conflicting objectives requires selecting desirable trade-offs from the Pareto set. In this work, we study preference-guided multi-objective optimization, where a predefined preference function is minimized over the weak Pareto set of multiple nonconvex objectives. Leveraging a merit function that vanishes on the weak Pareto set, we propose a penalty-based min-max-min formulation, termed the M$^3$ problem, which unifies preference optimization and the enforcement of weak Pareto optimality in a single objective. We further develop ParetoM$^3$, a single-loop first-order algorithm for computing stationary solutions of the resulting M$^3$ problem. Under a local Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz assumption, we prove that ParetoM$^3$ finds an $ε$-stationary point of the M$^3$ problem that is also approximately weakly Pareto optimal for the original multi-objective problem when the penalty parameter is sufficiently large, with explicit non-asymptotic convergence rates. We also show that this stationarity notion recovers existing optimality criteria, including approximate preference stationarity and approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, under the same assumptions used in prior works. Experiments on a synthetic benchmark, image classification, regression, and math reasoning demonstrate that ParetoM$^3$ reliably attains preferred weak Pareto optimal solutions while achieving strong practical performance. Code is available at https://github.com/tpgoodboy/ParetoM3.
