items.title: Dancing Tokens on the Vocabulary Network from LLM Generation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, yet how a particular generation relates to the geometry learned in pre-training remains unclear. The fundamental explainability of LLMs is elusive. Here, we build a similarity network from the input embeddings of six open LLMs and map generation onto it. The token-embedding network is scale-free while heavy-tailed, as are random embeddings with matched covariance, but far more fragmented. Distillation barely changes this topology because input embeddings are largely inherited. The knowledge space is thus deterministic from pre-training. Consecutive generated tokens are rarely graph neighbours and, in most models, no more often than in shuffled order, so generation is not a walk on the predefined network, although the tokens it visits are concentrated within it. Through the logit lens in a layer- wise manner, tokens settle late in depth in most models, and repetitive models remain confined to small domain-specific sub-graphs. These observables could serve as inference-time monitors of degeneration. We thus provide a fresh perspective on understanding LLM generation in the microscopic way from node or link prediction by graph learning.

items.title: Probabilities of Causation in Nondeterministic Causal Models
items.abstract: We study probabilities of causation in nondeterministic causal models, where mechanisms may remain intrinsically stochastic even after all latent variables are fixed. Focusing on binary treatments and outcomes, we develop a generic identification program that represents observational and interventional data as moment constraints on latent stochastic mechanism types and computes minimal/maximal values of counterfactual quantities via constrained optimization. Within this framework, we derive sharp analytic bounds on the probabilities of causation under several assumptions tailored to nondeterministic models. Resulting identification regions are often more informative than those attainable under deterministic alternatives. We illustrate the practical relevance of these results in a case study on personalized treatment decisions and experiments on semi-synthetic datasets. Our results clarify how classical bounds relate to nondeterministic causal semantics, generalizing previous works and providing a unified route from qualitative structural restrictions to computable partial identification regions.

items.title: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation
items.abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

items.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
items.abstract: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

items.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
items.abstract: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.

items.title: T2ST: Data-Efficient Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models via Temporal Data and Knowledge Transfer
items.abstract: Spatio-temporal foundation models (STFMs) require large-scale training corpora, yet synchronized observations and spatial metadata are costly to acquire and curate, limiting the availability of suitable data. By contrast, time-series data are abundant and easier to collect. Since observations at each location form a time series, this motivates a natural question: can abundant time-series data enhance STFMs when spatio-temporal observations are scarce? To bridge this gap, we propose T2ST, a data-efficient training framework that augments limited spatio-temporal observations with selected auxiliary time series and transfers knowledge from a frozen time-series foundation model. Our key insight is that temporal pattern learning can benefit from abundant external time series, while spatial dependency learning remains grounded in real spatio-temporal observations. Guided by this insight, T2ST retrieves matched sequences to reinforce sparsely observed temporal patterns and selects reliable complementary sequences to broaden temporal coverage. Temporal relation distillation aligns relationships among historical patches, while multi-scale prediction distillation transfers forecasting behavior at fine and coarse temporal resolutions, enabling knowledge transfer across heterogeneous architectures. Using only 10\% of the original spatio-temporal data, T2ST enables STFMs to achieve overall forecasting performance competitive with or superior to their full-data counterparts across six long-term and twelve short-term forecasting datasets. These results establish a new paradigm for data-efficient training of spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/T2ST-65F3/.

items.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

items.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
items.abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

items.title: An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model
items.abstract: TRIBE v2 (d'Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE's video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2's predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.

items.title: Exact stochastic theory of post-transcriptional gene autoregulation mediated by RNA-binding proteins
items.abstract: While analytical theories of transcriptional feedback loops have been well established, exact stochastic analyses of post-transcriptional feedback loops remain relatively scarce and are notoriously challenging. Here, we develop an exact theory of post-transcriptional gene autoregulation, in which reversible protein-mRNA binding modulates both translation and mRNA stability. We derive the state-dependent protein burst-size distribution, the steady-state protein number distribution in terms of confluent Heun functions, and an exact criterion for sub-Poissonian fluctuations. By comparing transcriptional and post-transcriptional networks, we reveal a reversal in their relative advantages in noise suppression and rhythm transmission: negative feedback favors post-transcriptional regulation, whereas positive feedback favors transcriptional regulation. Our results reveal how the regulatory pattern fundamentally shapes gene expression fluctuations and dynamic responses.

items.title: Striatal Optogenetic Modulation Shifts Seizure Onset Timing: A Survival-Analysis Reanalysis with Effect Sizes, Permutation Validation, and Sensitivity Analysis
items.abstract: We present a worked methods vignette, not a novel biological claim: a reanalysis of the public dataset accompanying Hyder and colleagues' report that optogenetic activation and inhibition of the dorsal striatum bidirectionally control seizures, applying a time-to-event framework to the pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus (SE) arm, the only arm with genuine per-animal event-level data rather than aggregate statistics. The original study compared latencies with a Mann-Whitney U test (ChR2 vs GFP: p = 0.0125; ArchT vs GFP: p = 0.0025). We first directly replicate that test on the same data (p = 0.0151 and p = 0.0025), confirming we analyze the same numbers, then designate the log-rank test as this reanalysis's pre-specified primary comparison, with a Cox model, a label-permutation test, a bootstrap confidence interval, and a leave-one-out analysis serving as validation checks rather than co-equal findings. ChR2 activation delays SE onset relative to its paired GFP control (hazard ratio 0.338, 95% CI 0.128-0.895; log-rank p = 0.023), and ArchT inhibition accelerates it (hazard ratio 9.18, 95% CI 1.91-44.09; log-rank p = 0.0011); a Schoenfeld-residual check found no significant proportional-hazards violation, though this check has limited power at n = 8-11 per group. Both results are confirmed by a 2,000-shuffle permutation test and survive leave-one-out, though the ChR2 comparison loses significance in 2 of 20 leave-one-out iterations, a fragility we report rather than omit. We do not claim this demonstrates anything the field did not already believe; its value is methodological, a reusable survival-analysis template with a Cox-derived effect size and documented sensitivity, extending naturally to future datasets with genuine censoring, which this one does not have.

items.title: Vision-Language Models Reproduce a Human Mental-Extrapolation Bias in the Watanabe Illusion
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for visual judgments, yet whether they share human perceptual biases, and where in the model such biases arise, is unclear. We addressed this with the Watanabe Illusion, a stimulus not previously studied quantitatively: an oblique segment inside a circle whose extension geometrically hits the topmost of 11 dots, yet human observers (n = 131) reported a dot near the middle of the column. Five VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 7B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash), given the identical stimulus and wording, all deviated in the same direction. In the open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-32B, linear probes on the vision encoder recovered the line angle and the target dot six to eight times more accurately than its behavioral responses. A layer-wise logit lens showed that the correct answer dominates in the middle layers of the language model and is overwritten in late layers only under a visual-judgment frame. Naming the illusion, requesting suppression of prior knowledge, forcing a visual chain of thought, and 390 semantic preambles left the response center unchanged; only disclosing the correct answer moved it. VLMs may therefore carry human perceptual biases at the language-generation stage, where they resist declarative correction.

items.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
items.abstract: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

items.title: TOI-1699A: a sub-Neptune and a super-Jovian in an S-type planetary system
items.abstract: We present the detection and characterization of the TOI-1699A (TYC 3415-00428-1) S-type planetary system, hosted by the G5 V primary of a wide binary with an M3 V stellar companion at a projected separation of $\sim$348 au. The inner planet, TOI-1699A b, was initially detected by TESS and confirmed with targeted CHEOPS photometry, ground-based photometry, and HARPS-N follow-up. With an orbital period of $\sim$4.55 d, radius of $3.096^{+0.057}_{-0.056}$ $R_\oplus$, mass of $13.9^{+1.9}_{-1.8}$ $M_\oplus$, and bulk density of $2.58^{+0.40}_{-0.39}$ g cm$^{-3}$, TOI-1699A b lies firmly in the sub-Neptune regime and requires a substantial volatile envelope. The HARPS-N data additionally reveal a massive outer companion, TOI-1699A c, with an orbital period of $108.75 \pm 0.10$ days, a low but significant eccentricity of $0.0737 \pm 0.0034$, and a minimum mass of $5.54 \pm 0.21$ $M_\mathrm{Jup}$. Assuming coplanarity with the inner planet, TOI-1699A c is not expected to transit, and our dynamical stability analysis disfavors a stellar-mass nature and limits its true mass to $M_\mathrm{c} \lesssim 18$ $M_\mathrm{Jup}$. Our combined data-driven and dynamical detection-limit analysis excludes additional planets between 54 and 235 days, and planets more massive than 27 $M_\oplus$ at shorter periods. TOI-1699A joins the still limited sample of S-type multiplanet systems, while upcoming Gaia DR4 astrometry together with radial velocity monitoring can constrain the true mass and inclination of the outer planet.

items.title: Eleven Trans-Neptunian Objects and Eight Candidates Discovered by TESS
items.abstract: We report a blind search for trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) in Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) full-frame images from 2018 July 25 through 2026 November 6. We search 572 CCD fields near the ecliptic across 95 TESS sectors. After modeling and subtracting Gaia stars with the TESS-Gaia Light Curve package, we stack the residuals along curved trial paths and link detections across sectors. We identify eleven new TNOs, each detected blindly in two to five TESS sectors and independently in archival ground-based images, with arcs of 2-20 years. They have V = 20.8-22.1, heliocentric distances of 25-57 au, inclinations of 16-27 deg, and diameters of about 120-910 km for an assumed albedo of 0.08. They lie 9-26 deg from the ecliptic, and the largest is 5 deg from the Galactic plane. Eight additional objects linked across two or three TESS sectors lack secure independent recovery in the archives examined and remain candidates. The search recovers 314 known TNOs and Centaurs, with an empirical recovery fraction of 50% at V = 21.6 before quality cuts. Nine were discovered after TESS imaged them, including 2026 ED138 6.8 years before its discovery by Rubin. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of TESS for finding bright outer Solar System objects and extending their observational arcs.

items.title: The effect of vertical mixing on oxygen sequestration by refractory elements in the atmosphere of giant planets
items.abstract: The most widely used route to study the formation history of giant exoplanets is the C/O ratio, usually derived from H$_2$O, CO, CO$_2$ and CH$_4$. However, refractory elements can sequester a significant fraction of O, causing the observed C/O ratio to be overestimated with respect to the intrinsic one. Previous calculations of this bias relied on chemical equilibrium models. Here we quantify the impact of vertical mixing using the 1-D chemical kinetics code VULCAN, expanded with a Mg-Si-Fe network including the condensation and settling of enstatite, forsterite and metallic iron. We compute 168 models spanning equilibrium temperatures $T_{eq} \in$ [700, 1500] K, eddy diffusion coefficients $K_{zz} \in$ [$10^6$, $10^{10}$] cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$ and metallicities $Z \in$ [0.9, 7.2] $Z_\odot$, derived self-consistently from planet formation simulations. We find that vertical transport causes magnesium silicates to destabilize already at $T_{eq} \sim 900$ K regardless of metallicity, releasing oxygen to H$_2$O and to minor gas-phase carriers such as SiO and Mg(OH)$_2$. Therefore, while equilibrium models predict a nearly constant C/O overestimation up to 1100-1300 K, in disequilibrium it drops sharply between 900 and 1200 K. In this transitional range the C/O overestimation is controlled by $K_{zz}$ and is partially degenerate with metallicity, while outside it is robust against both mixing intensity and the probed atmospheric layer, ranging from 14.5-23\% at 700 K to 4.5-7\% at 1500 K. Metallic iron condensation prevents Fe from sequestering oxygen, lowering the overestimation by about one third with respect to previous estimates. Finally, CH$_4$, CO$_2$ and the CH$_4$/CO ratio are most sensitive to $K_{zz}$ in the transitional range, and can provide a constraint on vertical mixing.

items.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
items.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

items.title: The directions of science: How we search the unknown
items.abstract: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. This Perspective distinguishes the visible diversity of scientific activity from its effective diversity: apparently different researchers, institutions, or projects need not provide genuinely different routes of exploration or evaluation. Our principal contribution is to introduce cross-stage dependence, which occurs when selection processes operating at different stages of science are not fully independent in the grounds through which they favour scientific trajectories. We hypothesize that, under uncertainty, repeated filtering through overlapping criteria, information, prior selections, or technological infrastructure can reduce the capacity of science to maintain plausible alternatives and redirect effort when evidence changes their relative promise. Artificial intelligence makes this problem increasingly consequential because it can simultaneously expand scientific search capacity and participate across multiple stages of production and selection. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce more knowledge, but to preserve sufficiently distinct routes of exploration, verification and correction while retaining the ability to change direction.

items.title: A Multiscale Analysis of an Interplanetary Shock from IMAP, SOLAR-1, and the L1 Constellation to Earth
items.abstract: Collisionless shocks are primary sites of particle acceleration throughout the Universe. Transient, mesoscale structures forming around these shocks influence their energy conversion efficiency, yet remain poorly observed at interplanetary (IP) shocks: spacecraft sample the shock transition briefly, and single-point measurements cannot disentangle temporal evolution from spatial structure. Here, we examine a fast, CME-driven IP shock of 2026 January 19, observed by IMAP, SOLAR-1, Wind, ACE, DSCOVR, and Aditya-L1 at L1 and by ARTEMIS and MMS near Earth, to determine its spatial and temporal structure. At MHD scales, a pre-existing solar wind flux tube is overtaken by the shock as it crosses the L1 fleet. This inflates the apparent magnetic compression ratio far beyond the ideal strong-shock limit of 4, showing that upstream and downstream intervals can sample different plasma and bias single-spacecraft estimates. At kinetic scales, IMAP and SOLAR-1, separated by only $\sim$7 $R_E$ ($\sim$340 ion inertial lengths), sample the same foreshock yet record localized structures that differ measurably; these are the first candidate signatures of large-scale foreshock transients at an IP shock. Further upstream, shocklets appear hundreds of $R_E$ ahead of the shock, consistent with steepening of ambient solar wind waves. Near Earth, the shock-to-flux-tube arrival lag increases to approximately six minutes, corresponding to a nominal sheath extension of $\sim$50 $R_E$, indicating sheath expansion over $\sim$200 $R_E$ of propagation. Together, these results show that the IP shock, its foreshock, and its sheath evolve across multiple scales from L1 to Earth, underscoring the need for multipoint measurements to resolve the underlying processes.

items.title: JCMT--Venus: Daily Monitoring of HDO and SO$_2$ Absorption in Venus' Mesosphere
items.abstract: We present three multi-week, disc-integrated James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) campaigns monitoring HDO and SO$_2$ absorption in Venus' upper mesosphere at altitudes of approximately 80--110 km. Obtained in February 2022, July 2023, and August--September 2023, these observations provide dense temporal sampling and complementary observing geometries, enabling the disentanglement of short-term, long-term, and local solar time (LST) variability, which has been challenging in previous studies. We have four main findings. First, SO$_2$ in the upper mesosphere, being largely absent in February 2022 but present in both 2023 campaigns, may follow the same long-term trend observed at cloud tops. Second, long-term variability in H$_2$O is identified here for the first time and is interpreted as an anticorrelated response to the long-term change in SO$_2$, likely through H$_2$SO$_4$ formation. Third, H$_2$O is broadly stable within each campaign, although occasional short-term variability is present in the form of a depletion event. Finally, short-term variability is likely present for SO$_2$, but it does not dominate the overall behaviour. In the absence of strong long-term differences, the daily SO$_2$ abundance evolution is consistent with an asymmetric LST profile peaking near midnight, which is well reproduced by an independent model. These results are enabled by a dedicated reduction and retrieval pipeline that mitigates the strong standing-wave baseline structure in the spectra and quantifies systematic uncertainties, providing a methodological framework for future studies facing similar challenges.

items.title: JWST/NIRISS-SOSS Spectroscopic Variability and Auroral Modelling of Warm Ultracool Dwarf LSR J1835+3259
items.abstract: Auroral variability in ultracool dwarfs (UCDs) has been proposed as a key source of optical and infrared modulation, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. We present JWST Near Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph/Single Object Slitless Spectroscopy (NIRISS/SOSS) time-series spectroscopy of the M8.5 UCD LSR J1835+3259. These observations probe the object's wavelength-dependent rotational variability, providing insight into the atmospheric processes underlying its infrared behaviour. Additional GTC/MEGARA optical spectra reveal that its H$α$ emission has declined markedly since earlier epochs, suggesting a reduced activity state during the JWST observations. We detect no emission from H$_3^+$ or absorption by hydronium in the NIRISS spectra. We use principal component analysis to identify two distinct modes of spectral variability: one dominated by FeH modulation near 1 $μ$m and another contributing broadband variability across the H and K bands. We find that no model atmosphere grid provides a reasonable fit to the average NIRISS spectrum. However, a blended model comprising an M-dwarf photosphere and a cooler blackbody component provides an improved fit to the mean spectrum, the broadband spectral energy distribution and the NIRISS broadband variability. By adding perturbations to PICASO model grids, we demonstrate that a combination of atmospheric heating and non-equilibrium chemistry can successfully mimic a blend of unperturbed photosphere and a blackbody, and that the presence of these effects may explain the unusual spectrum and variability of LSR J1835+3259.

items.title: Model Choice or Model Bias? How stellar spectral libraries and activity modelling choices influence Ariel spectra- I. Forward model
items.abstract: The Ariel mission will conduct a population-level survey of approximately 1000 exoplanet atmospheres across its nominal lifetime, requiring unprecedented consistency in the treatment of stellar contamination of transmission spectra. We present a systematic comparison of stellar spectral libraries and modelling approaches for computing facular and spot contamination spectra across the full Ariel wavelength range (0.5-7.8 microns) for six stellar spectral types spanning F3 to M2. Using a surface resolved forward model with approximately 200 randomly generated active region configurations per spectral type, we compute contamination spectra at Ariel Tier 3 resolution and compare three 1D spectral libraries against 3D MHD stellar atmosphere spectra as a physical ground truth. We find that library-dependent differences in the facular treatment introduce systematic biases exceeding the Ariel Tier 3 sensitivity threshold of approximately 20 ppm across most of the wavelength range, for most spectral types and activity levels considered. These biases align with the absorption bands of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane, rendering them indistinguishable from genuine atmospheric signals at Ariel's precision. Our results demonstrate hat the choice of stellar spectral library, in particular the faculae treatment is a critical and currently underappreciated source of systematic error for Ariel atmospheric characterisation. The impact on atmospheric retrievals is quantified in a companion paper.

items.title: Separability defects in artificial satellite theory: intermediaries, zonal harmonics and secular separatrices
items.abstract: A five-input Poisson-bracket operator, which reproduces the Levi-Civita separability expressions and is cubic in the Hamiltonian, is used as a diagnostic of artificial satellite theory, in a modified polar-nodal chart regular at prograde equatorial orbits. For the general intermediary proposed by the author in 2020, covering those of Sterne, Garfinkel, Brouwer, Aksnes, Cid and Lahulla and Deprit, the linearised defects vanish if and only if the integrability ansatz holds, the condition for additive first-order Hamilton-Jacobi separation in polar-nodal variables. Second-order defects follow in closed form, and the coupling with the nodal pair comes from the dependence on the physical latitude, shared by the zonal term, Aksnes's intermediary and the originals of Sterne and Garfinkel. For every axisymmetric field the radial defect is linear, with a torque form, and the first-order zonal defect is the operator response to the first-order Lie generator, which also gives the second-order mean radial defect per revolution. In its gauge the long-period second-order average is common to intermediaries without latitude terms. Oblate structures with a displaced centre separate the zonal field exactly if and only if its coefficients satisfy the recurrence of Vinti's translated spheroidal potential, and along orbits propagated over 300 periods in the field truncated at $J_4$ they conserve the approximate third integral better than the centred structure, by median factors of 23 to 77. On secular separatrices the integrated defect is the derivative of the Melnikov function, tested in the eccentric Kozai-Lidov problem, and transverse zero sets of the operator define event surfaces.

items.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
items.abstract: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

items.title: Symbolic Regression Fitting for Roche Lobe Radius
items.abstract: We present a compact approximation to the dimensionless, volume-equivalent Roche lobe radius $R_{\rm L}/a$, obtained by applying symbolic regression to radii calculated from the full Roche potential. Over $10^{-5}\leq q\leq10^5$, the expression reduces the root mean square error from $1.97\times10^{-3}$ for Eggleton's formula to $5.95\times10^{-4}$, while its maximum relative error is $1.39\%$, compared with Eggleton's $0.83\%$. Calculations at additional mass ratios give a mean relative error of $0.331\%$. The formula is monotonic, recovers the $q^{\frac{1}{3}}$ scaling at small mass ratio, and approaches a large-mass-ratio limit within $0.036\%$ of the limiting Roche model. In a NumPy float64 benchmark of $10^7$ direct formula evaluations, the SR expression takes $0.217$~s compared with $0.450$~s for Eggleton, a speed-up of $2.08$. These results quantify the accuracy and evaluation cost of a compact algebraic alternative for binary-system calculations.

items.title: Spatial scaling of heterogeneity transfer from boron concentration to absorbed dose in boron neutron capture therapy
items.abstract: We investigate how the amplitude and spatial correlation length of boron-concentration fluctuations affect the boron-induced absorbed-dose distribution in boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT). The spatial energy-deposition response of alpha particles and lithium nuclei is obtained using Geant4 and convolved with three-dimensional correlated lognormal boron fields under a uniform neutron field. Approximately $90\%$ of the reaction-product energy is deposited within a radius of $6.00~μ\mathrm{m}$, with a characteristic deposition length of $\ell_B\approx2.05~μ\mathrm{m}$. Dose heterogeneity increases with both the fluctuation amplitude $H$ and correlation length $ξ$, while the transfer factor $S=CV_D/H$ exhibits an approximate scaling collapse as a function of $ξ/\ell_B$. Analytical Gaussian and lognormal--Gaussian models provide reference predictions for this behavior. At short correlation lengths, the Geant4 response yields a higher transfer factor than a Gaussian response with the same characteristic length, highlighting the influence of the energy-deposition shape on dose smoothing. For $D_{95}$, defined as the dose received by at least $95\%$ of the modeled volume, the relative difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous boron-dose models reaches $(86.62\pm1.07)\%$ at $H=1.2$ and a target ratio $ξ/\ell_B=6$. We show that mean boron concentration alone is insufficient to characterize spatial nonuniformity of the boron-dose component.

items.title: On the Existence of a Third Planet and an Apsidal Resonance Chain in the Kepler-396 System through TESS Data
items.abstract: The possible existence of a third planet in the Kepler-396 system has been previously proposed. Given that the planetary mass is poorly constrained and the orbit could be either interior or exterior to planet Kepler-396 c, that proposal is not clearly known in the community. In order to address this and further investigate Kepler-396 system's configuration, new TESS data are employed to form a long baseline of transit timing. Using the pixel-level decorrelation technique, the mid-transit times are determined. Through long baseline transit-timing-variation technique, we perform a comprehensive exploration of the parameter space of the third planet. Two best-fit solutions, derived from different priors of orbital inclinations, have led to the reduced chi-square values as 2.24 and 2.34 respectively, compared to 12.97 for the two-planet model. This result strongly suggests the existence of the third planet, i.e. Kepler-396 d. Based on these two best-fit solutions, the masses of Kepler-396 b, c, d are updated to be around 9, 4, 4 Earth Mass, and the corresponding orbital periods are 43, 89, 144 days, respectively. With these updated masses, Kepler-396 b is on the border between rocky or volatile-rich, Kepler-396 c is confirmed to be a volatile-rich super-puff planet, and both planets lie in the Neptune savanna. Dynamical simulations with three planets are performed, showing that they are stable for a timescale of $10^6$ years. The examination on resonant angles leads to the conclusion that planets Kepler-396 b, c, d form a three-body apsidal resonance chain.

items.title: DART ejecta reveal the recoil momentum budget of a kinetic impact
items.abstract: Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated that ejecta recoil enhances asteroid deflection, but the ejecta processes generating and distributing this recoil remained unclear. We reconstruct three-dimensional ejecta evolution from time-resolved morphology and brightness observations, recovering previously missing constraints on momentum transfer and material transport. Integrating reconstructed momentum yields momentum enhancement factors $β_\mathrm{D}=2.13 \pm 0.19 (1σ)$ for Dimorphos and $β_\mathrm{sys}=2.04 \pm 0.19 (1σ)$ for the Didymos system. Combined with the measured deflection, the reconstructed recoil constrains Dimorphos's bulk density to $1435.18_{-153.71}^{+112.59} \mathrm{kg m^{-3}}$ without assuming its mass. By linking observed orbital deflection to the released material, this reconstruction provides ejecta-based constraints for assessing kinetic-impact effectiveness and investigating how natural collisions drive mass loss and debris transport among small Solar System bodies.

items.title: Protocol for isolation of murine neural stem cells from the adult subventricular zone and reprogramming into induced pluripotent stem cells.
items.abstract: Reprogramming of neural stem cells (NSCs) into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offers a promising strategy for studying neurological disorders and developing cell-based therapies. Here, we present a protocol for the isolation and expansion of adult subventricular zone (SVZ)-derived NSCs and their reprogramming using a two-factor Oct4/Klf4 strategy. We describe steps for tissue dissection, NSC culture, viral transduction, colony selection, and pluripotency validation. This streamlined approach enables efficient generation of stable iPSC lines while improving safety and reproducibility. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Lázaro-Carot et al. 1 .

items.title: Protocol for generating parasympathetic neurons from hiPSCs and their coculture with hiPSC-atrial cardiomyocytes.
items.abstract: Peripheral parasympathetic ganglia lie adjacent to their target organs and are difficult to access for primary culture; their dysfunction contributes to diseases like atrial fibrillation. Here, we present a protocol to differentiate human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into parasympathetic neurons and assess their function by electrophysiological recordings, nicotinic receptor activity, and expression of cholinergic and autonomic markers. We also describe how to establish a coculture system with hiPSC-atrial cardiomyocytes that allows neuromodulation of cardiomyocyte activity.

items.title: Explaining Human Psychology Evolutionarily
items.abstract: Abstract Evolutionary psychology aims to fulfil Darwin’s vision—articulated towards the end of The Origin of Species— of providing a new foundation for the scientific study of human psychology. The field holds that human behavior should be explained using the same biological principles and empirical approaches applied to non-human animals, emphasizing how different evolutionary forces have influenced the functioning of their psychological mechanisms. Scholarly debate has long centered on issues such as adaptationism, testability, cognitive modularity, and the role of culture. More recently, however, evolutionary psychology has faced a new wave of critiques. These include that it presupposes, but cannot support, that human psychological mechanisms are “vertically homologous” with those of their ancestors; that it neglects several important evolutionary processes; that it relies on an outdated computationalist view of the mind; and that it does not yet satisfy the criteria for a mature, normal science. This article aims to present a balanced account of these emerging critiques, along with a set of original responses that, to date, have not been fully articulated in the literature. In general, we argue that the critiques involve unsound argumentation with false premises, attack a straw man position, are vulnerable to reductios , or rely on an implausible philosophical model of how scientific works ought to be evaluated.

items.title: Probable post-traumatic stress disorder after miscarriage: psychological, social, and healthcare-related factors in a mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Miscarriage is commonly managed as a short-term obstetric condition, yet its psychological consequences may extend beyond physical recovery. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after miscarriage and to examine psychological, social, and healthcare-related factors shaping PTSD symptom severity and recovery experiences. Methods: A theory-informed sequential mixed-methods study was conducted at the Post Abortion Care clinic of a tertiary Grade-A women’s and children’s hospital in Sichuan Province, China. In the quantitative phase, 293 women who had experienced miscarriage before 20 completed weeks of gestation completed a digital survey assessing PTSD symptoms, psychological resilience, perceived social support, rumination, coping style, distress disclosure, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic growth. Probable PTSD was defined as a Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist–Civilian Version score of 38 or higher. Between-group comparisons, Spearman correlations, and hierarchical multivariable linear regression models were used. In the qualitative phase, nine women participated in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings. Results: The mean PCL-C score was 33.5 ± 12.1, and 95 women (32.4%) screened positive for probable PTSD. Women with probable PTSD had lower psychological resilience than those without probable PTSD (55.4 ± 12.7 vs. 66.4 ± 16.4) and lower perceived social support (59.3 ± 14.0 vs. 66.3 ± 13.8). Higher resilience and perceived social support were associated with lower PTSD symptom severity, while intrusive rumination showed the strongest positive association. Hierarchical regression showed that sociodemographic and reproductive variables alone explained little variance in PTSD symptom severity (adjusted R² = 0.007), whereas adding healthcare-related, psychosocial, and psychological process variables increased explanatory power (adjusted R² = 0.161 and 0.538). Qualitative interviews identified four themes: self-regulation after miscarriage, partner and family support, social safety and stigma, and healthcare communication and care-process burden. These findings contextualized the quantitative associations and highlighted modifiable family, social, and health-service factors. Conclusions: Probable PTSD was common after miscarriage and was shaped by more than individual psychological vulnerability. Post-miscarriage care should move beyond procedure-centered management toward trauma-informed, partner- and family-sensitive, and patient-centered support that includes psychological screening, clear communication, stigma reduction, and attention to care-process burden.

items.title: Efektivitas Pengelolaan Sumber Daya Alam dalam Memenuhi Kebutuhan Ekonomi Masyarakat
items.abstract: Natural resource management is often assumed to improve community welfare, yet empirical evidence shows mixed outcomes. This article synthesizes research on natural resource management in forestry, fisheries, mangroves, and related sectors, internationally and in Indonesia, to assess how far such management meets the economic needs of communities. Using a library research approach, it synthesizes 29 scholarly journal articles through thematic grouping and interprets the findings with economic concepts such as property rights, scarcity, opportunity cost, externalities, and benefit distribution. The findings show that natural resources contribute roughly 22–38% of rural and coastal household income, and that various management schemes are reported to raise income or food security by 18–45%. However, Indonesian studies indicate that abundant resources do not automatically generate stable income, owing to land tenure problems, weak coordination and regulatory enforcement, pollution, and technological constraints. Management effectiveness should be assessed across four dimensions: economic, ecological, equity, and institutional. Policies should recognize community management rights, strengthen regulatory implementation, and provide alternative livelihoods when resource use is restricted

items.title: From intracellular force maps to organelle and organism physiology.
items.abstract: The mechanical properties of the cell interior are heterogeneous, varying across components and compartments according to function, location and time. However, many current mechanical models of the cell do not fully reflect this, either treating the cell as a simplified isotropic mechanical continuum or focusing on complex mechanics of isolated cellular structures, leaving the integration of mechanical features at cellular-to-tissue levels unresolved. To link mechanics with biological function, complete, spatially and temporally resolved maps of subcellular to mesoscopic mechanical properties in living systems and organisms are needed. Despite major technical advances in mechanobiology over the past decade, only snapshots of these heterogenous material properties have been obtained. Crucially, the integration of quantitative force measurements with microscopy approaches remains a challenge in connecting cell mechanics with biological structure and function. This limitation underlines the urgent need for novel imaging methods to visualize how different organelles, cells and organisms respond to forces and how their mechanical properties are coupled to function and physiology. In this Review, we outline recent developments in this rapidly advancing field and discuss what lays ahead in order to bring spatially and temporally resolved imaging of subcellular mechanics into a quantitative and broadly accessible framework for cell biology.

items.title: The Cylinder Test: Development and clinical validation of a tool for assessing hand opening.
items.abstract: Background Impaired hand opening following neurological injury can limit functional grasp and object handling. Existing upper limb assessments do not specifically evaluate functional hand opening or distinguish between active and passive components. Purpose To describe the development of the Cylinder Test (CyT) and evaluate its preliminary face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance among clinicians and individuals with neurological upper limb impairment. Study design Clinical measurement, cross-sectional study. Methods The CyT was developed through iterative clinical refinement and literature review. The final CyT version comprises 14 plastic cylinders (20-150 mm diameter) and four subtests assessing active and passive functional hand opening. Face validity was evaluated in 33 individuals with neurological upper limb impairments due to cervical spinal cord injuries (cSCI) or spasticity and 31 clinicians experienced in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. Clinicians reviewed the CyT manual and completed a study-specific questionnaire assessing clarity, perceived clinical usefulness, relevance of the subtests, and scoring criteria. Participants performed the CyT and subsequently rated its relevance and perceived effort. Data were summarized descriptively. Results All clinicians (31/31, 100%) reported that the manual provided sufficient guidance for independent administration, and all considered the CyT potentially useful in clinical practice. The purpose of the CyT was rated as clear or very clear by 26/31 clinicians (84%), and no clinician rated any subtest or scoring criterion as inappropriate. All participants (33/33, 100%) rated the overall CyT as relevant or very relevant, and ratings of the individual subtests were predominantly relevant or very relevant. Six of 15 participants with spasticity rated the test as demanding compared with 2/18 participants with cSCI. Conclusions Preliminary evaluation supports the face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance of the CyT for assessing functional hand opening in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. The CyT may provide hand therapists with a clinically feasible approach to assessing active and passive hand opening. Further evaluation of reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness is required.

items.title: Molecular detection of Borrelia puertoricensis and a Coxiella endosymbiont in Ornithodoros puertoricensis from northern Veracruz, Mexico.
items.abstract: Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a neglected zoonosis caused by Borrelia spp. and transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros. Although Mexico has a long history of human TBRF, the current distribution of relapsing fever borreliae and their associated vectors remains poorly understood, particularly in the Mexican Gulf Coast region. This study investigated the presence of tick-borne bacteria in ticks collected at a​ veterinary clinic in northern Veracruz, Mexico. A total of 164 Ornithodoros puertoricensis ticks were identified using morphological characteristics and 16 S mitochondrial ribosomal RNA sequencing. DNA extracts were screened by conventional PCR for Borrelia, Rickettsia, Bartonella, Coxiella, and Ehrlichia/Anaplasma, followed by DNA sequencing and phylogenetic analyses of positive samples. Borrelia puertoricensis DNA was detected in six ticks (3.66%), in four nymphs and two females. Phylogenetic analyses of the flaB gene confirmed that all sequences clustered within the B. puertoricensis clade with strong bootstrap support. In addition, a Coxiella endosymbiont was detected and assigned to clade B based on 16 S rRNA phylogenetic reconstruction, representing the first molecular evidence of this lineage in O. puertoricensis. None of the DNA samples were positive for Rickettsia, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, or Anaplasma. These findings provide the first molecular evidence of B. puertoricensis and a Coxiella clade B endosymbiont in O. puertoricensis from Veracruz, extending the known distribution of both microorganisms in Mexico. The detection of these bacteria in ticks collected at a veterinary clinic capable of treating wild animals highlights the importance of integrated acarological and molecular surveillance at wildlife-domestic animal-human interfaces to improve understanding of the ecology and public health significance of neglected tick-borne zoonoses.

items.title: The wild avian resistome: metagenomic insights into antimicrobial resistance ecology.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in wild birds is increasingly studied as an ecological component of the wider One Health resistome, yet the evidentiary meaning of a resistance gene detected in avian material varies markedly with study design. This review synthesizes culture-based, whole-genome and metagenomic evidence with emphasis on what modern sequencing can and cannot establish about acquisition, persistence, mobility and transmission. Wild birds encounter antimicrobial-resistant bacteria and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through wastewater, landfills, livestock-associated environments, surface waters, sediments and food webs; resident synanthropic species can be as informative as long-distance migrants. Shotgun and genome-resolved metagenomics have expanded the known avian resistome, enabled host assignment and revealed links with mobile genetic elements and viromes, but DNA detection alone does not demonstrate viable carriage or directional dissemination. We therefore organize the evidence through an evidence-to-inference framework of five complementary domains: ARG detection, microbial-host assignment, genomic mobility, viable carriage and persistence, and transmission, the last separated into sharing between compartments and direction of movement. Applying the framework to published sequencing studies shows that most reach only detection or host assignment, rely on relative abundance, rarely report negative controls and come predominantly from China. The framework clarifies why wild birds are often best regarded as ecological sentinels unless persistence, viable hosts and directionality are shown. Combining metagenomics with long-read sequencing, targeted culture, isolate genomics, environmental sampling and movement ecology offers the strongest route toward biologically meaningful One Health surveillance.

items.title: From subjects to experts: Methodological reflections on interviewing preschool-aged children about sensitive topics.
items.abstract: Preschool-aged children remain underrepresented in research on illness, death, and bereavement, reflecting ethical concern and the fit between conventional interview methods and children's developmental and communicative capacities. This article draws on three Danish studies. These were a home-based sand tray interview with parentally bereaved children, a laboratory timeline task on understanding death, and a practice-based evaluation of a family bereavement network. Across the three studies, participants were aged three to eight at data collection. We use preschool-aged children throughout to refer to this broad group, recognizing that the term is defined more narrowly in some national systems, and we note where age-related differences within the group mattered for participation. Together the three studies show how children can be included in sensitive research. Participation depended less on simpler questions than on designing encounters that gave children ways to engage, supported distance from difficult material, and visible opportunities to continue, pause, or stop. Setting, interviewer judgment, and infrastructure shaped the ethics of participation and the knowledge produced. Recognizing children's expertise means broadening what counts as data, including play, gesture, objects, silence, and advice. The task is not to make children speak like adults, but to build methods that recognize what they communicate.

items.title: Measurement properties of instruments assessing self-stigma and help-seeking stigma in youth: a systematic review protocol.
items.abstract: Objective This systematic review will evaluate the measurement properties and methodological rigor of self-report instruments assessing internalized self-stigma and self-stigma of seeking help among youth and emerging adults (aged 12-25 years). The review will map global evidence to identify geographical gaps in psychometric equity, focusing on instruments validated for Arabic-speaking youth as a critical test of cross-cultural validity and measurement invariance. Introduction The transition between ages 12 and 25 years represents a critical period for mental health. Internalized self-stigma is a significant proximal barrier to professional help-seeking; however, existing tools often lack sufficient evidence of cross-cultural validity. Without psychometric equity, particularly in collectivist, Arabic-speaking contexts, current instruments may contain measurement bias. Eligibility criteria We will include original peer-reviewed primary research and academic dissertations reporting the development, translation, cross-cultural adaptation, or validation of self-report instruments measuring internalized self-stigma or the self-stigma of help-seeking in youth (aged 12 to 25 years) across any cultural context, with a secondary focus on Arabic-speaking populations (including regional dialects). Studies published in English, Arabic, or French published from January 1, 1996, to the date of the final search, will be eligible. Methods This review will follow the COSMIN framework. We will search PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Citation Index, and the Index Medicus for the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Two independent reviewers will screen studies for eligibility, assess methodological quality using the COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist v.3.0, and extract data using a standardized tool. Findings will be synthesized following COSMIN guidance, and certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the modified GRADE approach tailored for measurement properties. Review registration PROSPERO CRD420261290064.

items.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
items.abstract: Purpose The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females. Methods Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness. Results Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p Conclusions The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

items.title: Supporting Males with Suicidal Ideation: Evaluation of an E-Learning for Healthcare Providers.
items.abstract: Suicide remains an important public health issue. Males are at increased risk for suicide, yet display reduced help-seeking, increased drop-out and less lasting engagement. Despite calls for more gender-responsive care, practical training for healthcare providers (HCPs) remains scarce. To address this gap, a training module (e-learning) was developed to support HCPs in offering gender-responsive suicide prevention care to males. This study aimed to evaluate changes in HCPs' self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies, and their satisfaction with the training. This pre-post trial has been registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06810713). A single-group pre-post design was used. HCPs completed questionnaires before and after completing the 30-60 minute e-learning module. The surveys assessed self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies in supporting males experiencing suicidal ideation. In addition, participants evaluated the e-learning using Likert-scale items. A total of 109 HCPs participated, of whom 75 completed the posttest. Results showed statistically significant improvements in both self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies with moderate to large effect sizes of d = 0.55 and d = 1.98. Participants evaluated the module positively (M = 8.0/10), with good evaluations of its content and format. The psychoeducational model on gender socialization and suicidality, as well as the downloadable summary sheets, were well received. The e-learning module significantly improved HCPs' confidence and gender-responsive competencies in working with males experiencing suicidal ideation. Given its self-paced, freely accessible online format, the training appears feasible and acceptable. Further research is needed to examine its long-term impact, behavioral outcomes in clinical practice, and applicability to more diverse male populations.

items.title: Contribution of risk factors to racial/ethnic disparities in tuberculosis among US-born persons.
items.abstract: In the United States, tuberculosis (TB) incidence rates are substantially higher among racial/ethnic minorities compared with non-Hispanic White persons. However, few analyses have investigated the mechanisms driving these disparities. To assess the contribution of geographic factors and individual TB risk factors to racial/ethnic disparities in TB incidence among U.S.-born individuals. We analyzed TB case data for 2012-2019 from the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System, stratified by race/ethnicity, age, sex, and Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA). Age-sex standardized incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were calculated to quantify disparities across racial/ethnic groups. We decomposed these IRRs to quantify the contribution of differences within and between PUMAs to overall disparities. We also estimated the contributions of racial/ethnic differences in the prevalence of established TB risk factors-diagnosed diabetes, current smoking, HIV infection, and excess alcohol use-to TB disparities. Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native and non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander persons had the highest TB incidence rates compared to non-Hispanic White persons (IRR: 15.3 (95% CI: 12.5, 18.6) and 18.1 (12.3, 26.2) respectively). Within-PUMA TB incidence differences accounted for most of the differences in incidence by race/ethnicity, representing 52-96% of total IRRs for each racial/ethnic population. Racial/ethnic differences in the prevalence of individual risk factors had minimal impact on total TB incidence disparities. Eliminating racial/ethnic disparities in TB will require more than addressing individual risk factors. Combatting structural or community-level determinants of TB, including treating infection to prevent disease, will be important for accelerating TB elimination.

items.title: Multiparametric ultrasound characterizes pediatric cystic fibrosis hepatobiliary involvement.
items.abstract: The contemporary European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN)/North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (NASPGHAN) framework broadens the definition of cystic fibrosis hepatobiliary involvement (CFHBI), but the biological interpretation of individual multiparametric ultrasound parameters within this framework remains unclear. We evaluated the biological associations of shear wave elastography (SWE), shear wave dispersion (SWD), and attenuation imaging (ATI) with histopathological phenotypes in children with cystic fibrosis (CF). In this ambispective cohort study, 119 children with CF underwent hepatobiliary assessment, including SWE, SWD, ATI, Doppler ultrasonography, clinical and laboratory evaluation. Histopathological assessment was performed when clinically indicated. CFHBI was classified according to the ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN framework, with the Debray criteria used as a secondary exploratory comparison. Exploratory phenotype-oriented analyses evaluated ultrasound parameters according to corresponding histopathological phenotypes. Exploratory phenotype-oriented analyses demonstrated significantly higher ATI values in histopathologically defined steatosis (p < 0.001), with good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.813) and an optimal threshold of 0.655 dB/cm/MHz. In contrast, SWE was not associated with histopathologically defined fibrosis (p = 0.151), whereas SWD showed no significant phenotype-specific associations. Secondary exploratory analyses demonstrated significant overall CFHBI discrimination by all three ultrasound parameters, with the highest AUC observed for SWD. The ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN and Debray classifications demonstrated significant disagreement (McNemar p < 0.001), with 22.7% of patients classified as Debray-negative but ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN-positive. Multiparametric ultrasound should be interpreted within the contemporary ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN CFHBI framework rather than as a single diagnostic tool for hepatobiliary involvement. The distinct biological associations of SWE, ATI, and SWD support a phenotype-oriented interpretation of individual ultrasound parameters, whereas overall CFHBI discrimination should be interpreted as a secondary exploratory finding requiring prospective multicenter validation.

items.title: Creatine and CoQ10 with physical activity on muscle function in children with myositis: a proof-of-concept trial.
items.abstract: We aimed to evaluate whether Creatine (Cr) and Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) supplementation, combined with a self-paced physical activity program, enhances muscle function in juvenile idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (JIIM). Fifteen participants, (8 male/ 7 female) aged 9-17, from SickKids' JIIM clinic were recruited for a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized, multiple-baseline trial. All participants participated in both the placebo and intervention periods. The primary outcome, muscle function, was measured by the Wingate Test. Secondary outcomes included improvements in jumping height, disease activity, and quality of life. There was a significant increase in peak power (mean difference (MD)=95 Watts; p = 0.02), mean power (MD = 74 Watts; p = 0.02), and minimum power (MD = 47 Watts; p = 0.01) in the intervention periods compared to placebo periods. Vertical jump peak power also increased significantly in the intervention period (MD = 493 Watts; p = 0.02). However, these significant findings were not replicated in the prespecified sensitivity analyses, which incorporated linear mixed models to adjust for individual baseline values. Cr+CoQ10 supplementation combined with physical activity showed positive effects; however, these findings may be attributable to chance imbalances in baseline values. Alternatively, the lack of statistical significance in the sensitivity analyses may reflect a Type II error, as the study size was set for the more powerful primary analysis. Further research is necessary to fully understand the impact of Cr and CoQ10 supplementation in children with JIIM. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04286178.

items.title: Maternal mean arterial pressure and serum inhibin A as early predictors of hypertensive disorders in low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria: A prospective cohort study.
items.abstract: This study evaluates the role of maternal mean arterial pressure (MAP) and serum inhibin-A level as early predictors of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) among low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria. This was a prospective cohort study of 254 consecutively consenting, low-risk, normotensive, and non-proteinuric pregnant women at 13-19 weeks of gestation. Receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curves and validity tests were used to determine the performance of serum levels of inhibin A, MAP, and a combination of both in predicting HDP (gestational hypertension and preeclampsia). The mean age and parity of the participants was 30.3 ± 4.9 years and 1 (0-2), respectively. The area under the ROC curves of serum inhibin A (0.9981, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.9946-1.000) was higher than for MAP (0.7531, 95% CI 0.6641-0.8421), in predicting the composite endpoint of HDP. The optimum cut-offs for predicting HDP as calculated from Youden's index were 476.8 pg/mL (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 98.7%) for serum inhibin A and 81.3 mm Hg (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 50.1%) for MAP. There was no statistically significant difference between the combined predictive ability of inhibin A and MAP compared to that of serum inhibin A alone for predicting HDP (AUC of 0.9984 vs. 09981, P-value = 0.7259. This study demonstrated that serum inhibin A alone and MAP have good and moderate performance, respectively, in predicting HDP in the low-risk cohort of Nigerian pregnant women. The combination of serum inhibin A and MAP has a similar predictive performance as serum inhibin A alone.

items.title: Inside the battery box: a cross-technology assessment of PFAS uses, functions, and substitution potential.
items.abstract: Understanding where and why per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are used in batteries is essential for evaluating their substitution potential, yet detailed information across battery technologies is scarce. We analyzed more than 5600 submissions to the Annex XV public consultation on the proposed universal PFAS restriction in the European Union and extracted information reporting use, associated substance(s), and stated function(s) of PFASs in batteries. 341 records were compiled into a database using our structured Battery Use & Function Framework that incorporates the Functional Substitution Framework. Among these records, 78 contained sufficient information to qualify as a potential PFAS use and were organized into 36 potential PFAS uses, accounting for overlaps. Each potential PFAS use was evaluated using supporting evidence from previous use-mapping studies, input from battery stakeholders, teardown-analysis studies, and other targeted academic literature. Across all lines of evidence, two PFAS uses in batteries were contradicted, indicating already large-scale availability of PFAS-free alternatives, while 16 PFAS uses were confirmed, primarily in cathode components across several battery technologies and chemistries. PFAS-free alternatives were identified for 13 PFAS uses across battery applications, with an additional five uses showing PFAS-free options for certain applications within the broader use category. The findings indicate that few technical barriers remain for substituting PFASs in most battery components. Our mapping provides a detailed foundation for future alternatives assessments, supports essential-use evaluations, and highlights opportunities and challenges relevant to monitoring and recycling.

items.title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge.
items.abstract: Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM). Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings. Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM. BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.
